title: Queen's Gambit Declined
description: The "QGD" is a solid repertoire against 3/4 major White openings: d4, c4, and Nf3. This repertoire is based on 3...a6, the Janowski Variation.

r1b1k1nr/1pp1qppp/p1n1p3/8/P1pP4/2N1PN2/.text:
When White opens an attack on c4 with 8.e3...

Our queen, already on e7, can quickly jump to b4, defending the c4-pawn while pressuring b2.

r1b1k1nr/1pp2ppp/p1n1p3/8/PqpP4/2N1PN2/1.text:
9.Qc2 defends b2 and places the queen on a very common square in the QGD, where it usually works with Bd3 to form a battery. 

But with our pawn on c4, White can’t play Bd3 yet. 

We continue simple development with ...Nf6. 

There’s no need for ...Na5 immediately; we can improve our kingside first and prepare to castle.

r1b1k2r/1pp2ppp/p1n1pn2/8/PqpP4/2N1PN2/1.text:
White develops their kingside bishop and gets ready to castle. 

Now we play ...Na5, aiming at the b3-square and clearing the path for our c-pawn.

r1b1kb1r/1p3ppp/p3pn2/q1p5/P2P4/2N1P3/1P.text:
The bishop comes to d2, lining up with our queen. 

But if we take on d4, White has no useful discovered attacks, so we simply capture in the center.

r1b1kb1r/1p3ppp/p3pn2/q7/P2P4/2N5/1P1B1P.text:
White recaptures, leaving themselves with an isolated queen’s pawn, a structural weakness in endgames. 

Now we develop our bishop to b4. 

This both shields our queen from any discoveries and ensures we’ll trade pieces if the knight moves. 

When playing against an IQP, trades generally favor the side attacking it.

r1b1kbnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/4N3/P1pqP3/1nN5/1P.text:
Black can win a pawn. 

Our ideas against 5. a4 are powerful, and can result in completely winning positions like this one if White isn't careful.

r1b2rk1/1p3ppp/p3pn2/q7/Pb1P4/2N5/1P1BBP.text:
We can castle. 

In the next moves, you can bring your rook to d8 to attack d4, play ...Bd7 and ...Bc6.

r1b2rk1/1pp2ppp/p3pn2/n7/PqpP4/2N1PN2/1P.text: We can castle kingside ourselves and play ...c5 next.

r1b2rk1/4bppp/p7/Rp1qP3/2pP4/4B3/1P1N1PP.text:
And once White captures on a5, we've got many strong ideas. 

...f6 to undermine e5, followed by ...Bb4. Or ...Bb4 right away is strong for Black. 

The bishop pair reigns supreme in this position.

r1bq1rk1/4bppp/p3p3/np1NP3/2pP4/4BB2/1P1.text:
For illustration - no need to memorize this part - if White takes on d5...

 We recapture with the e-pawn.

r1bq1rk1/4bppp/p3pn2/np2P3/2pP4/2N1BB2/1.text:
Don’t fear the discovered attack after 13.e5.
 
We can block with the knight on d5.

For White to keep pressing, they’d need to dive into some wild Rxa5 ideas. But if they try to break through the center, we’ll emerge with a superior pawn structure, active pieces, and the bishop pair.

r1bq1rk1/4bppp/p7/np1BP3/2pP4/4B3/1P1N1P.text:
And if White continues naturally by taking again on d5, restoring material balance... 

We centralize our queen with the recapture.

r1bqk1nr/1pp1Bppp/p1n1p3/8/P1pP4/2N2N2/1.text:
White accepts the trade. 

Our development speeds up after 7...Qxe7. 

Our queen gains freedom on the dark squares, and without White’s dark-squared bishop, it’s much harder for them to exploit any dark-square weaknesses.

r1bqk2r/1p2bppp/p1p1pn2/n7/P1pPP3/2N1B3/.text:
When Nd2 arrives...

We’re right on time: 10...b5 defends c4.

r1bqk2r/1pp1bppp/p3pn2/n7/P1pPP3/2N1BN2/.text:
As mentioned, 9.Be3 is the only real plan to recapture the pawn. 

White first defends the d4-pawn, then aims for Nd2 to attack c4. 

Since Nd2 is coming, we play 9...c6 with the idea of following up with ...b5 to secure our c4-pawn.

r1bqk2r/1pp2ppp/p3p3/n2PN3/PbpP4/2N1BP2/.text:
White may happily take our knight.

We simply recapture, and now c4 is completely consolidated. 

We’ve traded a knight for two powerful central pawns, that’s our first source of compensation.

r1bqk2r/1pp2ppp/p3pn2/n3N3/PbpPP3/2N1BP2.text:
White plays 9.f3, but this weakens the dark squares, making our future ...c5 much stronger. 

It also removes the natural retreat square for the e5-knight. 

Thanks to all this, the beautiful 9...Nd5 becomes possible.

r1bqk2r/1pp2ppp/p7/n2pN3/PbpP4/2N1BP2/1P.text:
White continues developing with 10.Be2, preparing to castle. 

Our second source of compensation is that the f3-square is blocked by a pawn, so 11...f6 hits the knight with greater force.

r1bqk2r/1pp3pp/p4p2/3p4/PbpP2N1/1nN1BP2/.text:
If White places the rook on the “safest” square, they’ll face a problem: the rook on a2 is completely passive. 

It can’t go to a1 (covered by our knight), nor to a3 (covered by our bishop), and the entire second rank is blocked by its own b2-pawn. 

We develop our light-squared bishop to e6 to support the whole pawn chain. 

We need that support because we won’t be playing ...c6, our idea is the thematic ...c5!

r1bqk2r/1pp3pp/p4p2/n2p4/PbpP2N1/2N1BP2/.text:
The knight must retreat to g4, where its only idea is to eye f2. 

It’s a miserable piece, and with our d5/c4 structure we can jump our knight into b3.

r1bqk2r/4bppp/p1p1pn2/nP6/2pPP3/2N1B3/1P.text:
White may choose to exchange their a-pawn, hoping to open the a-file for the rook. 

Always be careful in these situations, don’t blunder the knight on a5, which is currently defended by our queen. 

In this position we can simply recapture.

r1bqk2r/4bppp/p3pn2/np6/2pPP3/2N1BB2/1P1.text:
And if the bishop heads to f3 to attack our a8-rook...
 
We just castle.

r1bqkb1r/1p3ppp/p3pn2/N1p5/P2P4/2N1P3/1P.text:
White exchanges, the most popular choice.

This lets us recapture and develop our queen at the same time, pinning the knight.

r1bqkb1r/1p3ppp/p3pn2/n1P5/P1p5/2N1PN2/1.text:
Some players can’t handle the tension and release it by taking on c5. 

Here we play 9...Bd7 to avoid a queen trade. 

It’s actually White who feels cramped because of our c4-pawn, so we shouldn’t give them an easy way out.

r1bqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p3pn2/n3N3/P1pPP3/2N1B3.text:
If White goes 8.Ne5, adding another attacker to c4, we develop our bishop, pinning the knight on c3. 

The point is to build enough pressure on e4 that White feels forced to defend with f3.

r1bqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p3pn2/n7/P1NP4/2N1P3/1P.text:
White recaptures.

We follow with 8...c5 - one of the core points behind 6...Na5 - freeing the c-pawn.

r1bqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p3pn2/n7/P1pP4/2N1PN2/1.text:
White castles. 

Now we strike with our strong ...c5 pawn break, undermining White’s central control.

r1bqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p3pn2/n7/P1pPP3/2N2N2/1.text:
White castles. 

We also prepare to castle with 8...Be7.

r1bqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p1n1p3/6B1/P1pP4/2N2N2/.text:
6.Bg5 is the third most popular option. 

It attacks our queen, but we can calmly block and develop with 6...Be7, proposing an exchange and neutralizing the threat.

r1bqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p1n1p3/8/P1pP4/2N1PN2/1.text:
6.e3 is the second most popular move, and it also opens an attack on c4. 

We can continue with our usual idea: 6...Na5, defending the c4-pawn with the knight.

r1bqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p1n1p3/8/P1pPP3/2N2N2/1.text:
Now 6.e4 is the most popular attempt, opening a direct attack on our c4-pawn with the f1-bishop. 

Here we reveal the point of our setup: 6...Na5!, defending c4 and forcing White to work hard to recover the pawn.

r1bqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/n3N3/P1pP4/2N1P3/1.text:
If White adds another attacker with 7.Ne5... 

We simply ignore the threat to c4 and play 7...Nf6. 

It’s actually good for us that White had to twist their pieces around with Nf3–Ne5–Nxc4; that lost time won’t come back.

r1bqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/n3N3/P1pPP3/2N5/1P.text:
White’s most popular reply, 7.Ne5, appears to pressure c4 but actually fails tactically. 

It allows our knight to hop into b3, hitting both d4 and the rook.

r1bqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/n7/P1pP4/2N1PN2/1P.text:
Simple development with 7.Be2, aiming for quick castling, is also an option for White. 

We continue naturally with 7...Nf6.

r1bqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/n7/P1pPP3/2N1BN2/1.text:
7.Be3 defends the d4-pawn and prepares to maneuver toward the c4-pawn. 

Against this we have a neat idea starting with 7...Nf6, but it relies on White playing Ne5 and f3 in the next couple of moves.

r1bqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/n7/P1pPP3/2N2N2/1P.text:
Some players choose simple development with 7.Be2. 

You might see this even from opponents who aren’t sure of the plan. 

If they do know the idea, they’ll try to reroute the bishop to f3, but that requires preparing the knight move with Be3 first. 

In the meantime, we calmly develop with 7...Nf6.

r2qk2r/1p4pp/p3bp2/2pp4/PbpP2N1/1nN1BP2/.text:
And here comes 14...c5, to finally undermine White's last central pawn. 

It’s worth analyzing positions after natural moves like Kh1 or Re1; Black’s central control is superb, and in many lines White even has to give back material.

r2qkb1r/1p1b1ppp/p3pn2/n1P1N3/P1p5/2N1P3.text:
If the knight jumps to e5, attacking our bishop and the c4-pawn... 

We simply develop our queen to c7, preparing ...Bxc5 and clearing d8 for one of the rooks.

r3k2r/1pqb1ppp/p3pn2/2b5/P1B5/2N1P3/1P3P.text:
So after ...Bxc5, our queen indirectly sees the bishop on c4. 

We'll continue with moves like ...Bc6, 0-0 and Rfd8.

r3kb1r/1pqb1ppp/p3pn2/2P5/P1B5/2N1P3/1P3.text: White recaptures, and this trade conveniently places the bishop on c4 where it’s undefended.

r3kb1r/1pqb1ppp/p3pn2/n1P5/P1N5/2N1P3/1P.text:
When the knight eventually takes on c4, this shouldn’t concern us. 

White had to go Nf3–Ne5–Nxc4 to recover the pawn. 

We capture on c4, trading knights.

rnbqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/3p4/2PP4/2N2N2/PP2.text:
Most players are taught that the Queen's Gambit isn't a true gambit: Black cannot win and hold on to the c-pawn. 

But this isn't the case in the 3...a6 QGD! 

A simple, developing move like 4. Nf3, while a natural continuation that many players choose to go for, actually allows us to take on c4. 

Thanks to ...a6, we can capture on c4, posing difficult problems for White.

rnbqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/8/P1pP4/2N2N2/1P2P.text:
The first variation of this chapter arises after 5.a4, aiming to prevent ...b5. 

But I’ve prepared a way to complicate matters for White despite this move. 

We continue with 5...Nc6, intending to jump to a5, where the knight defends the c4-pawn and eyes b3.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
Many players now go for the Queen’s Gambit. 

This challenges our central control, but instead of taking on c4, we support our own center. 

We play 2...e6, defending the d5-pawn with another pawn in true QGD style.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/2PP4/2N5/PP2PPP.text:
White often develops the queenside knight to c3, increasing pressure on d5. 

Now comes our key move: 3...a6. 

This multipurpose move fights for b5 control, prevents a white piece from landing there, and prepares ...b5. 

Combined with 4...dxc4, 3...a6 can even become a real threat to hold on to the c-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to this course on the 3...a6 Queen’s Gambit Declined! 

In this first chapter we’ll explore what happens when White allows us to capture on c4 with 4...dxc4. 

As you’ll see, our move 3...a6 carries real venom, and if White isn’t precise, not even 5.a4 will help them recover the pawn. 

White begins with 1.d4, a solid move supported by the queen that prepares solid development. 

We respond symmetrically with 1...d5.

2r1k2r/1bq1bppp/p3pn2/2n5/PpB5/1P2PN2/1B.text:
You can always overprotect your knight on c5.

...0-0, ...Rfd8 are sound moves you could continue with, centralizing your pieces. 

When the rook comes to d8, ...Nd5 will also become a solid choice.

r1bqkbnr/2p2ppp/p1n1p3/8/PppPP3/5NN1/1P3.text:
Once the knight moves to g3 to reopen the bishop's diagonal... 

We can jump to a5 and secure the c4-pawn.

r1bqkbnr/2p2ppp/p3p3/n7/PppPP3/5NN1/1P2B.text:
If White develops the bishop to prepare castling, we continue with 9...Bd7. 

We’ll follow up with ...Nf6 and ...Be7, putting pressure on e4 while enjoying our active queenside knight and pawn structure.

r2q1rk1/1b3ppp/p1n1pn2/2b5/PpB5/1P2PN2/3.text:
Here we'll castle and after Bb2 we may even go for ...Na5 and ...Nxc4. 

We'll also centralize rooks on d8 and c8. I like Black's piece coordination here.

r2qk2r/1b2bppp/p3pn2/n7/Pp1N4/1P2P3/NB2B.text:
After 13...Be7 Black has the same advantages related to piece activity and coordination. 

We'll play ...0-0, ...Rc8, ...Qb6 to develop our pieces.

r2qk2r/1b3ppp/p1n1pn2/2b5/PpB5/1P2PN2/3N.text: And once again, with e3 on the board, you'll most likely see b3 for White to play Bb2.

r2qk2r/1b3ppp/p1n1pn2/2b5/PpB5/4PNN1/1P2.text:
White might try a move like this to prepare Rd1. 

But continuing with 12.Na5, attacking White's bishop, is always a good strategy.

r2qk2r/1b3ppp/p1n1pn2/P1b5/1pB5/4PN2/NP1.text:
Black recaptures with the bishop, defending b4.

The a5-pawn isn’t the strongest, but we must stay alert since the rook is on the a-file.

...0-0, ...Qe7 at some point also adds a defender on b4.

r2qk2r/2p1bppp/p1n1pn2/8/PpBPb3/4BN2/NP3.text:
We can develop with 11...Be7, looking to castle soon and place our bishop on d5 where it will have a safer home.

Black is a pawn up out of the opening, and White still has to solve the knight on a2 situation.

r2qkb1r/1b3ppp/p1n1pn2/2P5/PpB5/4PN2/1P1.text:
When that capture finally happens, we’re quite happy - White has given up their d4-pawn and loosened their central control. 

We simply recapture the c5-pawn.

r2qkb1r/1b3ppp/p1n1pn2/2P5/PpB5/4PNN1/1P.text:
And indeed, we may see that capture. 

I recommend taking back with the bishop, which reinforces the b4-pawn that controls key queenside squares and restricts White’s normal development. 

If White trades queens on d8, we recapture with the rook and enjoy the open file.

r2qkb1r/1b3ppp/p1n1pn2/2p5/PpBP4/1P2PN2/.text:
If White continues to ignore the tension... 

I like capturing on d4, giving them an IQP. 

They can recapture with the e-pawn and accept the isolated pawn, or recapture with a piece and surrender central control.

r2qkb1r/1b3ppp/p1n1pn2/8/PpBN4/1P2P3/NB3.text:
Capturing with the knight is the move you’ll see most often, avoiding the IQP and keeping the dark-squared bishop on the board. 

Here I really like 12...Na5, going after White's light-squared bishop.

r2qkb1r/1bp2ppp/p3pn2/n7/PppPP3/5NN1/1P2.text: But our moves are very natural, and our pieces are active on the squares that are available to them (in contrast to White's knight on g3 and the e2 bishop).

r2qkb1r/2p2ppp/p1n1pn2/8/PpBPb3/4BN2/NP3.text: If the bishop comes to e3 to defend the d4 pawn...

r2qkbnr/1b3ppp/p1n1p3/P1p5/1pBP4/4PN2/NP.text:
So at some point White will have to resort to Bxc4. 

We simply keep developing, maintaining control over the d5-square with 10.Nf6.

r2qkbnr/1bp2ppp/p3p3/n7/PppPP3/5NN1/1P2B.text: White may castle at this point.

r2qkbnr/2p2ppp/p1n1p3/3bP3/Pp1P4/2p2N2/N.text: 10...c3, attacking the bishop on d2 and with a discovered attack on the a2 knight!

r2qkbnr/2p2ppp/p1n1p3/3bP3/PppP4/5N2/NP1.text: The very natural Rc1, adding an attacker on c4, runs into a tactic:

r3k2r/1b3ppp/pq2pn2/n1b5/PpB5/4PNN1/1P2Q.text:
Our queen is safe on b6. 

We're on the light-squared bishop, which we'll take if we get the chance. 

...0-0 and centralizing our rooks on d8 and c8 are our next moves if we do not take on c4 first.

r3k2r/1bqn1ppp/p3pn2/2b5/PpB5/1P2PN2/NB3.text:
Noting that Rc1 may come, ...Nbd7 protects the c5-bishop. 

We won't be surprised on the c-file. 

We've got ...0-0 coming up and if Rc1 White will be cramped, without any way out for their a2-knight. 

We even have ...Rd8 coming to x-ray their queen, and in this case we have a more direct threat to White's own queen.

r3k2r/1bqnbppp/p3pn2/2P5/PpB5/1P2PN2/1B1.text:
White may develop the knight, preparing Rc1. 

Now is a good moment for us to recapture on c5 with the knight.

r3kb1r/1bqn1ppp/p3pn2/2P5/PpB5/1P2PN2/1B.text:
White develops their bishop to b2. 

Fortunately, after ...Nbd7, our knight on f6 gains support. 

This setup is very sound for Black after 12...Be7, delaying the capture on c5 so the knight on f6 remains protected.

rn1qk2r/1bp1bppp/p3p3/1p1nP3/2pP4/P1N2N2.text:
And we'll get castled soon enough. 

We're up a pawn with a better position!

rn1qk2r/1bp2ppp/3bpn2/p7/PpBP4/4PN2/NP1B.text:
And we're placing our bishop on d6, on a more active diagonal than if it were placed on e7.

We've got ...0-0 coming up, followed by ...Nbd7 and we'll prepare the e5-pawn break for middlegame counterplay.

rn1qkb1r/1b3ppp/p3pn2/2P5/PpB5/4PN2/1P3P.text:
If White chooses to take... 

We place our queen on c7. 

We’re not interested in trading pieces and helping White coordinate - coordination becomes easier with fewer pieces. 

We’d rather watch them untangle the b1-knight and the c1-bishop while we keep developing smoothly.

rn1qkb1r/1b3ppp/p3pn2/2P5/PpB5/4PN2/NP3P.text:
And if White takes on c5, once again, we’re not trading queens.

We develop our queen instead and watch White struggle to untangle their queenside pieces - the knight on a2 and the bishop on c1.

rn1qkb1r/1b3ppp/p3pn2/2p5/PpBP4/1P2PN2/N.text:
White may also choose to ignore the pawn with 10.b3. 

In that case, we continue exactly as before: ...Nc6, increasing the pressure on d4 and trying to provoke White into taking on c5.

rn1qkb1r/1b3ppp/p3pn2/2p5/PpBP4/4PN2/1P1.text:
White may also refuse to take on c5 with 10.Nbd2. 

In this case, I like adding pressure on d4 with 10...Nc6 to force them into releasing the tension.

rn1qkb1r/1b3ppp/p3pn2/2p5/PpBP4/4PNN1/1P.text:
Most players will castle here. 

In that case, as in other lines where White doesn’t take on c5, I like 
…Nc6 to increase pressure on d4. 

This move often provokes dxc5 because of the tension on the pawn.

rn1qkb1r/1bp2ppp/p3pn2/1p2P3/2pP4/P1N2N2.text:
If they try to fix that problem by pushing the e-pawn, they only weaken the light squares further.

It allows us to immediately take advantage with a knight jump to d5.

rn1qkb1r/1bp2ppp/p3pn2/8/PpBP4/4PN2/1P3P.text:
White castles.

We challenge the center with ...c5.

rn1qkb1r/1bp2ppp/p3pn2/8/PpBP4/4PN2/NP3P.text:
White castles. 

We immediately undermine the d4-pawn with 9...c5.

rn1qkb1r/1bp2ppp/p3pn2/8/PpBP4/4PNN1/1P3.text:
Once White recovers the c4-pawn...

We continue with …c5. 

This move undermines the center, and White cannot capture without losing castling rights. 

Even though we’re no longer a pawn up, we reach a completely healthy position.

rn1qkb1r/2p2ppp/p3pn2/8/PpBPb3/5N2/NP3PP.text:
10.Re1 is a very natural idea, pressuring the e-file and eyeing our bishop. 

I recommend developing the knight to c6 and soon bringing the bishop to d5.

rn1qkbnr/1b3ppp/p3p3/P1p5/1ppP4/4PN2/NP1.text:
And what if White tries Bd2 to avoid the queen trade and increase pressure on b4? 

They delay dxc5, so it looks logical.

Yet 9...Nc6 solves everything: it adds another defender to b4, and if dxc5 now, ...Bxc5 follows and the bishop defends b4 as well.

rn1qkbnr/1bp2ppp/4p3/p7/PpBP4/4PN2/NP1B1.text:
White has already lost time with Bd2. 

They could take on c4 now, but our development flows smoothly. 

We continue with kingside development with 9...Nf6 since we’re going to castle. 

We’re perfectly happy with the a5–b4 pawn chain, there’s not much to do on the queenside for the moment.

rn1qkbnr/1bp2ppp/p3p3/1p6/2pPP3/P1N2N2/1.text:
Many players now just continue developing, thinking their central pawns and the stable knight on c3 are enough compensation. 

But that isn’t true. 

With 7...Nf6, we already put pressure on the center.

rn1qkbnr/1bp2ppp/p3p3/4P3/PppP4/5N2/NP3P.text:
If White makes this pawn push, they give up control of the e4- and the d5-squares. 

We immediately make use of that by placing our bishop on d5 as an outpost. 

From d5, the bishop also defends the c4-pawn.

rn1qkbnr/1bp2ppp/p3p3/8/PpBP4/4PN2/1P3PP.text:
The bishop finally recaptures the pawn.

We continue with 8...Nf6, we’ve achieved very natural development while White still has a knight sitting on b1.

rn1qkbnr/1bp2ppp/p3p3/8/PpBP4/4PN2/NP3PP.text:
White recaptures on c4. 

Our moves here are very easy to remember: 8...Nf6, and ...c5. 

The knight on f6 helps control e4 and d5. 

And remember: if 9.Bd2, you can simply play 9...a5.

rn1qkbnr/1bp2ppp/p3p3/8/PpBPP3/5N2/NP3PP.text:
If White recaptures on c4... 

We simply take on e4.

rn1qkbnr/1bp2ppp/p3p3/8/PppP4/4PN2/NP1B1.text:
If you ever see 8.Bd2... 

Remember you have ...a5 to defend everything. 

This keeps the b-pawn protected and maintains annoying control over the queenside squares. 

White’s development becomes awkward.

rn1qkbnr/1bp2ppp/p3p3/8/PppP4/4PNN1/1P3P.text:
White, of course, must move the knight - this is the main continuation. 

I suggest we develop our knight to f6, taking control of key central squares like e4 and d5.

rn1qkbnr/1bp2ppp/p3p3/8/PppPP3/5N2/1P3PP.text:
We can play Bb7 with a tempo on e4, and now White has no convenient defense. 

If 8.Bxc4 Bxe4.

If 8.Nbd2 c3!

If 8.e5 Bd5

And we proceed with c7-c5 when necessary, as well as kingside development.

rn1qkbnr/1bp2ppp/p3p3/P7/1ppP4/4PN2/NP3P.text:
What if White plays 8.a5 themselves, preparing Bd2 to attack our b4-pawn?

Here I like the immediate 8...c5. 

This move creates practical problems: ...c5 helps defend b4, and if dxc5, we get a favorable queen trade. 

White becomes even more cramped on the queenside.

rn1qkbnr/2p2ppp/p3p3/3bP3/PppP4/5N2/NP1B.text:
White can’t take either pawn and plays 9.Bd2, targeting b4. 

We respond with 9...Nc6, which defends the b4-pawn.

rn1qkbnr/2p2ppp/p3p3/8/PpBPb3/5N2/NP3PPP.text:
Castling is the most common move afterwards.

White often tries to compensate for the pawn with activity - especially along the e-file with Re1.

But we develop harmoniously with 9...Nc6, controlling key light squares and defending our bishop, while maintaining excellent coordination. 

White still has lingering issues, especially the misplaced Na2.

rn2k2r/1bq2ppp/p3pn2/2b5/PpB5/1P2PN2/NB3.text: The awkward thing for White is that they'd like to play Rc1 but they also have to retrieve their knight with some Nc1 maneuver.

rn2kb1r/1bq2ppp/p3pn2/2P5/PpB5/1P2PN2/5P.text:
Once again, you’ll often see b3 from White to get their pieces out. 

There’s no need to play ...Qxc5; the queen is safer on c7 than on c5. 

We’re also not forced to recapture immediately, so we play 11...Nbd7.

rn2kb1r/1bq2ppp/p3pn2/2P5/PpB5/1P2PN2/N4.text:
White will likely have to adopt a b3–Bb2 setup to get developed, since they played e3. 

We can capture on c5 with the bishop, clearing the way for castling.

rnbqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/3p4/2PP4/2N2N2/PP2.text:
White develops with 4.Nf3. 

Their logic is that the Queen’s Gambit isn’t a true gambit, that they can always recover the c-pawn. 

But 4.Nf3 actually allows us to capture it immediately.

rnbqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/8/2pP4/2N1PN2/PP3P.text:
5.e3 is a more modest way of targeting the c4-pawn. 

It doesn’t try to claim both central squares with e4, but simply aims to stay solid and recover the pawn.

Against 5.e3, we can already pose problems by threatening to hold on to it with 5...b5.

rnbqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/8/2pPP3/2N2N2/PP3P.text:
After our capture, the reflex move 5.e4 is very common. 

White wants to claim the central e4-square we just vacated and hit c4 at the same time. 

Thanks to 3...a6, we can play 5...b5 to prevent Bxc4 - you’ll soon see that the a6/b5 structure not only defends the pawn but can also enable ...b4 to kick the knight and disrupt White’s coordination.

rnbqkbnr/2p2ppp/p3p3/1p6/2pPP3/P1N2N2/1P.text:
6.a3 is occasionally played with the idea of preventing ...b4. 

The problem is that it lets us keep our strong pawn chain led by the extra pawn. 

We can simply fianchetto our light-squared bishop on a beautiful diagonal. 

Our light-square control becomes extensive: the a6–c4 chain dominates the queenside, while the bishop on b7 targets the kingside.

rnbqkbnr/2p2ppp/p3p3/1p6/P1pP4/2N1PN2/1P.text:
But White can undermine our structure with 6.a4. 

We respond just as in the main line: the familiar …b4 push.

rnbqkbnr/2p2ppp/p3p3/1p6/P1pPP3/2N2N2/1P.text:
6.a4 is White’s most popular attempt to undermine the c4-pawn.

But 6...b4 hits the knight and asks a serious question: where should it go? 

The best engine move is 7.Ne2, but it’s not even the most common choice.

rnbqkbnr/2p2ppp/p3p3/8/PppP4/4PN2/1P3PPP.text:
Some players bring the knight back to b1. 

This is obviously not ideal for development. 

Our moves stay the same: We'll start with  7...Bb7, then ...Nf6, and ...c5. 

The bishop goes to b7 to control the long diagonal, and our grip on e4 and d5 becomes a major asset.

rnbqkbnr/2p2ppp/p3p3/8/PppP4/4PN2/NP3PPP.text:
7.Na2 places the knight on a bad square. 

The b4-pawn is defended by our bishop on f8, and after 7...Bb7 our bishop exerts long-range control over the light squares. 

Without a pawn on e4, that bishop becomes even more powerful.

rnbqkbnr/2p2ppp/p3p3/8/PppPN3/4PN2/1P3PP.text:
Since White hasn’t placed a pawn on e4, they actually gain an extra square for the knight. 

This is the most popular move. 

We answer with 7…Bb7, attacking the knight and strengthening our grip on the light squares.

rnbqkbnr/2p2ppp/p3p3/8/PppPP3/5N2/1P2NPP.text:
Finally, 7.Ne2 is liked by the engine but not very popular, and it creates coordination issues. 

The knight on e2 blocks the f1-bishop, and since that bishop is shut in, we can freely develop our knight to c6. 

This gives us extra time to play ...Na5 and defend c4.

rnbqkbnr/2p2ppp/p3p3/8/PppPP3/5N2/1P3PPP.text: 7. Nb1, a hard reset on the knight, is what many others have played.

rnbqkbnr/2p2ppp/p3p3/8/PppPP3/5N2/NP3PPP.text:
The main move is 7.Na2. 

White avoids the attack but places the knight on the rim, and it’s not even threatening b4, since our bishop on f8 defends it. 

We continue with ...Bb7, a perfect square for the bishop, where it cuts across the long diagonal and targets the e4-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White continues with the Queen’s Gambit, 2.c4. 

We decline it with 2...e6, supporting the d5-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/2PP4/2N5/PP2PPP.text:
White usually follows with 3.Nc3. 

As mentioned in the previous study, c3 is the ideal square for the queenside knight in the QGD because it reinforces pressure on d5. 

We respond with 3...a6, preparing ...b5, stopping White’s pieces from using b5, and supporting our light-square structure.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
This second study will show you how to handle the very natural 5.e4 and 5.e3. 

After Black plays ...dxc4, many Queen’s Gambit players instinctively push the e-pawn to attack c4 with a discovered threat from the bishop. 

But this actually gives us everything we want from the opening - and in some lines, we even keep the pawn! 

White begins with the queen’s pawn.

We mirror with our own, aiming for our traditional QGD setup.

1n2k1nr/2p2ppp/4p3/8/1qpP4/2N1PP2/1P3P1P.text:
White recaptures, ending up with doubled f-pawns. 

These pawns will be weak in endgames, and even in the middlegame Black can often generate play against the king. 

Now we take on b2, since c4 is weak and doubled regardless.

1n2k1nr/2p2ppp/4p3/8/Q1pP4/2N1PP2/1q3P1P.text: The game could continue with 14. Qa4+.

4k1nr/2pn1ppp/4p3/8/Q1pP4/2N1PP2/1q3P1P/.text:
We'll develop a piece and block the check. 

After this, we'll bring our other knight out and castle kingside.

Black has an active queen and a better pawn structure out of the opening.

bn2k1nr/2p1qppp/4p3/1N6/2pP4/4PN2/1P3PPP.text:
The knight takes on b5, grabbing material. 

We give a check with the queen, attacking both the knight and the b2-pawn.

bn2k1nr/2p2ppp/4p3/8/1qpP4/2N1PN2/1P3PPP.text:
White must block with the knight to save the piece. 

Now comes a nice detail: we take on f3 first, damaging their pawn structure.

r2qk2r/1bpn1ppp/p3pn2/1p6/P1pP1B2/2P1PN2.text:
We won't have any trouble dealing with the queenside counterplay. 

We'll castle kingside and enjoy being a pawn up.

rn1qkbnr/1bp2ppp/p3p3/8/PppP4/2N2NP1/1P2.text:
We can attack that knight, and it'll have to retreat to b1. White is worse out of the opening.

We'll continue with moves like ...Nf6 and ...c5, going for comfortable development that we have earned.

rn1qkbnr/2pb1ppp/p3p3/1N6/Q1pP4/5N2/PP2P.text: 6...Bd7 pins the knight and it's game over.

rn2k1nr/1b2qppp/p1p1p3/1p6/3P4/1QN2N2/PP.text:
At which point, you can just get your bishop on b7, and in the following moves, conclude your development adopting this setup: ...Nd7, ...Ngf6 and ...0-0. 

Black has sound development and a very robust queenside pawn diamond.

rn2k1nr/1bp1qppp/p3p3/1P6/2pP4/2N1PN2/1P.text:
And indeed, White may play exactly that. 

We recapture, and because our queen is on e7, the tactical idea ...Qb4+ becomes available if Nxb5.

rnb1k1nr/1p2qppp/p1p1p3/8/2QP4/2N2N2/PP2.text:
White recovers the pawn, but there’s a price to pay: we will gain a tempo on the queen and build a strong queenside pawn structure.

After 8...b5 we hit the queen and create a square for our bishop. 

Getting our light-squared bishop to b7 with tempo is a big win - normally in the QGD the light-squared bishop is a problem piece, sometimes needing a long route via d7–e8 and even ...f6 to activate it!

rnb1k1nr/1pp1qppp/p3p3/8/2pP4/2N1PN2/PP3.text:
Among beginners, 7.e3 is the most popular continuation, aiming at our c4-pawn. 

We respond with 7...b5, reinforcing the c4-pawn.

rnb1k1nr/1pp1qppp/p3p3/8/Q1pP4/2N2N2/PP2.text:
This check is a good move. 

We cannot play 7...b5 here because the knight can take on b5 (8.Nxb5), and if we try to pin with 8...Bd7, White has Nxc7+. 

That’s why we need a different idea: 7...c6, preparing ...b5.

rnb1k1nr/2p1qppp/p3p3/1p6/P1pP4/2N1PN2/1.text:
White’s most logical reply is to challenge our b-pawn and exploit the pin on the a-file. 

We solve this by developing our light-squared bishop to b7, removing the pin so that after axb5 axb5 our rook remains defended.

rnb1k1nr/4qppp/p1p1p3/1p6/3P4/1QN2N2/PP2.text:
b3 is a very natural square for the queen. 

I'm willing to bet most d4 players would go here.

rnbqk1nr/1pp1Bppp/p3p3/8/2pP4/2N2N2/PP2P.text:
If they accept the trade, which is the most common choice...

We recapture with the queen, activating it on the dark squares.

rnbqk1nr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/8/1bpP1B2/2N1PN2/P.text:
Many players follow up with e3 to attack c4. 

With the dark-squared bishop already outside the pawn chain on f4, they feel comfortable doing so.

But we have our signature ...b5, defending the pawn. 

Once again, White lacks an effective way to pressure c4, and we may simply remain a pawn up.

rnbqk1nr/2p2ppp/p3p3/1p6/1bpP1B2/2N1PN2/.text:
Some players just continue developing and prepare to castle. 

We do the same with 7...Nf6, aiming at the central squares e4 and d5, and getting ready to castle.

rnbqk2r/2p2ppp/p3pn2/1p6/1bpP1B2/2N1PN2/.text:
Once White castles... 

We can take the knight. 

After 9.bxc3, we will control the queenside more easily because White no longer has the b3 pawn break. 

With only a4 left, their queenside play is much easier to handle.

rnbqk2r/2p2ppp/p3pn2/1p6/2pP1B2/2P1PN2/P.text:
White recaptures. 

We develop our bishop to b7, onto the strong diagonal.

rnbqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/3p4/2PP4/2N2N2/PP2.text:
White develops normally with 4.Nf3, but this move allows us to enter our desired line with 4...dxc4.

We’re temporarily a pawn up, and as seen in the previous studies, recovering it is far from trivial for White.

rnbqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/6B1/2pP4/2N2N2/PP2.text:
5.Bg5, attacking our queen, is the most popular sideline. 

But we can calmly block the attack with 5...Be7, offering a bishop trade. 

With dark-squared bishops off, White will struggle to attack our dark squares.

rnbqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/8/2pP1B2/2N2N2/PP2.text:
5.Bf4, developing the bishop, is the second-most popular choice. 

The bishop eyes c7, but thanks to our earlier 3...a6, Nb5 is impossible. 

I suggest we pin the knight here with 5...Bb4. 

If we later trade it and the b-pawn recaptures, controlling the queenside becomes much easier since White will only have one pawn break left (a4).

rnbqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/8/2pP4/2N2NP1/PP2P.text:
White may try to play 5.g3 in a Catalan style, aiming for compensation and quick control of the h1–a8 diagonal. 

But this idea is flawed: after 5...b5, our bishop will reach the same diagonal just as quickly, so White gains no special advantage.

rnbqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/8/Q1pP4/2N2N2/PP2P.text:
5.Qa4+, developing the queen with check, is a very popular choice. 

White’s idea is to recapture the pawn immediately, and they may also assume - incorrectly - that ...b5 is impossible because of Nxb5 and the pin on the a-file.

But we can play 5...b5.

rnbqkbnr/2p2ppp/p3p3/1N6/Q1pP4/5N2/PP2PP.text:
If White takes this pawn, yes 6...axb5 loses the rook on a8. 

But we don't have to take. 

We can just counter pin the knight and win it.

rnbqkbnr/2p2ppp/p3p3/1p6/2pP4/2N2NP1/PP2.text:
White gets their bishop onto the diagonal. 

We do the same, and the position offers White nothing extra.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White continues with the Queen’s Gambit. 

We decline it with ...e6, supporting the d5-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/2PP4/2N5/PP2PPP.text:
White usually develops with 3.Nc3, since from c3 the knight puts pressure on d5. 

Once again, we follow with our signature move 3...a6, taking control of b5 and preparing ...b5 should we need it.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
This third study reviews the sidelines White may choose after 4...dxc4. 

Some options, like 5.Bf4 or 5.Bg5, allow harmonious development. 

Others, such as 5.Qa4+ and 5.g3, are more dubious and let us comfortably fight for an advantage.

 White begins with the queen’s pawn.

We mirror with our own, heading toward our standard QGD structure.

1r1q1rk1/1p1n1ppp/p1pb1n2/3p1bB1/3P4/1QN.text:
The cool, calm and collected 11...Rb8 defends the important b7 pawn. 

We'll continue with moves like ...Qc7 (always wary of not losing a pawn with Nxd5) and ...Re8. 

We don't have any weaknesses that White could attack.

2rq1rk1/3n1ppp/p1pb1n2/1p1p1bB1/3P4/1Q2P.text:
But after 12...Rc8, we're defending our only weakness, our bishops are better, and the burden is on White to try to trade one of the bishops. 

Moves like Bd3 or Bf4 come to mind. 

If Bd3, we can play ...Be4. 

If Bf4, we can keep the bishop with ...Be7 and play ...Re8.

R2qkb1r/3n1ppp/2p2n2/1p1p1bB1/3P4/1QN1PN.text:
After a trade of rooks...

We recapture. Our queen sits well and fully controls the a-file.

q3kb1r/3n1ppp/2p2n2/1p1p1bB1/3P4/1QN1PN2.text:
White develops the bishop to its only square and prepares to castle.

 We also get ready to castle, placing our bishop on d6. 

Notice how after 12...Bd6 both our bishops have better diagonals and are more active than White’s.

q4rk1/3n1ppp/2pb1n2/1p1p1bB1/3P4/1QN1PN2.text:
And so will we. 

Because our queen controls the a-file, White will most likely play their rook to c1, x-raying our one weakness: the c6 pawn. 

Thus, Rc8 from us should be considered, along with further destabilizing ideas like b4 at some point.

r2q1rk1/1p1n1pp1/2pbbn1p/p2p4/3P3B/P1NBP.text:
f White insists, they may prepare b4 with 13.a3. 

The point of …a5 is that when b4 finally comes, we’ll capture it and activate our a8-rook. 

So we'll allow b5 and bring our other rook into play with 13.Re8, improving our position.

r2q1rk1/1p1n1pp1/p1pbbn1p/3p4/3P3B/2NBPN.text:
12.Rab1 aims for queenside play. 

We respond with 12...a5, controlling the b4-square. 

Together with our bishop’s influence, this makes White’s idea much harder to execute.

r2q1rk1/1p1n1pp1/p1pbbn1p/3p4/3PP2B/2NB1.text:
If e4, remember that e5, forking our bishop and knight, is a threat. 

So we simply capture on e4 to remove it.

r2q1rk1/1p1n1pp1/p1pbbn1p/8/3PN2B/3B1N2/.text: The knight recaptures, adding pressure to our pinned Nf6 and attacking our bishop.

r2q1rk1/1p1n1ppp/p1pb1n2/3p1bB1/3P4/1QN1.text: If the queen comes to attack the base of our pawn chain...

r2q1rk1/1p1nBppp/p1p5/8/3Pn3/3Q1N2/PP3PP.text:
White trades on e7, as our bishop and queen were pressuring g5. 

We recapture.

r2q1rk1/1p1nbpp1/p1p1bn1p/8/3PN2B/3B1N2/.text:
We simply retreat the bishop to e7, both defending the knight and breaking the pin.

And you’ll notice that after the 12.e4 operation, White is left with an IQP, which isn’t easy to manage.

Our pawn structure is far more solid, and in any endgame we’ll be better off.

r2q1rk1/1p1nbppp/p1p2n2/3p2B1/3PP3/2NQ1N.text:
When e4 comes...

We take on e4 and leave White with an isolated queen’s pawn.

r2q1rk1/1p1nbppp/p1p2n2/6B1/3PN3/3Q1N2/P.text:
White must recapture with the knight. 

We welcome the trades, it is well known that exchanges favor the side playing against the IQP.

r2q1rk1/1p1nbppp/p1p2n2/6B1/3PN3/P2Q1N2/.text: We can retreat to e7 and simply enjoy the advantages of a safer king, connected rooks, and a healthier pawn structure - since we’re once again fighting against an IQP.

r2q1rk1/3n1ppp/p1pb1n2/1p1p1bB1/3P4/1Q2P.text: 12.Nd1 reveals an attack on the c6-pawn.

r2qk2r/1p1n1pp1/p1pbbn1p/3p4/3P3B/2NBPN2.text:
White castles.

We castle as well. 

Now White has two typical choices: e4 or Rab1 for queenside play.

r2qk2r/1p1n1ppp/p1p2n2/6B1/1b1PN3/3Q1N2/.text:
12.Kf1 steps out of the check and essentially claims that the knight on e4 will stay put - after all, it pressures the pinned knight on f6. 

But from Black’s perspective, we can castle and have a much safer king, while the knight on e4 doesn’t create any real threats. 

We have more than enough resources to handle the pin.

r2qk2r/1p1n1ppp/p1pb1n2/3p1bB1/3P4/2N1PN.text:
The rook comes to c1, becoming active on the semi-open c-file. 

We can now get our king to safety by castling short.

r2qk2r/1p1nbppp/p1p2n2/3p2B1/3P4/2NQPN2/.text:
White places the rook on e1 to prepare the e-pawn push. 

Thus we get our king out of the center quickly by castling.

r2qk2r/3n1ppp/p1pb1n2/1p1p1bB1/3P4/1QN1P.text:
White places a rook on the c-file, x-raying the c6-pawn. 

We castle as well - c6 isn’t under direct attack yet, so we have time to bring the king to safety.

r2qkb1r/1p1n1pp1/p1p1bn1p/3p4/3P3B/2NBPN.text:
The bishop arrives on d3, but thanks to …h6 it lacks its usual impact. 

We develop our bishop on the long diagonal.

r2qkb1r/1p1n1ppp/p1p2n2/3p1bB1/3P4/2N1PN.text:
White castles. 

We continue normal development, placing our bishop on the diagonal toward h2. 

White’s setup isn’t challenging, and the pin on f6 means little if d5 isn’t under pressure.

r2qkb1r/1p1n1ppp/p1p2n2/3p2B1/3P4/2NQPN2.text:
Castling is the slower - but better - approach. 

Getting the king safe first is more logical than rushing e4 and walking into ...Bb4+. 

Since e4 is coming, we also want to develop and get our king out of the center.

r2qkb1r/1p1n1ppp/p1p2n2/3p2B1/3PP3/2NQ1N.text:
The immediate 10.e4 is also possible. 

We simply take, and when White recaptures, we have a very common idea.

r2qkb1r/1p1n1ppp/p1p2n2/6B1/3PN3/3Q1N2/P.text:
The knight recaptures, allowing us accelerated development: 

...Bb4+, developing with tempo and forcing White to make a difficult choice.

r2qkb1r/3n1ppp/p1p2n2/1P1p1bB1/3P4/1QN1P.text:
White can still trade on a8, which is their best way of activating the rook. 

We simply recapture with the a-pawn - capturing with the c-pawn would drop d5.

r2qkb1r/3n1ppp/p1p2n2/1p1p1bB1/3P4/1QN1P.text:
White castles kingside.

Our bishop comes to d6. 

Once again, both of our bishops are more active than White’s in this position.

r2qr1k1/1p1n1pp1/2pbbn1p/3p4/1P1P3B/2NBP.text:
And once they recapture, b5 is a positional threat. 

Just as a fork on e5 with a pawn is a tactical threat, b5 threatens to weaken our structure and activate the White pieces on the kingside.

r2qr1k1/1p1n1pp1/2pbbn1p/p2p4/1P1P3B/P1N.text:
White gets their desired b4 push.

We simply take it.

r2qr1k1/3n1pp1/2pbbn1p/1p1p4/1P1P3B/2NBP.text:
Hence I suggest we play b5 ourselves. 

We have the idea of playing Nb6-c4, making sure we don't have queenside weaknesses.

r4rk1/1p1n1pp1/p1pq3p/6N1/3P3R/3Q4/PP3PP.text:
If the knight tries to be cool by coming to g5 and threaten checkmate with the queen, by all means, don't take! 

Because that's checkmate with the queen and rook!

r4rk1/1p1n1ppp/p1pq4/8/3P3R/3Q1N2/PP3PPP.text:
White may try to play actively with their rook, attacking h7. 

This is exactly what IQP players must do: create activity. 

We simply defend h7 by pushing the h-pawn. 

It becomes considerably tougher to target the kingside pawns after 16...h6.

r4rk1/1p1nqppp/p1p5/8/3PR3/3Q1N2/PP3PPP/.text:
White recaptures on e4 with tempo on our queen.

We escape the threat by centralizing it to d6, hitting d5 and keeping the IQP under pressure.

r4rk1/1p3pp1/p1pq1n1p/6N1/3P3R/3Q4/PP3PP.text:
Just defend against checkmate with the knight. 

Up next, you should play moves like Rae8 and take control of the open e-file! 

Black has a small edge out of the opening because of a better pawn structure (no IQP), a robust kingside defense, and the control of the e-file coming up.

rn1q1rk1/5ppp/p1p2n2/1p1p2B1/3P4/1QNNP3/.text:
After Kxh2...

We play the discovered attack 13...Ng4+, and the bishop on d3 will fall next.

rn1q1rk1/5ppp/p1p5/1p1p2B1/3P2n1/1QNNP3/.text: White's best bet is to hide away on g1.

rn1q1rk1/5ppp/p1pb1n2/1p1p2B1/3P4/1QNNP3.text:
Many players will castle here automatically. 

And now we have the classic Greek Gift sacrifice on h2.

rn1qk2r/5ppp/p1pb1n2/1p1p2B1/3P4/1QNNP3/.text:
The knight recaptures. 

We castle immediately. 

This often tempts White to castle as well, and if they do, 12.0-0 runs straight into Bxh2+!

rn1qk2r/5ppp/p1pb1n2/1p1pNbB1/3P4/1QNBP3.text:
If the bishop comes to d3, we can trade and set a small trap. 

We take on d3.

rn1qkb1r/1p3pp1/p1p1bn1p/3p4/3P3B/2N1PN2.text:
Good players avoid taking on f6 and retreat the bishop to h4. 

Here we develop our queenside knight to d7.

rn1qkb1r/1p3ppp/p1p1bn2/3p2B1/3P4/2N1PN2.text:
White plays 8.e3 to develop the bishop to d3 and pressure the d3–h7 diagonal. 

We challenge the bishop once with 8...h6; if White trades, we’re happy to win the bishop pair. 

If it moves to h4, White's Bd3/Qc2 battery won’t threaten h7.

rn1qkb1r/1p3ppp/p1p2n2/3p1bB1/3P4/1QN1PN.text:
Some players, whenever you go 
…Bf5 in Queen’s Pawn games, like to place their queen on b3 to pressure the now undefended b7-pawn. 

But since we already played …c6 to defend d5, all we need to do is protect b7 - and we can do that easily. 

Thus, we play 8…b5, achieving a strong queenside pawn structure and neutralizing the threat.

rn1qkb1r/1p3ppp/p1p2n2/3p1bB1/3P4/2N1PN2.text:
8.Be2 is a natural move, avoiding the bishop trade.

Without the exchange, our bishop on f5 becomes very strong, controlling the h7–b1 diagonal.

We calmly develop our b-knight to d7 - Be2 is passive and poses no immediate issues.

rn1qkb1r/1p3ppp/p1p2n2/3p1bB1/3P4/2NBPN2.text:
White plays 8.Bd3, proposing a trade. 

And as mentioned, we should absolutely accept it. 

In QGD structures, Black gladly trades the light-squared bishop.

rn1qkb1r/1p3ppp/p1p2n2/3p2B1/3P4/2NQPN2/.text:
White recaptures with the queen, activating it. 

One of the queen’s main ideas is to support the upcoming e4 push. 

We continue developing with 9...Nbd7, supporting our f6-knight.

rn1qkb1r/5ppp/p1p2n2/1p1p1bB1/3P4/1QN1PN.text:
9.Be2 is simple and reasonable development. 

Here we just bring out our queenside knight.

And we can get our bishop out to f5, controlling e4 and d3, which are squares White would like to control themselves. 

One of the best ideas White has now is placing their knight on e5, followed by Bd3 at some point. 

If they don't find that, our development is simple: ...Bd6 and ...0-0.

rn1qkb1r/5ppp/p1p2n2/1p1p1bB1/P2P4/1QN1P.text:
9.a4 tries to break apart our queenside and threatens axb5, not only to win a pawn but also to activate the rook. 

That’s why 9...Nbd7 is necessary: it connects our queen and rook and reduces the danger of axb5.

rn1qkb1r/5ppp/p1p2n2/1p1pNbB1/3P4/1QN1P3.text:
We’ve discussed the Ne5 idea before, but it’s worth repeating: from e5 the knight pressures c6 and supports a potential Bd3. 

We simply develop the bishop to d6 and prepare to castle.

rn3rk1/5ppp/p1p5/1p1p2q1/3P2n1/1QNNP3/PP.text: After which we can recover our piece with interest, and we're up a pawn with a strong attack.

rnb1k2r/1p3ppp/p1p2q2/8/1b1P4/2N2N2/PP3P.text: White has nothing better than to retreat to block the check...

rnb1kb1r/1p3ppp/p1p2q2/3p4/3PP3/2N2N2/PP.text:
8.e4 attacks our d5-pawn, but it won’t help White. 

It opens the position, which favors us because we have the bishop pair. 

Pawn exchanges benefit our bishops, so 8...dxe4 is strong. 

Tactically, after 9.Nxe4, we also have 9...Bb4+.

rnb1kb1r/1p3ppp/p1p2q2/8/3PN3/5N2/PP3PPP.text:
When the knight recaptures, it leaves the c3-square, opening the diagonal for our bishop. 

With 9...Bb4+ we develop and probe the dark squares.

rnb2rk1/1p3ppp/p1p2q2/8/1b1P4/2N2N2/PP3P.text:
After which we can just castle kingside.

We've castled before White, and we're playing ...Be6 and ...Nd7, with moves like ...Rfe8 coming in the future.

rnbq1rk1/1p3ppp/p1p2n2/6B1/1b1P4/2N2N2/P.text:
We can castle, with ideas of Re8 and Be6. 

Black is fighting against the IQP, so we should look to control the d5 square and take advantage of our e-file pressure.

rnbqk2r/1p3ppp/p1p2n2/6B1/1b1P4/2N2N2/PP.text: When the knight comes back to c3...

rnbqkb1r/1p3ppp/p1p2B2/3p4/3P4/2N2N2/PP2.text:
This capture, after we’ve played 
…c6 to reinforce d5, lacks toughness. 

We simply recapture and develop our queen.

rnbqkb1r/1p3ppp/p1p2n2/3p2B1/3P4/1QN2N2/.text:
7.Qb3, played after we’ve reinforced d5 with …c6, is another futile attempt to create pressure.

With d5 covered, we simply play 7...b5, solving any b7 issues. 

This gives us a strong queenside pawn formation that dominates the light squares, while our bishop is freed now that b7 is no longer a weakness.

rnbqkb1r/1p3ppp/p1p2n2/3p2B1/3P4/2N1PN2/.text:
7.e3 is the most natural move, enabling the development the light-squared bishop. 

And since White’s dark-squared bishop is already outside the chain, e3 is even more appealing. 

But we should exploit the fact that we can enter the h7–b1 diagonal first. 

If we trade light-squared bishops, we’re happy, our pawn structure already forms a strong light-square complex.

rnbqkb1r/1p3ppp/p1p2n2/3p2B1/3P4/2N2N2/P.text:
7.Qc2 is a natural queen move in many Queen’s Pawn openings. 

It prevents …Bf5, which is why we develop our light-squared bishop to e6 instead.

rnbqkb1r/1p3ppp/p1p2n2/3p2B1/3PP3/2N2N2/.text:
7.e4, immediately challenging the d5-pawn, is also popular, but it shouldn’t worry us. 

We simply capture the pawn, and after the knight recaptures, our f8-bishop develops more easily.

rnbqkb1r/1p3ppp/p1p2n2/6B1/3PN3/5N2/PP3P.text:
White recaptures, putting pressure on f6… 

But our bishop checks on b4, forcing White to block with a piece.

rnbqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p4n2/3p2B1/3P4/2N2N2/PP.text:
White plays 6.Bg5, a typical QGD move. 

The pin on our knight removes a defender of d5, and Qb3 ideas start to appear. 

That’s why I suggest solidifying the center with ...c6. 

One bonus of ...c6 is that it frees our c8-bishop - we’ll be able to play ...Bf5 before White goes Bd3.

rnbqkb1r/5ppp/p1p2n2/1p1p2B1/3P4/1QN1PN2.text: White plays e3 to develop their light-squared bishop, as they often do.

rnbqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/3P4/3P4/2N5/PP2PPP.text:
White may avoid the tricky 4.Nf3 and choose the “safe” approach with 4.cxd5. 

Whatever the reason, we recapture - and we get an added bonus: our c8-bishop will no longer be a problem piece. 

In many QGD lines, that bishop suffers, but with the diagonal open, development becomes effortless.

rnbqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p7/3p4/3P4/2N2N2/PP2PPP.text:
White develops the knight to f3, reinforcing central control. 

We continue with simple principles: develop our knight to f6 first, supporting d5 and avoiding Qb3 tactics before activating our bishops.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White plays the Queen's Gambit. 

These first moves are the same as the previous chapter.

As before, we decline it with 2...e6.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/2PP4/2N5/PP2PPP.text:
White develops the queenside knight to c3, increasing pressure on d5. 

We respond with 3...a6, keeping all our ideas of ...b5, holding the pawn, and building queenside counterplay.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to Chapter 2! 

Some players like to exchange pawns with cxd5. 

If this happens, does it make our 3...a6 idea useless? 

Not at all. 

In fact, cxd5 often helps us develop, many players capture because they’re afraid of our ...a6–b5 idea! 

White begins with the queen’s pawn.

We mirror with ours.

1r3rk1/2p2ppp/p1nq1n2/3p1b2/3P4/2N1PN2/P.text: If the queen retreats to its home square...

1r3rk1/2p2ppp/p1nq1n2/3p1b2/3P4/Q1N1PN2/.text: 12.Qa3 is another logical try, defending b2 and proposing a queen trade.

1r3rk1/2p2ppp/p2q1n2/3p1b2/1n1P4/Q1N1PN2.text:
But we've got the c2-square for the knight. 

If Rc1, ...Nc2+ wins the exchange. 

If 0-0-0, ...Rfc8 is strong, for ...c5.

White is lost here as well.

5rk1/2p2ppp/p1nq1n2/3p1b2/3P4/2N1PN2/Pr3.text:
Not only do we recover the pawn, but we activate all our pieces on the queenside. 

If Be2, ...Qb4. 

If Rc1, ...Nb4 for ...Nc2+. 

White is totally lost.

r2q1rk1/1Qp2ppp/p1nb1n2/3p1b2/3P4/2N1PNB.text: Once again, this cannot be played.

r2q1rk1/1pp2ppp/p1nb1n2/3p1b2/3P4/1QN1PN.text:
Instead of taking on b7, White may opt for simple development once they realize they cannot win any pawns. 

In that case, we capture on g3 and bring our queen to d6, securing control over the dark squares.

r2qk2r/1Qp2ppp/p1nb1n2/3p1b2/3P1B2/2N1PN.text: If White takes thinking that ...Rb8 cannot be played, they would be right.

r2qk2r/1Qp2ppp/p2b1n2/n2p1b2/3P1B2/2N1PN.text: But 9...Na5 can be played and the queen doesn't have any squares!

r2qk2r/1pp2ppp/p1nB1n2/3p1b2/3P4/1QN1PN2.text:
White may try to eliminate our bishop first. 

After we recapture, our queen no longer protects the a8-rook.

r3k2r/1Qp2ppp/p1nq1n2/3p1b2/3P4/2N1PN2/P.text:
So can they take the pawn now?

Not really - the queen is still nearly trapped, and White loses too much time trying to save it.

We castle our king.

r4rk1/1pp2ppp/p1nq1n2/3p1b2/3P4/1QN1PNP1.text:
And our control is quite nice. 

Our bishop is on f5 so h7 has some reinforcement. 

We've got sound moves like ...b6 and ...g6 to safeguard our weak points. 

If Qxb7 here, the queen still gets trapped with ...Na5.

r4rk1/1ppn1ppp/p2q1n2/3p4/3P4/2NQPN2/PP3.text:
After 11...Nbd7 the development is complete.

As per usual, we will reinforce the center with ...c6 next.

In the future, we'll bring the rooks to the center and possibly try to jump into e4 with our knight!

This line just goes to show that sometimes chess can be very calm, with many trades and balanced, equal positions.

r4rk1/2p2ppp/p1nq1n2/3p1b2/3P4/1QN1PN2/P.text:
When White finally retreats the queen... 

We slide our a-rook to b8, attacking it and x-raying the b2-pawn.

rn1q1rk1/1pp2ppp/p2b1n2/3p1b2/3P4/1QN1PN.text:
If White targets b7 immediately with the queen...

9...Nc6 is a tricky response because of the queen trap on b7.

rn1q1rk1/1pp2ppp/p2b1n2/3p4/3P1B2/2NQPN2.text:
We get our king to safety.

White has given us everything we need out of the opening; we are developed and castled, with no real weaknesses.

Next, we'll reinforce the center with ...c6, and after dealing with the dark-squared bishop tension, develop the knight and centralize the rooks.

rn1qk2r/1p3ppp/p1pb1n2/3p1bB1/3P4/2N1PN2.text:
...But before they get to develop it, we jump in with ...Bf5 and control the d3-square, as in the Bg3 line!

We are ready to castle and develop the knight from b8.

If White tries to be aggressive with moves like Qb3 now, ...b5 is very strong again.

As mentioned, some of the themes we play are repetitive, which makes them important to remember!

rn1qk2r/1pp2ppp/p2b1n2/3p1b2/3P1B2/1QN1P.text:
White may also go for the b7-pawn. 

Here I recommend the very tricky 8…Nc6.

rn1qk2r/1pp2ppp/p2b1n2/3p1b2/3P1B2/2NBPN.text:
This time White wants to trade immediately. 

We don’t mind - developing the light-squared bishop is often difficult for Black in QGD positions anyway.

rn2k2r/1pp2ppp/p2q1n2/3p1b2/3P4/2NBPN2/P.text:
White immediately looks for a trade of light-squared bishops, which is no problem for us.

We accept the trade.

rn2k2r/1pp2ppp/p2q1n2/3p4/3P4/2NQPN2/PP3.text:
White recaptures, activating the queen. 

We castle.

rnb1k2r/1pp2ppp/p2q1n2/3p4/3P4/2N1PN2/PP.text:
White plays the usual e3. 

And once again, we develop our light-squared bishop faster than White with ...Bf5.

rnbq1rk1/1pp2ppp/p2b1n2/3p4/3P4/2N1PNB1/.text:
e3 is a very common move in structures where the bishop went to f4. 

White only needs to develop the light-squared bishop, so e3 is enough. 

But we answer just in time with 8...Bf5, preventing White from taking over key diagonals.

rnbqk2r/1p3ppp/p1pb1n2/3p2B1/3P4/2N1PN2/.text: With 8.e3, White opens the door for their own bishop on f1...

rnbqk2r/1pp2ppp/p2B1n2/3p4/3P4/2N2N2/PP2.text:
The most common response is for White to trade. 

We recapture with the queen, placing it actively on d6.

rnbqk2r/1pp2ppp/p2b1n2/3p2B1/3P4/2N2N2/P.text:
Some players who don’t want to trade will move the bishop again to g5, pinning our knight and threatening to win d5.

We simply reinforce the center with 7…c6, forming the familiar pawn chain.

rnbqk2r/1pp2ppp/p2b1n2/3p4/3P1B2/2N1PN2/.text:
The last option is 7.e3, opening the diagonal for the f1-bishop and defending the bishop on f4 with a pawn. 

White likely wants to meet …Bf5 with Bd3 and trade bishops, but this setup doesn’t challenge us at all.

We activate our bishop to f5 once again.

rnbqk2r/1pp2ppp/p2b1n2/3p4/3P4/2N2NB1/PP.text:
Many players familiar with London-style positions will drop the bishop back to g3, hoping that if we take on g3, hxg3 activates the rook on the h-file. 

We should avoid helping White - so instead of taking, we castle and activate our own rook.

rnbqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p4n2/3p4/3P1B2/2N2N2/PP.text:
In this line White plays the natural 6.Bf4. 

One of the best reactions is simply to challenge that bishop. 

That’s why I like 6...Bd6, proposing a trade and getting quick development.

rnbqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/3P4/3P4/2N5/PP2PPP.text:
To avoid our ...dxc4 ideas, White may take on d5. 

We recapture, opening the diagonal for our traditionally problematic c8-bishop.

rnbqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p7/3p4/3P4/2N2N2/PP2PPP.text:
White develops the knight, increasing central control. 

We answer with 5...Nf6, overprotecting d5 and keeping Bg5/Qb3 ideas under control.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White plays the Queen’s Gambit.

We decline as usual.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/2PP4/2N5/PP2PPP.text:
White develops the knight to c3, once again putting pressure on d5.

We follow with 3...a6, with the familiar ideas of preparing ...b5 and restricting White’s pieces from using b5.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
In this second study, we examine what happens when White trades on d5 and develops the bishop to f4 instead of g5. 

Against this setup, we immediately challenge that bishop with 6...Bd6, proposing a trade. 

Our goal is to simplify, develop quickly, and reach a sound position. 

White starts with the queen’s pawn.

We mirror.

r1bq1rk1/1p1nbppp/p1p2n2/3p4/3P1B2/2N2NP.text:
White activates the dark-squared bishop before pushing e4, which is one of the key benefits of playing 6.g3. 

We stay with our idea: activating our rook on the semi-open e-file and freeing the f8-square for the knight.

r1bqr1k1/1p1nbppp/p1p2n2/3p4/3P1B2/P1N2N.text: White's 11.a3 prevents a possible ...Bb4, pinning the knight to the rook.

r1bqrnk1/1p2bppp/p1p2n2/3p4/3P1B2/P1N2NP.text:
We finish our knight maneuver by landing it on f8. 

Notice we’ve delayed developing our light-squared bishop - it can easily become a target of Ng5 or Nh4. 

But once the knight reaches g6, Nh4 won’t be possible, as we can trade. Only then do we bring the bishop out to f5!

rn1q1rk1/1pp2ppp/p2b1n2/3p4/3P4/2NQPN2/P.text:
We do the same.

While White might try to push e4 at some point and activate the dark-squared bishop, we will counter that by either taking or playing ...c6.

Then, we will develop our knight and enjoy a comfortable position!

rn1qk2r/1pp2ppp/p2b1n2/3p4/3P4/2NQPN2/PP.text: Once White brings the king to safety...

rn1qkb1r/1pp2ppp/p4n2/3p1b2/3P4/1QN1PN2/.text: However, that does leave the b7-pawn undefended and vulnerable to various queen attacks...

rn1qkb1r/1pp2ppp/p4n2/3p1b2/3P4/2NBPN2/P.text:
Instead of launching queen pressure, White may try to trade our active light-squared bishop with 7.Bd3. 

Trading is completely fine - it makes our development smooth and leaves our position free of problems.

rn1qkb1r/1pp2ppp/p4n2/3p4/3P4/2NQPN2/PP3.text:
White recaptures. 

Since they already played 6.e3, we don’t have to worry about Bg5 ideas. 

That’s why 8...Bd6 is the best developing move for our dark-squared bishop.

rn1qkb1r/2p2ppp/p4n2/1p1p1b2/3P4/1QN1PN2.text:
But we simply go with our standard approach and push ...b5!

In the future, we might support our structure with ...c6, develop our knight to d7, move our dark-squared bishop and castle.

On the other hand, White has blocked their dark-squared bishop in, and now has trouble developing the light-squared one too! The only available square is e2.

rnbq1rk1/1p2bppp/p1p2n2/3p4/3P4/2N2NP1/P.text:
The rook comes to the e-file, hinting at a future e4. 

We continue developing for now, 9...Nbd7 is our next move. 

Our plan in this variation is to place the knight on f8, from where it helps defend the kingside and can reroute to g6.

rnbq1rk1/1pp1bppp/p4n2/3p4/3P4/2N2NP1/PP.text:
White castles too.

So we implement ...c6 idea, creating a solid pawn chain and stabilizing the center.

rnbqk2r/1pp1bppp/p4n2/3p4/3P4/2N2NP1/PP2.text:
White continues with their plan, also preparing to castle. 

Before the battle begins, both kings must be safe, so we castle short.

rnbqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p4n2/3p4/3P4/2N1PN2/PP3.text:
One sixth-move option for White is 6.e3. 

White wants to develop the light-squared bishop naturally and strengthen the center, but this also shuts in the dark-squared bishop.

We take advantage of the open diagonal and develop our bishop to f5 so it won’t be stuck anymore.

rnbqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p4n2/3p4/3P4/2N2NP1/PP2.text:
Another line is 6.g3, aiming to fianchetto the light-squared bishop instead of developing it normally. 

We’ll eventually push ...c6 to reinforce the center. 

First, we bring the bishop out to e7 and prepare to castle.

rnbqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/3P4/3P4/2N5/PP2PPP.text:
But here White prevents that and captures on d5 first. 

We recapture, activating our light-squared bishop, which is the biggest benefit for Black when White plays cxd5 early.

rnbqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p7/3p4/3P4/2N2N2/PP2PPP.text:
The knight jumps to its natural f3-square...

We also continue developing with 5...Nf6, and now the fun begins.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
The Queen's Gambit is on the board.

We decline it with ...e6, supporting the center.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/2PP4/2N5/PP2PPP.text:
White develops with more pressure on d5. 

As we’ve already learned, 3...a6 is the main idea of this course - preparing to capture on c4 and support the pawn with ...b5.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
In this third study of Chapter 2, we look at what happens when White skips both 6.Bg5 and 6.Bf4 and instead plays 6.e3 or 6.g3. 

There are a few simple ideas to remember. 

White begins with the queen’s pawn.

We mirror, aiming for our QGD structure.

r1b1kbnr/1pp1qppp/p1n5/3P4/4N3/8/PP2QPPP.text:
The natural pawn push only gives us another tempo. 

We jump into d4, hitting the queen.

r1b1kbnr/1pp1qppp/p1n5/8/3PN3/5N2/PP2QPP.text:
If White tries to simply develop...

We’ll get the trades we want, and the IQP will soon come under unbearable pressure.

We start by adding pressure on Ne4 with 8...Bf5.

r1b1kbnr/1pp1qppp/p7/3P4/3nN3/3Q4/PP3PPP.text:
Once the queen retreats to d3 to defend the knight, cover c2, and keep an eye on our knight... 

We attack the knight with our light-squared bishop. 

As mentioned, trades favor the side playing against the IQP.

r1b1r1k1/1p1nqpp1/p1p4p/3p4/3PB3/1QN1PN2.text:
White usually trades off our strong e4-knight next. 

We take with the pawn, forcing the f3-knight away.

r1b1r1k1/1p1nqpp1/p1p4p/8/3Pp3/1QN1P3/PP.text: This knight may come to d2, putting pressure on our pawn.

r1b1r1k1/1p2qpp1/p1p2n1p/8/3Pp3/1QN1P3/P.text:
But our knight arrives on f6 right on time. 

We have ...Bf5 ideas and ...Rad8 to continue our development. 

In the middlegame, we're looking to exploit the fact that our e4-pawn helps us control White's position. 

If we can trade our light-squared bishop for a knight, this would also be good since our pawns are mostly on light squares.

r1b1r1k1/1pp2p1p/p1nq1np1/3p4/3P4/2NBP1N.text: White activates the rook on the e-file, with plans of playing e4 in the future if possible.

r1b1r1k1/1pp2ppp/p1nq1n2/3p4/3P4/2NBP1N1.text:
The knight continues its journey toward g3, probably aiming for f5.

Although it weakens our king a little, 11...g6 is necessary - we must stop anything from landing on f5 or h5.

r1bq1rk1/1p1n1ppp/p1pb1n2/3p2B1/3PP3/2N2.text:
10.e4 strikes in the center! 

We must not allow e5 and the fork, so we capture. 

This gives White the chance to activate their knight…

r1bq1rk1/1p1n1ppp/p1pb1n2/6B1/3PN3/5NP1/.text:
…and they do, now attacking our pinned knight and our bishop simultaneously.

11...Be7 is essentially forced - retreating the bishop and unpinning the knight. 

After the bishop retreat, we threaten to capture on e4.

r1bq1rk1/1p1nbpp1/p1p2n1p/3p4/3P1B2/1QNB.text:
In all likelihood, White will do the same. 

Since we cannot trade dark-squared bishops, we can aim for it with our knight - 11…Nh5 fits the QGD strategy perfectly, since dark squares are key.

r1bq1rk1/1p1nbpp1/p1p2n1p/3p4/3P3B/1QNBP.text:
White castles as well.

With 11…Re8, we prepare …Ne4, which gives us chances to trade pieces.

r1bq1rk1/1p1nbpp1/p1p4p/3p3n/3P4/1QNBPNB.text:
The bishop may try to keep structure by going to g3. 

We take.

r1bq1rk1/1p2bpp1/p1p2n1p/3p4/3P4/1QNBPNP.text:
And now with the knight on f6 we control the e4-square, because White may try to push e4 at some point. 

We have ideas of ...Bd6 and ...Re8 to improve our pieces, and even a5-a4 to kick the queen out of b3.

With the bishop pair, we should have a slightly more comfortable position.

r1bq1rk1/1p2bppp/p1p2n2/6B1/3P4/5NP1/PP3.text:
...And we take back, activating our knight from d7.

We have successfully dealt with White's quick development, advancement in the center and kingside aggression!

Next, we will develop our light-squared bishop, kick out White from g5 and bring our rooks to the game, having equalized.

r1bqk2r/1p1nbpp1/p1p2B1p/3p4/3P4/1QNBPN2.text: If White gives up this bishop, we'll gladly accept it.

r1bqk2r/1p1nbpp1/p1p2n1p/3p4/3P1B2/1QNBP.text:
The bishop can stay on the board by retreating to f4, keeping an eye on e5. 

We calmly castle.

r1bqk2r/1p1nbpp1/p1p2n1p/3p4/3P3B/1QNBPN.text:
The most logical is 10.Bh4, keeping influence along the diagonal. 

Here we castle and prepare …Re8.

r1bqk2r/1p1nbppp/p1p2n2/3p2B1/3P4/1QNBPN.text:
White will usually continue developing as well.

We push h6, forcing the g5-bishop to make a decision. 

It has three legitimate choices.

r1bqk2r/1p2bpp1/p1p2n1p/3p4/3P4/1QNBPN2/.text:
The dark-squared bishop is the most important bishop in Queen's Gambit Declined positions because Black has placed many pawns on dark squares.

Black can aim for ...0-0, Bd6 and Qc7, controlling the dark squares.

r1bqr1k1/1p1nBpp1/p1p4p/3p4/3Pn3/1QNBPN2.text:
The bishop will most often take.

We recapture.

r1bqr1k1/1p1nbpp1/p1p2n1p/3p4/3P3B/1QNBP.text:
In most QGD structures, White places a rook on c1. 

Now we go for 12…Ne4, with a discovered attack on the bishop on h4 and forcing White to react.

r3kb1r/1pp1nppp/p7/5b2/1n1P4/2N2N2/PP3PP.text:
We recapture, and ...Nc2+ is still a problem.

...Rd8 is coming, but not before ...Nc2, attacking the rook on a1.

White's position is crumbling and most likely castling won't be possible for them.

r3kbnr/1pp1Qppp/p7/5b2/1n1P4/2N2N2/PP3PP.text: Trading queens just accelerates our development.

r3kbnr/1pp1qppp/p1n5/5b2/3P4/2N2N2/PP2QP.text:
If White tries to save the knight... 

The problems only increase after we play 9...Nb4 threatening ...Nc2+. 

Just to illustrate, suppose White trades here.

r3kbnr/1pp1qppp/p7/3P1b2/3QN3/8/PP3PPP/R.text:
White takes on d4.

We capture on e4, forcing a queen trade.

r3kbnr/1pp2ppp/p7/3P1b2/4Q3/8/PP3PPP/R1B.text:
White is forced to exchange queens.

We recapture, also attacking d5.

r3kbnr/1pp2ppp/p7/3P4/2B5/8/PP3PbP/R1B1K.text:
Because g2 is unprotected. 

This should be an easy win for Black.

r3r1k1/1ppb1p1p/p1nq1np1/3p4/3P4/2NBP1N1.text:
And we complete queenside development with 12...Bd7.

White cannot push e4 yet because the d4 pawn would be hanging.

Next, we will activate the a8 rook, and sometimes go for the ...h5 push, to try and put pressure on White's oddly placed knight on g3.

Our knight could also rotate to e7 and become useful on the kingside, in some positions.

rnb1k2r/1p2qpb1/p1p4p/5p2/P1BP4/1Q2pP2/1.text: And even though White can win this pawn...

rnb1k2r/1p2qpb1/p1p4p/5p2/P1BPp3/1QN2P2/.text:
If 13.f3, we cannot let White open the f-file - the f-file is where our weaknesses live. 

So we push the pawn forward.

rnb1k2r/1p3ppp/p1p2q2/8/3P4/1Q3N2/PP3PPP.text:
White defends and develops. 

We castle, bringing our rook into the game.

rnb1k2r/1pp2ppp/p2q1n2/3p4/3P4/2NBP3/PP3.text:
A simple developing move from White, 8.Bd3. 

We bring our king to safety.

rnb1kb1r/1p2qp2/p1p2p1p/8/P1BPp3/1QN5/1P.text:
After White develops their other knight... 

We support the e4-pawn with 11...f5. 

The structure may not be pretty, but our opening problems are solved. 

With …Bg7 coming, our entire kingside becomes developed.

rnb1kb1r/1p2qp2/p1p4p/5p2/P1BPp3/1QN5/1P.text:
White castles.

We fianchetto and begin pressuring the isolated queen’s pawn.

rnb1kb1r/1p2qpp1/p1p2B1p/8/P1BPp3/1QN5/1.text:
White will often take, damaging our pawns. 

But since we are a pawn up, this is acceptable. 

We recapture with the g-pawn and then follow with …f5 and a kingside fianchetto, controlling central squares.

It’s White who must find a way to challenge our e4-pawn.

rnb1kb1r/1p2qppp/p1p2n2/6B1/P1BPp3/1QN5/.text:
White is advised to play a4 to stop b5.

Our reply is to kick the bishop off the diagonal with 9...h6.

rnb1kbnr/1pp1qppp/p7/8/3PN3/8/PP2QPPP/R1.text:
White must defend the knight while breaking the pin with 7.Qe2. 

We develop our knight to c6 with tempo, attacking d4. 

White has no good way to meet this pressure.

rnb1r1k1/1p3ppp/p1p2q2/8/3P4/1Q3N2/PP2BP.text:
But after 12...Re8, it's safe to say we have some nice pressure in this position because of the pin. 

To increase the pressure, we have ideas of trading White's strong queen on b3 with ...Qe6. 

We'll also aim to develop our queenside knight to d7 and then to f6.

rnb1r1k1/1pp2ppp/p2q1n2/3p4/3P4/2NBP3/PP.text:
Before moving forward with their idea, White castles.

We answer with the peculiar-looking 10...Nc6. 

Developing the knight to c6 isn’t typical here, but White’s setup allows it. 

The knight pressures d4, making e4 much harder to achieve.

rnb2rk1/1p2qpb1/p1p4p/5p2/P1BP4/1Q2pP2/1.text:
We should allow them to take, because we're not in the business of giving up excessive piece activity for a pawn. 

We'll continue with ...Re8, ...Nd7 to develop, keeping in mind we always have pressure on d4 if White isn't careful with that pawn.

rnb2rk1/1p3ppp/p1p2q2/8/3P4/1Q3N2/PP2BPP.text: White will develop and block the e-file.

rnb2rk1/1pp2ppp/p2q1n2/3p4/3P4/2NBP3/PP2.text:
Instead of Nf3, White plays 9.Nge2, planning a knight route toward g3 and maybe f5 if allowed. 

We activate our rook, discouraging the e4 break.

rnbq1rk1/1p3ppp/p1pb1n2/3p2B1/3P4/2N2NP1.text:
White uses the fact that they haven’t moved the e-pawn yet and pins our knight. 

We reinforce it with 9...Nbd7, developing.

rnbqk2r/1p2bppp/p1p2N2/6B1/3P4/1Q6/PP3PP.text:
White has nothing better than to trade pieces.

We recapture with the bishop, keeping a clean structure.

rnbqk2r/1p2bppp/p1p2n2/3p2B1/3P4/1QNBP3/.text:
This is one of the few lines where White stops our bishop from reaching f5. 

We simply develop the pieces we can, now with 8...Nbd7.

rnbqk2r/1p3ppp/p1p2B2/8/3P4/1Q6/PP3PPP/R.text:
White continues trading.

We recapture and develop our queen, with pressure on d4.

rnbqk2r/1p3ppp/p1pb1n2/3p4/3P4/2N2NP1/PP.text:
With the king safe, White now begins to think seriously about e4. 

We also get our king out of the center.

rnbqk2r/1pp2ppp/p2B1n2/3p4/3P4/2N1P3/PP3.text:
White chooses to trade bishops, develop quickly and castle. 

We recapture with the queen.

rnbqkb1r/1p3ppp/p1p2n2/3p2B1/3P4/1QN1P3/.text:
One is 7.e3, reinforcing d4 and opening the diagonal for the light-squared bishop. 

But this slow move prevents us from playing …b5 (too committal) and …Bf5 is impossible due to the b7-weakness. 

When there’s nothing active to do, we follow opening principles and develop calmly, 7...Be7 is our move.

rnbqkb1r/1p3ppp/p1p2n2/3p2B1/3PP3/1QN5/P.text:
White can try to break in the center with 7.e4. 

Some aggressive players think the pin makes this possible. 

We simply take, there’s no reason to fear Nxe4 or Bc4.

rnbqkb1r/1p3ppp/p1p2n2/3p4/3P4/2N2NP1/PP.text:
White finishes kingside development and prepares to castle. 

We do the same by playing 7...Bd6.

rnbqkb1r/1p3ppp/p1p2n2/6B1/2BPp3/1QN5/PP.text:
If Bc4 appears, targeting f7... 

We defend both pawns with the calm 8...Qe7.

rnbqkb1r/1p3ppp/p1p2n2/6B1/3PN3/1Q6/PP3P.text:
If White just captures on e4...

We break the pin with 8…Be7, as is common in QGD structures.

rnbqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p4n2/3p2B1/3P4/1QN5/PP2.text:
If White pins our knight...

We support the center with ...c6. 

From here, White has a few natural developing tries.

rnbqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p4n2/3p4/3P1B2/2N1P3/PP.text:
With the dark-squared bishop developed, 6.e3 prepares to develop the light-squared bishop as well.

We aim to trade our bishop for White’s active f4-bishop. 

This line resembles the 6.Bf4 variation, except White hasn’t played Nf3 yet - allowing them tricky alternatives we’ll look at.

rnbqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p4n2/3p4/3P4/2N3P1/PP2P.text:
White continues with their plan. 

As seen in the previous study, ...c6 is often useful against g3/Bg2 structures.

rnbqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/3P4/3P4/2N5/PP2PPP.text:
White tries to neutralize 3...a6 by taking on d5, but they only help our development.

We recapture on d5, and our light-squared bishop gains a clear path.

rnbqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p7/3p4/3P1B2/2N5/PP2PPP.text:
The most critical choice is 5.Bf4. 

White delays Nf3, and we’ll soon see why.

We simply continue developing and strengthen our center with 5...Nf6.

rnbqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p7/3p4/3P4/1QN5/PP2PPPP.text:
White can choose to attack the d5-pawn and put pressure on b7.

We respond with a sound developing move that also defends the pawn, 5...Nf6.

rnbqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p7/3p4/3P4/2N3P1/PP2PP1.text:
Another line, often interchangeable with 5.e3, is 5.g3. 

White prepares to fianchetto the light-squared bishop.

We develop our knight to f6, adding central support.

rnbqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p7/3p4/3PP3/2N5/PP3PPP/.text:
5.e4 is a popular try, but White isn’t ready to open the position. 

After 5…dxe4, White is left with a weak d4-pawn and must play with an isolated queen’s pawn.

rnbqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p7/8/3PN3/8/PP3PPP/R1BQ.text:
White can recapture, of course. 

But after 6...Qe7, we guarantee trades - always good for the side playing against an IQP.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White plays the Queen’s Gambit.

We decline it with 2...e6, supporting our center.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/2PP4/2N5/PP2PPP.text:
White develops naturally, adding pressure to d5.

We once again play our thematic 3...a6, dreaming of ...dxc4 and ...b5 - but White has other plans.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to Study 4 of Chapter 2 in our QGD course. Here we examine White’s 5th-move deviations, such as 5.Bf4, 5.e3, and 5.g3. 

In the 5.Bf4 line, White can even avoid Nf3 entirely!


White begins with 1.d4, taking space in the center. 

We respond symmetrically.

r2q1rk1/1b1nbppp/pp2pn2/2p5/2PP4/2NBPN2/.text:
White slides their f-rook to d1, which now eyes our queen, so we must be careful about tactics if White opens the d-file with dxc5. 

Whenever the rook comes to d1, it’s wise to move away from discovered attacks, so we play 12...Qc7.

r2q1rk1/1b2bppp/p3pn2/1pn5/8/2N1PN2/PPB2.text:
We castle, leaving us with a lead in development and good control of the e4 square.  

In case White trades the queens, we recapture on d8 with the f-rook, so the a-rook can be placed on c8. 

Otherwise, we play ...Qc7 with the idea of playing ...Rfd8 and ...Rac8, centralizing the rooks.

r2qk2r/1b1nbpp1/p3p3/2p4p/Pp1P2nP/3BPNN1.text:
We end the variation with 13...Ng4, placing the knight on a very active square.

h4 is now under some serious pressure and Black has great attacking potential.

In addition, the ...g5 move is always an idea, initiating the attack.

r2qk2r/1b1nbpp1/p3pn2/2p4p/Pp1P3P/3BPNN1.text: White tries to block the attack but simultaneously makes some weaknesses around their king.

r2qk2r/1b1nbppp/p3p3/1ppNP3/3P4/3B1N2/PP.text: White gets rid of our strongly positioned d5-knight.

r2qk2r/1b1nbppp/p3pn2/1pP5/8/2NBPN2/PP3P.text:
White releases the tension. 

This allows our knight to recapture on c5 and occupy an excellent square. 

The bishop comes under attack, and our pieces are more active than White’s.

r2qk2r/1b1nbppp/p3pn2/1pp1P3/3P4/2NB1N2/.text:
White pushes the e-pawn, attacking our knight.

We place it on d5, its best square.

r2qk2r/1b1nbppp/p3pn2/2p5/Pp1P4/3BPNN1/1.text:
A popular move for White is 12.Ng3, activating the knight.

Now White's knight on g3, we strike on the kingside with 12...h5.

r2qk2r/1b1nbppp/p3pn2/P1p5/1p1P4/3BPN2/1.text: Another popular move here is to play a5, fixing our pawn on a6.

r2qk2r/1bpnbppp/p3pn2/1p6/3P4/2NBPN2/PP3.text:
Another option for White is to develop the rook to e1. 

Our …c5 advance remains essential.

r2qk2r/1bpnbppp/p3pn2/1p6/3PP3/2NB1N2/PP.text:
Instead of 10.a4, White expands in the center with 10.e4. 

We continue with our ...c5 plan.

r2qk2r/1bpnbppp/p3pn2/1p6/P2P4/2NBPN2/1P.text:
White tries to challenge our queenside pawns... 

But a4 is always met by ...b4.

r2qk2r/1bpnbppp/p3pn2/8/Pp1P4/3BPN2/1P2N.text:
White retreats.

We challenge the center with ...c5 while expanding on the queenside. 

Black’s position is extremely comfortable - White’s c1-bishop has yet to move, and our development is nearly complete.

r2qk2r/3nbppp/p3p3/1ppbP3/3P4/3B1N2/PP3P.text:
We recapture with our bishop.

We will castle next. 

The backward d-pawn will be successfully undermined. 

The e5-pawn presents some attacking chances for White, so we must be careful and defend our king accordingly.

r3k2r/1bqnbppp/p3pn2/P1p5/1p1P4/3BPN2/1P.text:
In that case, we should put the queen on c7 in order to prepare a "battery" with ...Bd6. 

The rooks will also sit nicely on the 
d- and c-files.

r4rk1/1bqnbppp/p4n2/1ppP4/8/2NBPN2/PB2QP.text:
We have a very strong queenside pawn chain that can be pushed with ...c4 or ...b4 should good, tactical opportunities present themselves. 

...Rfe8 and ...Bd6 are also some plans, playing for control of the e5-square.

r4rk1/1bqnbppp/pp2pn2/2p5/2PP4/2NBPN2/PB.text:
We respond by simply stepping out of the d-file, also connecting the rooks. 

White will most likely play for the d5 pawn push. 

In that case, the plan for Black revolves around playing ...b5 and expanding on the queenside.

r4rk1/1bqnbppp/pp2pn2/2pP4/2P5/2NBPN2/PB.text:
White confronts our pawn structure by pushing their d-pawn.

d5 should always be taken, so that's what we do, 13...exd5 comes next.

r4rk1/1bqnbppp/pp3n2/2pP4/8/2NBPN2/PB2QP.text:
White recaptures on d5.

Now the plan of queenside expansion with ... b5 is very strong.

rn1q1rk1/1b2bppp/pp2pn2/2P5/2P5/2NBPN2/P.text: White opts to take on c5 immediately.

rn1q1rk1/1b2bppp/pp2pn2/2p5/2PP4/2NBPN2/.text:
White connects the rooks and gets the queen off the dangerous d-file.

We now have multiple development options. 

One is 11...Nbd7, supporting the c5-pawn without blocking our b7-bishop.

White instead chooses 11.Qc2, planning to form a battery along the b1–h7 diagonal, but this is a mistake. 

The knight now has only one defender - the pawn in front of White’s king - so we capture it to ruin White’s structure.

rn1q1rk1/1b3ppp/pp2pn2/2b5/2P5/2NBPN2/PB.text:
Capturing with the bishop keeps the b- and a-pawns intact. 

The queen as usual will be moved to  c7 and we will play ...Nbd7. 

The c4-pawn could be a weakness that we could attack at some point.

rn1q1rk1/1bp1bppp/pp2pn2/3p4/2PP4/1PNBPN.text:
White castles. 

We take on c4, releasing the tension immediately after. 

This leaves our light-squared bishop with a much better scope.

rn1q1rk1/1bp1bppp/pp2pn2/8/2PP4/2NBPN2/P.text:
White recaptures. 

We challenge White’s center with 10...c5.

rn1q1rk1/4bppp/pp2pn2/8/2Pp4/2NBPP2/PBQ2.text:
It is a good idea to open things up since White's King can become weak. 

We also have ideas of playing ...Nc6 to b4. 

After exd4, White will have doubled isolated f-pawns. 

It is worth noting that the immediate ...Qxd4 wouldn't be a good move because of a discovered attack on our queen.

rn1qk2r/1bp1bppp/p3pn2/1p6/3P4/2NBPN2/PP.text:
White castles.

We finish development with 9...Nbd7. 

Our plan is simple: play ...c5 and castle with a very comfortable position

rnbq1rk1/1pp1bppp/p3pn2/3p4/2PP4/1PN1PN2.text:
White develops their dark-squared bishop on the main diagonal. 

Our next move, 7...b6, supports ...c5 and prepares the b7-square for our bishop.

rnbq1rk1/2p1bppp/pp2pn2/3p4/2PP4/1PNBPN2.text:
White plays 8.Bd3, developing the light-squared bishop on an active diagonal toward h7. 

We fianchetto ours, which sits well on the a8–h1 diagonal.

rnbqk2r/1pp1bppp/p3pn2/3p4/2PP4/1PN1PN2/.text:
White may defend c4 with 6.b3, avoiding an immediate ...b5. 

This also prepares to develop the dark-squared bishop, which was blocked by the early e3.

It's time for us to hide our king.

rnbqk2r/1pp1bppp/p3pn2/3p4/2PP4/2NBPN2/P.text:
White develops the bishop on an active diagonal. 

Now we make use of our 3...a6 idea and capture on c4.

rnbqk2r/1pp1bppp/p3pn2/8/2BP4/2N1PN2/PP3.text:
White must recapture, wasting another tempo with the bishop.

We attack the bishop while gaining queenside space with 7...b5. 

The b7-square is now open for our own bishop.

rnbqk2r/2p1bppp/p3pn2/1p6/3P4/2NBPN2/PP3.text:
White retreats to d3.

Our bishop will be beautifully placed on b7.

rnbqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p3pn2/3p4/2PP4/2N1PN2/P.text:
White does the same. 

Here the knights come out quickly to support a solid center, but White’s bishops aren’t very active.

We prepare to castle with 5...Be7.

rnbqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/3p4/2PP4/2N1P3/PP3.text:
White chooses the quiet 4.e3, simply aiming to develop the pieces.

We bring out our knight to its natural square, f6.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
The Queen’s Gambit appears on the board. 

We decline it with 2...e6, supporting our d5-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/2PP4/2N5/PP2PPP.text:
White develops the knight to c3, adding pressure on d5.

We play the key move once again: 3...a6. 

Later we may expand on the queenside with ...b5.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to Chapter 3! 

We now cover White’s second most popular reply to 3...a6: 4.e3. 

White opens with the queen’s pawn.

We mirror with 1...d5, fighting for the center.

r1b1k2r/1pp2ppp/p1n1pq2/8/2PP4/5N2/PP3PP.text:
