We end the variation with 9...Nc6. 

The plan is to castle and put pressure on the d-pawn by playing ...Rd8. 

If White pushes d5, we simply trade first and retreat our knight to e7.

r1bqk1nr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/n7/PbpP1B2/2N1PN2/.text:
White prepares to castle.

We develop the knight to f6, controlling e4 and d5.

r1bqk2r/1pp2ppp/p3p3/n2N4/PbpP1B2/4PN2/1.text: White sees the threat and captures on d5.

r1bqk2r/1pp2ppp/p3pn2/n7/PbpP1B2/2N1PN2/.text:
White castles, and the knight is no longer pinned.

We increase pressure on c3, threatening to win another pawn with 9...Nd5.

r1bqk2r/1pp2ppp/p7/n2p4/PbpP1B2/4PN2/1P2.text:
We recapture with our e-pawn. 

White will most likely aim for the e4 pawn push in the future.

Our plan is to castle, put the rook on e8, and push ...b5 to support the pawn on c4.

With a pawn up and space advantage on the queenside, we have a great position.

r1bqkb1r/1p3ppp/p1n1pn2/2pP4/2P5/2N2N2/P.text:
White pushes their d-pawn with tempo on our knight. 

We capture on d5 first before advancing our knight to b4.

r1bqkb1r/1p3ppp/p1n2n2/2pP4/8/2N2N2/PP3P.text:
White recaptures, and our knight must move. 

We jump to b4, escaping danger and attacking the d5-pawn.

r1bqkb1r/1p3ppp/p4n2/2pP4/1nB5/2N2N2/PP3.text: White develops their light-squared bishop to c4, defending d5 and getting ready to castle.

r1bqkb1r/5ppp/p4n2/1ppP4/1nB5/2N2N2/PP3P.text:
But our typical move ... b5 gives us a better position. 

We have to be careful a little bit since our king isn't safe yet, but a quick ...Be7 and castling is good for us.

r1bqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p1n1p3/8/P1pP1B2/2N1P3/.text:
White opens the light-squared bishop's diagonal and attacks c4.

A knight on the rim is often bad, but here it’s perfect, White will struggle to attack our c4-pawn once we place our knight on a5.

r1bqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/n7/P1pP1B2/2N1PN2/.text:
White develops the knight.

We place our dark-squared bishop on its typical active square in this variation, b4, pinning the knight on c3.

r2qk1nr/2p2ppp/p1n1p3/3b4/PpNP1P2/8/NP3P.text:
We end the variation by developing the knight.

The plan is to play ...Nh6-f5 and castle. 

The d4-pawn is under pressure, and the bishop on f1 cannot be developed so easily since g2 is hanging. 

The knight on a2 is placed very poorly. If White attacks the pawn, just defend with ...a5.

r3k1nr/1bB2ppp/p3p3/8/1pP5/4PN2/5PPP/3RK.text:
White recaptures.

With two passed pawns, simplifying is perfectly fine for us, so we trade more pieces with 15...Bxf3.

r3k1nr/1bB2ppp/pn2p3/8/1pB5/1P2PN2/5PPP/.text:
White takes the free pawn. 

We take the bishop on c4 as planned.

r3k1nr/1bp2ppp/p3p3/2n5/PpB2B2/4PN2/1P3P.text:
White can finally take the c-pawn now that g2 isn’t hanging… 

But now a4 is free for us to capture.

r3k1nr/1bp2ppp/p3p3/8/npB2B2/1P2PN2/5PPP.text:
White reinforces the c4-bishop and attacks our knight.

We retreat the knight to b6. 

If allowed, we’ll take on c4 and get a passed b-pawn.

r3k1nr/1bpn1ppp/p3p3/2P5/Ppp2B2/4PN2/1P3.text:
White develops the knight.

If Bxc7, we simply take on c5.

We capture on c5 anyway.

r3k1nr/2B2ppp/p3p3/8/1pP5/4PP2/5P1P/3RK2.text:
White captures.

We develop the knight to e7, from where it has better routes.

r3k2r/4np1p/3Bp1p1/p7/1pP5/4PP2/5P1P/3RK.text:
We defend the attacked pawn by pushing it to g6.

The plan is to utilize the passed pawns on b4, and a5, later supporting them with ...Nc6.

The king could be developed via playing ... f6 and ...Kf7.

r3k2r/4nppp/3Bp3/p7/1pP5/4PP2/5P1P/3RK1R.text: White activates the rook by placing it on the semi-open g-file, from where it attacks our g7-pawn.

r3k2r/4nppp/p2Bp3/8/1pP5/4PP2/5P1P/3RK2R.text:
White attacks b4.

We simply defend the passed pawn by advancing our a-pawn.

rn1qk1nr/1bp2ppp/p3p3/2P5/Ppp2B2/4P3/1P3.text:
White recaptures.

We go for a queen trade.

rn1qk1nr/2p2ppp/p2bp3/3b4/PpNP1B2/4P3/NP.text:
White finally takes the pawn… 

And we exchange White’s active dark-squared bishop.

rn1qkb1r/2p2ppp/p3pn2/3b4/P1pP1B2/1pN1PN.text:
We play 10...Nf6, developing the knight. 

With 9... b3 we have allowed the knight back in the game, but now White blocked the queen's attack on c4. 

We have a nice space advantage at our disposal on the queenside and future plans of playing ... c5.
Another plan is to play ...Nc6 and ...Na5, furthermore strengthening the pawn chain, with ...c5 coming later.

rn1qkb1r/2p2ppp/p3pn2/3b4/Pp1P1B2/1Pp1PN.text:
...but trap their own knight on a2.

We continue with normal development and we have a very good position.
 We are up a pawn and with a5 coming.  

White's position is very hard to untangle.

rn1qkbnr/1bp2ppp/p3p3/2N5/PppP1B2/4P3/1P.text:
White attacks our bishop.

We capture the strong knight - there's no better use for our dark-squared bishop.

rn1qkbnr/1bp2ppp/p3p3/8/PppP1B2/4PN2/NP3.text:
White plays 8.Nf3, blocking our bishop’s view of g2.

Our response is to anchor our light-squared bishop on d5, reinforcing the c4-pawn.

rn1qkbnr/2p2ppp/p3p3/3b4/P1pP1B2/1pN1PN2.text: 10.Nc3 is the only move for White.

rn1qkbnr/2p2ppp/p3p3/3b4/PppP1B2/4PN2/NP.text:
White may try to attack c4 with Rc1, but this is a mistake.

We reveal a discovered attack on the knight with 9...c3.

Another option for White is 9.Qc1, attacking our pawn.

We respond with 9...b3, attacking the knight.

rn1qkbnr/2p2ppp/p3p3/3bN3/PppP1B2/4P3/NP.text:
White's knight jumps to an active square, attacking c4.

We develop our dark-squared bishop to d6.

rn1qkbnr/2pb1ppp/p3p3/1N6/Q1pP1B2/8/PP2P.text: We can pin the knight to the queen.

rn2k1nr/1bp2ppp/p3p3/2P5/Ppp2B2/4P3/1P3P.text:
White recaptures with the rook.

We pressure c5 with 10...Nd7 - Bxc4 is impossible because of ...Bxg2.

rn2kbnr/2B2ppp/p3p3/8/b1pP4/8/PP2PPPP/R3.text: ...but we take theirs, leaving us up a piece.

rnb1k2r/1pp2ppp/p3pq2/8/1bPP4/5N2/PP1B1P.text:
White blocks. 

We’re happy to trade the dark-squared bishops - ours didn't have a better use.

rnb1k2r/2p2ppp/pp2pq2/8/2PP4/5N2/PP1Q1PP.text:
9...b6 allows for the bishop to be placed on the strong a8-h1 diagonal. 

We will castle, place the knight on d7, connect and centralize the rooks, and have a very comfortable position.

We can eventually plan the move
... c5 to challenge White's d-pawn.

rnb1kb1r/1pp2ppp/p3pq2/8/2PP4/5N2/PP3PPP.text:
White develops the knight to a natural square allowing Bg5, which would attack our queen.

We respond by developing our bishop with check, 7...Bb4+.

rnbqk2r/1pp1bppp/p3pN2/6B1/2PP4/8/PP3PPP.text:
White trades the knights.

We recapture.

rnbqk2r/1pp2ppp/p3pB2/8/2PP4/8/PP3PPP/R2.text:
White also trades dark-squared bishops, since retreating allows us to keep an active bishop on f6.

We recapture with the queen. 

Without dark-squared bishops on the board, we no longer have to fear any attack on our queen.

rnbqkb1r/1p3ppp/p3pn2/2p5/2PP4/2N2N2/PP3.text:
White defends the pawn. 

We develop the knight to c6, attacking d4.

rnbqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p3pN2/8/2PP4/8/PP3PPP/R.text:
White usually trades knights, retreating only wastes time.

We recapture on f6 with the queen, which now sits well on f6, where it cannot be challenged.

rnbqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p3pn2/6B1/2PPN3/8/PP3PP.text:
Instead of retreating, White pins the knight to our queen.

We break the pin by developing our dark-squared bishop to e7, and now the knight on e4 is hanging.

rnbqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p3pn2/8/2PP4/2N5/PP3PPP.text:
White may choose to retreat the knight.

The thematic ...c5 is excellent here, targeting d4 and undermining White’s center. 

If White advances, we capture, develop the dark-squared bishop, and castle.

rnbqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/3p4/2PP1B2/2N5/PP2.text:
White immediately develops the bishop to f4 - similar to a London setup, avoiding the issue of the bishop being stuck on c1. 

We simply take on c4, the most reliable counterplay in the position.

rnbqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/3p4/2PPP3/2N5/PP3P.text:
Another option is 4.e4, a very confrontational move. 

White tries to seize central control, but 4.e4 causes no real problems for Black.

We take immediately to prevent any expansion that could lead to a passive position.

rnbqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/8/2PPN3/8/PP3PPP/R.text:
White recaptures.

We challenge the centralized knight as it is unprotected.

rnbqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/8/2pP1B2/2N1P3/PP3.text:
5.e3 is White’s best and only try to avoid permanently losing the c4-pawn. 

We play 5...b4, reinforcing c4.

rnbqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/8/P1pP1B2/2N5/1P2P.text:
White tries to stop ...b5 with 5.a4, but this is not a good approach. 

They should play e3 first. 

Our plan is to put the knight on a5 to defend the c4-pawn, so 5...Nc6 is our move. 

Usually White defends with 6.e3, because that puts pressure on c4. 

If 6.Nf3, we play ...Bb4 first and then ...Na5.

rnbqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/8/Q1pP1B2/2N5/PP2P.text: White is trying to pick up the pawn on c4 next...

rnbqkbnr/2p2ppp/p3p3/1N6/Q1pP1B2/8/PP2PP.text:
White's point is that they can capture on b5 with the knight since the rook on a8 is hanging. 

This is a mistake.

rnbqkbnr/2p2ppp/p3p3/1p6/P1pP1B2/2N1P3/1.text:
White plays 6.a4, trying to break our queenside chain.

6...b4 is a typical response to a4 in the 3...a6 QGD: we gain space and hit the knight. 

Next, ...Bb7 stops White from taking on c4 because g2 would be hanging.

rnbqkbnr/2p2ppp/p3p3/8/PppP1B2/4P3/NP3PP.text:
The first knight retreat is 7.Na2.

After 7...Bb7 our bishop eyes g2. 

White cannot capture on c4 immediately - ...Bxg2 wins the exchange.

rnbqkbnr/2p2ppp/p3p3/8/PppPNB2/4P3/1P3PP.text:
The last knight move for White is 7.Ne4.

We continue with a light-squared bishop fianchetto, developing a piece and attacking the e4-knight.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
The Queen’s Gambit appears.

We decline it with 2...e6, supporting our d-pawn and opening the diagonal for our dark-squared bishop.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/2PP4/2N5/PP2PPP.text:
White develops the queenside knight, fighting for the center. 

We respond with 3...a6, preparing ...b5.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to the second lesson of this chapter! Here we examine White’s less popular reply to 3...a6: 4.Bf4. After that, we’ll also look at 4.e4. 

White begins with the queen’s pawn.

We mirror with 1...d5.

1n1qkb1r/1rp2ppp/p3pn2/1P2N3/2pP4/2N3P1/.text:
White exchanges again to open the a-file for the rook.

We recapture the pawn.

1n1qkb1r/rBp2ppp/p3pn2/1p2N3/P1pP4/2N3P1.text:
White trades. 

We recapture, also reinforcing the b-pawn.

1nbqkb1r/r1p2ppp/p3pn2/1p2N3/P1pP4/2N3P1.text:
White challenges our queenside pawns with 8.a4.

We fianchetto our light-squared bishop, attacking White's.

Rn1q1rk1/1rp2ppp/4pn2/1p2N3/1bpP4/2N3P1/.text:
We castle as well. 

In this position, we are up a pawn. White will most likely develop their bishop to g5.

In that case, we can even retreat with the bishop to e7 and prepare ...Nd5 and ...c5 with pressure on the queenside.

Rn1qkb1r/1rp2ppp/4pn2/1p2N3/2pP4/2N3P1/1.text:
White tries to activate the rook. 

We must get our king to safety quickly, so we develop the bishop and prepare to castle.

r1bqk2r/1p1n1ppp/p3pn2/2b5/2Q5/2N2NP1/PP.text:
White develops the knight to a natural square. 

Now that the knight blocks the bishop's vision, we play our typical ...b5 plan.

r1bqk2r/3n1ppp/p3pn2/1pb5/7Q/2N2NP1/PP2P.text:
White brings the queen toward the kingside.

We place our bishop on b7, countering White’s Catalan bishop.

r1bqkb1r/1p1n1ppp/p3pn2/2P5/2Q5/2N3P1/PP.text:
White trades. 

We recapture with the bishop, enabling castling.

r1bqkb1r/1ppn1ppp/p3pn2/8/2QP4/2N3P1/PP2.text:
White captures the pawn.

We strike back in the center with 7...c5. 

Both ...c5 and ...b5 are thematic for Black in this structure.

r2q1rk1/1b1n1ppp/p3pn2/1pb5/7Q/2N2NP1/PP.text:
We also castle. 

The plan is to put the rooks on d8 and c8 and attack on the queenside. 

We might anticipate a kingside attack from White. 

With active pieces and space on the queenside, we have a comfortable position.

rn1qk1nr/2p2ppp/p1b1p3/8/2pP4/6P1/PP1QPP.text:
And now we trade off White's strong bishop to save our rook. 

We are up a knight.

rn1qk1nr/2p2ppp/p3p3/1b6/1bpP4/6P1/PPQBP.text:
White blocks. 

We trade as planned.

rn1qkb1r/1bp2ppp/p3pn2/1p6/2pP4/2N2NP1/P.text: That allows for our bishop to be developed nicely, opposing White's bishop on g2.

rn1qkbnr/2p2ppp/p3p3/1b6/2pP4/6P1/PPQ1PP.text:
White retreats.

When ahead in material, trading pieces is always a good idea, so we give an in-between check with our dark-squared bishop, aiming to trade it for White’s before moving our rook out of danger.

rn1qkbnr/2pb1ppp/p3p3/1N6/Q1pP4/6P1/PP2P.text:
White tries to intensify the threat by attacking the a8-rook. 

But we simply capture the knight with tempo on the queen.

rnbqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p3pn2/8/2pP4/2N2NP1/PP2.text:
White may choose to develop their knight instead. 

But now the bishop on g2 is blocked, allowing us to push the b-pawn and protect the c-pawn.

rnbqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p3pn2/8/Q1pP4/2N3P1/PP2.text:
White goes after the c4-pawn with the queen. 

Note that 6...b5 doesn’t work here because the a8-rook hangs. 

We block the check with the knight; otherwise, b7 would be hanging.

rnbqkb1r/2p2ppp/p3pn2/1p2N3/2pP4/2N3P1/P.text:
White centralizes the knight and attacks our rook.

We move out of the attack, 7...Ra7 is our move.

rnbqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/3p4/2PP4/2N3P1/PP2.text:
But White can choose 4.g3, entering a Catalan-style setup. 

We keep to our theme and capture on c4.

rnbqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/8/2pP4/2N3P1/PP2PP.text:
After 5.Bg2 ...b5 is impossible... 

So we develop the knight, simultaneously controlling the central e4 and d5 squares.

rnbqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/8/Q1pP4/2N3P1/PP2P.text:
White tries to immediately recover the pawn on c4. 

But 5.Qa4+ is a blunder because the bishop is not on g2.

We block the check while also protecting c4 with 5...b5.

rnbqkbnr/2p2ppp/p3p3/1N6/Q1pP4/6P1/PP2PP.text:
White assumes they can take on b5 since the rook on a8 is hanging… 

But we now pin the knight to the queen.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
The Queen’s Gambit appears. 

This is a very solid way to begin the game. 

With 2...e6 we support d5, open the f8-bishop, and prepare our a6 setup.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/2PP4/2N5/PP2PPP.text:
White continues developing.

We play 3...a6, with the usual plan of ...dxc4 followed by ...b5.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to the third lesson of the third chapter of the a6 Queen’s Gambit Declined!

In this study, we examine the move 4.g3 for White. 

White begins with the Queen’s Pawn opening.

We mirror with our own.

r1b1k2r/1p3ppp/p1nqpn2/8/P1Pp4/4P3/1P3PP.text:
But we can develop and support the pawn. Notice our superior development. 

If exd4, ...Nxd4 and we've got ...Qb4+ for ...Qxb2 ideas.

r1b1kbnr/1pq2ppp/p1n5/3Q4/P7/2N5/1P2PPPP.text:
But we've got multiple moves to attack the queen. 

Our development is better and after ...Be6, ...Nf6, ...Bb4 to pin the c3-knight, we'll have a better middlegame and enough compensation for the pawn.

r1bqkb1r/1p3ppp/p1n1pn2/2pp4/P1PP4/2N1PN.text: We have this 4 knights position with tension between the c- and d-pawns just like in the 3. Nf3 lines.

r1bqkbnr/1p3ppp/p1n1p3/3P4/P7/2N1Q3/1P2P.text:
White may also try the “clever-looking” 7.Qe3, trying to pin the e-pawn.

But 7...Nb4 wins on the spot - we’re threatening a fork.

r1bqkbnr/1p3ppp/p1n1p3/3P4/P7/2N5/1P2PPP.text:
7.Qd1 is the most natural and popular retreat.

But we simply capture on d5. 

It may look like White will emerge a pawn up, but if they recapture with the knight, …Be6 gives Black a clear advantage.

r1bqkbnr/1p3ppp/p1n5/3Q4/P7/2N5/1P2PPPP/.text: The queen moves yet again to recapture.

r1bqkbnr/1p3ppp/p3p3/3P4/Pn6/2N5/1P1QPPP.text:
Once the queen moves again, we have enough pressure to win back the pawn.

White won’t even keep extra material for their poor position.

We take on d5, and …d4 next becomes a strong threat that White cannot easily stop.

If 9.e4, then 9...Nf6 increases the pressure, with …Bf5 coming once the pawn leaves e4 after something like exd5.

r1bqkbnr/1p3ppp/p7/3p4/Pn6/2N1P3/1P1Q1PP.text: If 9. e3 to control the d4-square, White cannot stop Black's other idea.

r2qkbnr/1p3ppp/p7/3p1b2/Pn6/2N1P3/1P1Q1P.text:
9...Bf5 adds another attacker to the c2-square.

...Nc2+ is coming. 

Kd1 is one of the best moves given by the engine, but it's already -6.

rnb1k2r/1p3ppp/p2qpn2/8/P1Pp4/4P3/1P3PPP.text: White may try to undermine the pawn.

rnb1kb1r/1p3ppp/4pq2/p1P5/PPPp4/8/4PPPP/.text:
But 8...a5 undermines the pawn chain and the defense of c5. 

White won't be able to hold on to c5. 

We're going to take on b4 and then win c5. 

We should be better because of our strong d-pawn.

rnb1kb1r/1p3ppp/p3pq2/2P5/PPPp4/8/4PPPP/.text: 8. b4 defends for one more turn.

rnbqk2r/1p3ppp/p2Ppn2/8/P1Pp4/8/1P2PPPP/.text:
The pawn recaptures…

But we take it back immediately, and our dominant d-pawn remains the strongest force in the position.

rnbqkb1r/1p3ppp/p2Npn2/2P5/P1Pp4/8/1P2PP.text:
White can try this check, but it isn’t challenging at all.

We take White’s only developed piece, recapture the pawn, and keep our knight developed on f6 - a win-win for Black.

rnbqkb1r/1p3ppp/p3pN2/2P5/P1Pp4/8/1P2PPP.text:
If this trade occurs...

We gain full control of d4 and our queen develops in the process. 

We’re also threatening to take on c5, which White cannot realistically prevent.

rnbqkb1r/1p3ppp/p3pn2/2pp4/P1PP4/2N1PN2/.text: And after White develops their knight...

rnbqkbnr/1p3ppp/p3p3/2P5/P1PpN3/8/1P2PPP.text:
White may jump into the center.

But we challenge the knight right away with ours, 6...Nf6 is our move. 

If White trades, we simply activate our queen.

rnbqkbnr/1p3ppp/p3p3/2Pp4/P1P5/2N5/1P2PP.text:
White may insert this capture, but it’s never good - because we immediately gain control of the d4-square.

Our pawn push, 5...d4, becomes very strong, dislodging the knight from its best square. 

White’s knight choices here are unpleasant.

rnbqkbnr/1p3ppp/p3p3/2pP4/P2P4/2N5/1P2PP.text:
If White plays 5.cxd5, this does not transpose back to our earlier chapters - but that’s fine, because the capture is simply bad for White!

We gain a tempo on the knight by taking on d5 first. 

If White recaptures with the queen, we gain yet another tempo hitting the queen.

rnbqkbnr/1p3ppp/p3p3/2pp4/P1PP4/2N1P3/1P.text:
5. e3 will also transpose to the 3. Nf3 lines.

We simply develop the kingside knight to f6.

rnbqkbnr/1p3ppp/p3p3/2pp4/P1PP4/2N2N2/1P.text: If this knight is brought out at move 5, we can transpose.

rnbqkbnr/1p3ppp/p3p3/3P4/P2Q4/2N5/1P2PPP.text:
When the queen captures on d4...

We develop with tempo. 

The pawn is pinned, so the queen must move again.

rnbqkbnr/1p3ppp/p3p3/3p4/P1Pp4/2N2N2/1P2.text:
This transposes to the 2 knights with 4. a4 and we've got ...e5 coming up. 

This is found in the 4. a4 study after 3. Nf3.

rnbqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/3p4/P1PP4/2N5/1P2P.text:
The difference now is the immediate 4.a4.

Nevertheless, we strike back right away with …c5. 

The point is simple: we undermine the center the moment White wastes time with a4.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White continues with the Queen’s Gambit. 

We are ready for this and go for the Queen’s Gambit Declined.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/2PP4/2N5/PP2PPP.text:
This line can transpose into the 3.Nf3 variations with an early 4.a4, but there are still some unique positions that may arise. 

We play 3...a6 here as well, just like in earlier studies.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to this new study, which I’m adding post-launch based on the 7th most popular move after 3...a6: 4.a4. 

The idea is to stop any …b5 ideas.

However, as you’ll see, 4.a4 gives up the b5-square and is actually premature - White falls behind in development trying to prevent 
…b5.

White begins with the queen’s pawn.

We respond symmetrically.

1n1qk2r/2p1bppp/2b1pn2/8/1p1P4/5NP1/2Q1P.text:
The plan is to castle.

We are up a pawn. 

...Bb5 and ...c6 might be played later in order to activate the pieces on the queenside.

1r2kbnr/1b3ppp/pq2p3/1p6/2pP4/6P1/PP2PPB.text:
We end the variation with 9...Bb7, challenging the defender of White's camp. 

Next, we finish up development on the kingside and castle.

1rb1kbnr/5ppp/pq2p3/1p6/2pP4/6P1/PP2PPBP.text:
White castles. 

Of course, if Bf4, we would have played ...Bd6 and not much would have changed.

2kr1bnr/1ppb1ppp/pq2p3/8/2QP4/6P1/PP2PPB.text:
We now castle queenside. 

Black develops very fast here. 

...Nf6, ...Bb5 coming quickly with pressure on d4. 

White's king is also still in the center and we might try to open up the position.

Bn1q1rk1/4bppp/4pn2/1p2N3/2pP4/6P1/1P2PP.text:
But we can just castle and have a completely safe position, with some more queenside space. 

Pressure d4, finish up your development, and you'll be great.

Bn1qk2r/4bppp/4pn2/1p2N3/2pP4/6P1/1P2PP1.text: The point is revealed - White recovers the piece, reaching material equality.

Bn2kb1r/5ppp/4pn2/qp2N3/2pP4/6P1/1P2PP1P.text: ...but ...Qa5+ picks up the piece since White hasn't castled yet.

Rn1qkb1r/1bp2ppp/4pn2/1p6/2pP4/5NP1/1P2P.text:
White trades the rooks.

We take back.

bn1qk2r/4bppp/2p1pn2/1N2N3/2pP4/6P1/1P2P.text:
Capturing on b5.

We recapture, and then…

bn1qkb1r/2p2ppp/4pn2/1p6/2pP4/1P3NP1/4PP.text:
White tries to disrupt our pawn chain with 10...b3.

We don’t want to leave tension on our c4-pawn, so our standard answer to b3 in this chapter is simply to capture on b3.

bn1qkb1r/2p2ppp/4pn2/1p6/2pP4/5NP1/1PQ1P.text:
Recapturing. 

This is a typical position, which may arise a lot of the time. 

We develop with ...Be7 and ...Nd7. 

If b3, we can play ...cxb3 and push ...b4. 

There are also plans of exchanging our light-squared bishop for either the knight on f3 or bishop on g2 with ...c6 coming later.

bn1qkb1r/2p2ppp/4pn2/1p6/3P4/1Q3NP1/4PPB.text:
White recaptures, and the b5-pawn is now attacked.

We push it to b4, from where it's defended by our dark-squared bishop.

bn1qkb1r/2p2ppp/4pn2/8/Qp1P4/5NP1/4PPBP/.text:
White creates a double attack on our bishop and king with 12.Qa4+.

We defend with tempo, 12...Bc6 is our move.

bn1qkb1r/5ppp/2p1pn2/1N2N3/2pP4/6P1/1P2P.text:
If White impatiently grabs the b5-pawn, it’s a blunder. 

We simply capture the knight.

bn1qkb1r/5ppp/2p1pn2/1p2N3/2pP4/2N3P1/1P.text:
White castles.

We also prepare castling with 11...Be7.

But White has one final trick…

bn1qkbnr/5ppp/2p1p3/1p2N3/2pP4/2N3P1/1P2.text:
The knight now “threatens” to take on b5, which would win our a8-bishop, but the threat isn’t real.

We can safely ignore Nxb5 and continue developing with 10...Nf6.

r1b1kbnr/1pp2ppp/p1N1p3/3q4/2pP4/6P1/PP2.text:
White moves the rook.

Now we recapture the knight. 

This queen maneuver avoids tripling our pawns on the c-file - a sound structural decision.

r1b1kbnr/1pp2ppp/p1q1p3/8/2pP4/6P1/PP2PP.text:
White develops the bishop and attacks our queen.

We place it on b6. 

Notice how poor the rook on g1 is.

The real question is: where will White castle?

r1b1kbnr/1pp2ppp/pq2p3/8/Q1pP4/6P1/PP2PP.text:
White wants to take the pawn on c4 by giving a check with the queen. 

We develop and block the check.

r1bqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p1N1p3/8/2pP4/6P1/PP2PP.text:
White trades knights. 

If instead White had captured on c4, we had ...Qd5, forking h1 and c4 and winning on the spot.

We don’t want to ruin our pawn structure by recapturing with the b-pawn, so we first attack the h1-rook with our queen.

r2qkbnr/1bpn1ppp/p3p3/1p6/P1pP4/2N2NP1/1.text: Once again, White plays the typical a4.

r2qkbnr/1bpn1ppp/p3p3/8/PppP4/2N2NP1/1P2.text:
After 8...b4 White's knight doesn't have many squares to move to and will be placed very awkwardly. 

With ...c5, ...Nf6, ...Be7, and castling coming we have a great position. 

We might play ...a5 to strengthen the pawn on b4.

rNb1kbnr/5ppp/pq2p3/1p6/2pP4/6P1/PP2PPBP.text:
White trades knights - there’s really nothing else, otherwise we play ...Bb7 next.

We recapture with the rook since it was under attack.

rn1qkb1r/1bp2ppp/p3pn2/1P6/2pP4/5NP1/1P2.text:
White immediately releases the tension by taking on b5.

We recapture.

rn1qkb1r/1bp2ppp/p3pn2/1P6/2pP4/5NP1/1PQ.text:
White trades to open up their rook.

We recapture.

rn1qkb1r/1bp2ppp/pp2pn2/8/P1pP4/5NP1/1PQ.text:
White attacks the c4-pawn with the queen.

But after ...Bb7, we can defend c4 with 8...b5 - the a8-rook is covered.

rn1qkbnr/1b3ppp/p1p1p3/1P2N3/2pP4/6P1/1P.text:
Once again, White trades on the queenside.

We recapture with the a-pawn.

rn1qkbnr/1bp2ppp/p3p3/1p6/2pP4/2N2NP1/PP.text:
White focuses on development first. 

We play 7...Nd7, from where it supports the upcoming …c5 break.

rn1qkbnr/1bp2ppp/p3p3/1p6/P1pP4/1P3NP1/4.text: White pressures the c- and b-pawns and frees up the b2-square for the bishop.

rn1qkbnr/1bp2ppp/p3p3/1p6/P1pP4/5NP1/1P2.text:
White uses the typical a4 push to pressure our queenside. 

We place the knight on the f6 square, eyeing e4 and d5.
...Bb7 also defends the rook on a8 in case of axb5.

rn1qkbnr/1bp2ppp/p3p3/1p6/P2P4/1p3NP1/4P.text: Our usual response is to take on b3 when this pawn tension arises.

rn1qkbnr/1bp2ppp/p3p3/8/Pp1P4/1Q3NP1/4PP.text:
And as in many similar lines, ...b4 is played to protect the pawn and gain some space on the queenside.

We are up a pawn and the plan is to play ... Nf6, ... Be7, ... Nbd7, and castle.

rn1qkbnr/1bp2ppp/pp2p3/8/P1pP4/5NP1/1P2P.text:
White castles. 

We place our kingisde knight on its best square, f6.

rnbqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/3p4/2PP4/5NP1/PP2P.text:
White goes for the Catalan system with g3. 

Staying true to our theme, we take on c4 and aim for ...b5.

rnbqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/4N3/2pP4/6P1/PP2PP.text:
5.Ne5 tries to win the pawn immediately, but it’s simply a mistake!

5…Nc6 challenges the centralized knight. 

Keep an eye on ...Qd5 next!

rnbqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/8/2pP4/5NP1/PP2PPB.text:
White places the bishop on g2. 

As usual, we follow up with the key move of the variation: 5...b5.

rnbqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/8/P1pP4/5NP1/1P2PP.text:
White tries to stop our ...b5 idea.

Since we can’t push the b-pawn, we play ...b6 and prepare ...Bb7.

rnbqkbnr/2p2ppp/p3p3/1p2N3/2pP4/6P1/PP2P.text:
White jumps to e5, with a discovered attack on our rook.

We simply block it with a move that appears to lose a pawn, 6...c6.

After 6...c6, White should react energetically with either Bxc6 or 7.a4. If they castle instead, we’ll develop the light-squared bishop, complete kingside development, and castle safely.

rnbqkbnr/2p2ppp/p3p3/1p6/2pP4/5NP1/PP2PP.text:
White chooses to castle instead- this isn’t the best way to play.

We respond with a natural move, challenging White’s strong bishop on g2 with our own.

rnbqkbnr/2p2ppp/p3p3/1p6/P1pP4/5NP1/1P2P.text: A sensible move. Yet again utilizing the a4 plan.

rnbqkbnr/2p2ppp/pp2p3/8/P1pP4/5NP1/1P2PP.text:
White develops the bishop.

We oppose the strong g2-bishop with our own.

rnbqkbnr/5ppp/p1N1p3/1p6/2pP4/6P1/PP2PPB.text:
White grabs the pawn. 

The position may look dangerous for us, but there are no real problems. 

Our queen was hit, yet after 7...Qb6 White’s knight is hanging.

rnbqkbnr/5ppp/p1p1p3/1p2N3/P1pP4/6P1/1P2.text:
White often repeats the same ideas in different positions, and usually the resulting structures remain similar.

We respond by developing our bishop to its typical square in this variation, 7...Bb7.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
The Queen’s Gambit appears. 

We support d5 with 2...e6, opening the dark-squared bishop.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/2PP4/5N2/PP2PPP.text:
White develops the kingside knight first. 

We prepare our ...b5 setup with our typical 3...a6.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to Chapter 4! Here we look at White’s setup with 3.Nf3, specifically when they choose the Catalan lines with g3. 

White starts with 1.d4.

We mirror by bringing our own d-pawn to the center.

rn1qk2r/1b3ppp/p3pn2/2b5/Pp6/3BPN2/1P3PP.text:
a4 is always met by ...b4 in this setup.

The development plan for us is very simple. 

We will castle, play ...Nbd7, and place the rooks on d8 and c8.

rnbqk2r/5ppp/p3pn2/1pb5/8/3BPN2/PP3PPP/R.text:
White castles. 

We develop our light-squared bishop to its ideal square, b7.

rnbqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p3pn2/3p4/2PP4/3BPN2/PP.text:
Only after White develops the bishop...

We take the pawn on c4.

rnbqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p3pn2/8/2BP4/4PN2/PP3PP.text:
White recaptures.

We play the desired 6…b5 with tempo.

rnbqkb1r/2p2ppp/p3pn2/1p6/3P4/3BPN2/PP3P.text:
White retreats.

The QGD light-squared bishop - usually a problem piece for us - won’t bother us here.

With 7...c5, using the support of our earlier ...b5, we strongly undermine White’s center.

rnbqkb1r/5ppp/p3pn2/1p6/3N4/3BP3/PP3PPP/.text:
If White takes on d4 with the knight... 

It can be attacked with 9...e5.

rnbqkb1r/5ppp/p3pn2/1pP5/8/3BPN2/PP3PPP/.text:
White captures on c5, a common idea. 

They do this to avoid …cxd4 followed by exd4 (creating an IQP), and to avoid …cxd4 Nxd4, where the knight can later be hit by …e5.

We recapture on c5 with the bishop.

rnbqkb1r/5ppp/p3pn2/1pp5/3P4/3BPN2/PP3PP.text:
Let’s say White castles in this position…

We simply take on d4.

rnbqkb1r/5ppp/p4n2/1p2p3/8/3BPN2/PP3PPP/.text: And White cannot go back to the knight's ideal square because of a fork.

rnbqkb1r/5ppp/p4n2/1p6/4p3/3BPN2/PP3PPP/.text: Therefore, many players just capture on c5 when they can.

rnbqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/3p4/2PP4/4PN2/PP3P.text:
4.e3 is a very non-specific move and often transposes into well-known lines. 

Our plans remain the same: take on c4, advance with …b5, and prepare …c5.

We first develop naturally with 4...Nf6 - we don’t want to take on c4 yet and help White develop with Bxc4.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White plays the Queen’s Gambit. 

We reinforce d5.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/2PP4/5N2/PP2PPP.text:
White develops the kingside knight first.

We go for step one of our setup, 3...a6.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to the second lesson of Chapter 4! 

In this study we cover White’s setup with 4.e3, which usually transposes into positions from previous chapters. 

White prepares a standard QGD structure.

We also bring our central pawn into play.

rnb1k1nr/1pp1qppp/p3p3/3P4/3P4/5N2/PP2PP.text:
White takes on d5, preventing any …dxc4 …b5 ideas. 

We recapture, and the upside is that our light-squared bishop now has a clear development route.

rnb1k1nr/1pp1qppp/p7/3p4/3P4/2N2N2/PP2PP.text: White develops the knight with an attack on the d5 pawn.

rnb1k2r/1pp1qppp/p4n2/3p4/3P4/2N2N2/PP2P.text:
We continue by placing the knight on a natural square, 7...Nf6, defending the pawn. 

The next steps are to castle, play 
...Nbd7, activate the bishop via ...Bf5 and centralize the rooks. 

The pawn on d5 will be supported with ...c6.

rnbqk1nr/1pp1Bppp/p3p3/3p4/2PP4/5N2/PP2P.text:
White captures - there’s no benefit in retreating.

We recapture with the queen, keeping the …Nf6 development available. 

This position also appeared in Chapter 1, though by a different move order.

rnbqk1nr/5ppp/pP2p3/2bp4/8/5N2/PP2PPPP/R.text:
...allowing for the dark-squared bishop to be developed.

We will recapture the pawn on b6, and develop very logically with ... Nf6 and ... Nc6.

 With a slight lead in development, we have a great position. Our open lines on the queenside will also give us great attacking chances.

rnbqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/2Pp4/3P4/5N2/PP2PP.text:
White plays 4.c5, a very uncommon move, but still possible.

The idea is to slow down …b5 and …c5. 

Although it may look annoying, 4.c5 poses no real threat. 

The advanced pawn is easily targeted with 4…b6.

So that's what we play, immediately threatening the pawn.

rnbqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/3p2B1/2PP4/5N2/PP2.text:
White develops the dark-squared bishop immediately, attacking our queen. 

We don’t mind trading off this bishop and offer the exchange with 4...Be7.

rnbqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/3p4/2PP1B2/5N2/PP2.text:
Another choice for White is 4.Bf4. 

This is very similar to Chapter 1 after we take on c4, just without the knight on c3. 

4.Bf4 doesn't serve White any deeper purpose and will likely transpose once again. 

The ideas of ...dxc4, ...b5, developing with ...Nf6 still remain.

rnbqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/8/2pP1B2/5N2/PP2PP.text:
Just remember the chapter 1 ideas.

If a4, for instance, ...Nc6 for ...Na5 is our idea.

rnbqkbnr/2p2ppp/1p2p3/2Pp4/1p1P4/P4N2/4P.text: ...we win a pawn since the rook on a1 is hanging.

rnbqkbnr/2p2ppp/1p2p3/p1Pp4/1P1P4/P4N2/4.text: If White tries to protect the pawn on b4...

rnbqkbnr/2p2ppp/pP2p3/3p4/3P4/5N2/PP2PPP.text:
White doesn't want to lose the pawn, so they capture it.

But that doesn’t stop us from playing 5…c5. 

Notice how the c5 push has weakened White’s queenside. 

With their structure undermined, we get excellent queenside play.

rnbqkbnr/2p2ppp/pp2p3/2Pp4/1P1P4/5N2/P3P.text:
White tries to protect c5 with 5.b4, but this is a bad move.

After 5…a5, White has a serious problem: the b4-pawn is hanging, and the defense of c5 collapses.

rnbqkbnr/5ppp/pP2p3/2Pp4/8/5N2/PP2PPPP/R.text: White decides to take it again...

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White plays the Queen’s Gambit. 

We choose one of the most reliable defenses and support the center.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/2PP4/5N2/PP2PPP.text:
White keeps things flexible with 3.Nf3 - many setups are still possible. 

We continue with our plan and play 3...a6.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to the third lesson of this chapter! 

Here we look at the only unique move order from White that we haven’t seen before: developing the dark-squared bishop before e3 or Nc3.

White begins with the Queen’s Pawn opening.

We mirror.

r1bq1rk1/1p2bpp1/p1n2n1p/2pp4/P2P1B2/2N2.text:
In this case we'll castle as well. 

Next we develop the rest of our pieces and stabilize our center.

r1bq1rk1/1p2bppp/p1n1pn2/2pp4/P1PP4/2N1P.text:
And we castle too. 

We have ideas of ...b6 and ...Bb7, going for development. 

Our rook is coming to e8 and if d5 is ever taken we'll recapture with the pawn.

r1bqk1nr/1p4pp/p1n5/4pp2/PbP5/3pPNN1/1P1.text:
Which allows us to advance 11...d3. 

Now, if Bxb4, ...Nxb4 and the d3-pawn is defended by the knight. 

We have ideas of ...e4 to reinforce the d3-pawn, normal developing moves like ...Nf6 and ...Qe7. We have more space and are restricting White's movement.

r1bqk1nr/1p4pp/p1n5/4pp2/PbPp4/4PNN1/1P1.text: After the bishop blocks, the queen no longer works to control d3.

r1bqk2r/1p2bpp1/p1n2n1p/2pp4/P2P1B2/2N2N.text: White could develop their bishop, refusing to take on c5.

r1bqkb1r/1p3pp1/p1n2n1p/2pp4/P2P4/2N2NP1.text:
White may also choose to ignore the c5-pawn and castle.

In that case, development is the name of the game. 

If there’s nothing better to do, we keep developing with 9...Be7.

Taking on d4 now brings no structural or dynamic benefit, so we improve our pieces. 

Whenever White captures on c5, we recapture with the bishop and castle.

r1bqkb1r/1p3ppp/p1n1pn2/2pp4/P1PP4/2N1PN.text:
The simple developing move preparing castling is normal and not challenging. 

We mirror and get ready to castle as well.

r1bqkbnr/1p3ppp/p1n1p3/3p4/P1P5/2N2N2/1P.text:
The queen is forced all the way back, which is terrible for White’s development.

The best way to challenge White’s setup is to push in the center with 7...d4; it becomes very hard for White to defend. 

8.Na2 is one of their better moves.

r1bqkbnr/1p3ppp/p1n1p3/8/P1PpN3/5N2/1P2P.text:
The knight may try e4, but centralized knights can be pushed around. 

With 8…f5 we control e4 and kick it away.

r1bqkbnr/1p4pp/p1n1p3/5p2/P1Pp4/5NN1/1P2.text:
The knight jumps to g3, looking safe - but now we switch gears.

We play 9...e5, with ideas of …e4.

r1bqkbnr/1p4pp/p1n5/4pp2/P1Pp4/4PNN1/1P3.text:
10.e3 is the only way White can develop the light-squared bishop. 

But it allows check on b4.

r2qk2r/1p2bppp/p1n5/3Pp3/P1P5/8/1PQ2PPP/.text: This pawn push, for example, allows us a great knight outpost.

r2qk2r/1p2bppp/p7/3Pp3/P1Pn4/8/1PQ2PPP/R.text:
We have ideas of ...Bb4 if Qc3 or Qd2, so White has to be careful not to lose their queen. 

If Qd3, moves like ...b5 are good to open up the position. 

If there's a rook trade on a8, the queen will become active on the a-file.

r2qk2r/1p3ppp/p1n1bn2/2b3B1/P2P4/2N2N2/1.text:
After the trade...

We recapture with the knight to preserve our bishop.

r2qk2r/1p3ppp/p1n1bn2/2bp2B1/P7/2N1PN2/1.text:
For example, if the standard 10.Rc1 is played…

10…d4 is simply better for Black, both dynamically and structurally.

Structurally, we eliminate our biggest weakness; dynamically, the position opens and White may not be ready.

r2qk2r/1p3ppp/p3bn2/6B1/P2b4/2N5/1P3PPP/.text:
...and we have to recapture as well. 

If a natural move like Bd3, we can capture on c3 with check (...Bxc3), followed by ...Qd5, forking g2 and the bishop on g5.

r2qkb1r/1p3p2/p1n1b2p/2p3p1/P2Pp3/4PNB1/.text:
We get a lot of pressure on the d4-pawn. 

It will be rather hard for White to keep the pawn structure intact. 

...cxd4 will be our next move no matter what.

r2qkb1r/1p3p2/p1n1b2p/2pp2p1/P2PN3/4PNB1.text: If White chooses to trade the knight off...

r2qkb1r/1p3p2/p1n1bn1p/2pp2p1/P2P4/2N1PN.text:
And once it reaches g3, it becomes quite a strong piece - so trading it is ideal.

We go for the trade with 11...Ne4, attacking the bishop that has nowhere to go. 

If White castles, we capture it, follow with …Bg7, and castle.

r2qkb1r/1p3pp1/p1n1bn1p/2pp4/P2P3B/2N1PN.text:
If White keeps the pin... 

We can even go 10…g5. 

It’s not always a QGD idea, but here we can afford it - we’re going straight after the dark-squared bishop, forcing it to go to g3.

r2qkb1r/1p3ppp/p1n1bn2/2pp2B1/P2P4/2N1PN.text:
White will likely develop the bishop to e2 to avoid …c4 against Bd3.

We challenge the dark-squared bishop with 9...h6. 

If White trades, we gain the bishop pair; if not, 9…h6 is useful to control g5.

r2qkbnr/1p4pp/p1n5/4pb2/P1PpNp2/5N2/1PQ1.text:
We just develop further. 

Our pawn chain is dominant and well-defended. 

We've got ideas of ...Bb4+ and ...Nf6 for quick development.

rn1qk2r/1p2bppp/p7/4p3/P1PP4/8/1PQ2PPP/R.text:
And once the queen arrives on c2...

We can even sacrifice a pawn with 12…Nc6. 

Even if White keeps a pawn, our development is superior and we gain tempi against the queen.

rn1qk2r/1p2bppp/p7/4pb2/P1PP4/8/1PN2PPP/.text:
And if White trades on d4, we don’t have to take back immediately...

We insert 11…Bxc2 first, capturing the knight and attacking the queen.

rn1qk2r/1p3ppp/p3bn2/2bp2B1/P7/2N1PN2/1P.text:
9.e3 tries to control d4 in front of the isolated pawn, but we develop and reinforce that square even more.

After 9...Nc6 we threaten to push and trade the isolated pawn, which is never good news for the side playing against it.

rn1qkb1r/1p2Nppp/p7/4pb2/P1Pp4/4P3/1PN2P.text:
So if White takes...

We recapture.

rn1qkb1r/1p3ppp/p3bn2/2Pp2B1/P7/2N2N2/1P.text:
White may think they’re giving us an IQP, but we’re not afraid of it - this actually accelerates our development.

After we recapture on c5, our bishop is out, castling is near, and …Nc6 is coming. White’s pressure on d5 isn’t significant.

rn1qkb1r/1p3ppp/p3bn2/2pp2B1/P2P4/2N1PN2.text:
Players usually play e3 after developing the bishop. 

The most natural square for our knight is c6, so that's what we play, 8...Nc6.

rn1qkbnr/1p3ppp/p7/3Npb2/P1Pp4/4P3/1PN2P.text:
You’ll often see 9.e3, challenging our pawn chain.

We go after the d5-knight with 9...Ne7. 

The idea is simple: we invite Nxe7 so we can answer with …Bxe7 and develop smoothly.

rnbqkb1r/1p3pp1/p4n1p/2pp4/P2P4/2N2NP1/1.text:
White fianchettoes. 

The bishop on g2 may add pressure on d5 once the f3-knight moves.

We simply develop our queenside knight to its best square.

rnbqkb1r/1p3ppp/p3pn2/2pp4/P1PP4/2N1PN2/.text:
White may add pressure by developing their knight to c3.

We play 6...Nc6, reaching a Four Knights setup.

White next chooses between bishop development or pawn captures.

rnbqkb1r/1p3ppp/p4n2/2pp2B1/P2P4/2N2N2/1.text:
White may try to pin our knight and undermine d5. 

But because our e6-pawn recaptured on d5, we defend comfortably with 7…Be6.

rnbqkb1r/1p3ppp/p4n2/2pp4/P2P4/2N2NP1/1P.text:
Some players may try a fianchetto with 7.g3. 

With 7...h6 we control the g5-square and prevent Bg5.

rnbqkbnr/1p3ppp/p3p3/2pP4/P2P4/5N2/1P2PP.text:
This capture is the second most popular move - but also the engine’s top choice. 

We simply recapture, opening the diagonal for our light-squared bishop.

rnbqkbnr/1p3ppp/p3p3/2pp4/P1PP4/2N2N2/1P.text:
White can go for the Two Knights setup here, but it isn’t particularly strong. 

Yes, a4 is already on the board -but so is our c5.

That’s why we can insert a favorable trade, 5...cxd4, reducing White’s central control.

rnbqkbnr/1p3ppp/p3p3/2pp4/P1PP4/4PN2/1P3.text:
White may choose to reinforce d4 with 5.e3, but this blocks their dark-squared bishop.

We usually develop the knight to f6 first in QGD positions, supporting d5.

rnbqkbnr/1p3ppp/p3p3/3p4/P1PN4/2N5/1P2PP.text:
Capturing with the knight is the most popular move.

But with the knight centralized, we attack it with 6…e5 and gain space.

Wherever the knight moves, we follow with 7...d4 and then develop normally. 

If this feels too sharp, you can simply develop and castle - just avoid the e6–e5 push.

rnbqkbnr/1p3ppp/p3p3/3p4/P1PQ4/2N2N2/1P2.text:
This move isn’t popular because the queen is unsafe on d4.

We develop and attack it, with tempo.

rnbqkbnr/1p3ppp/p7/2pp4/P2P4/2N2N2/1P2PP.text:
White may now develop the knight to c3. 

We develop our own knight to f6, supporting the d5-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/1p3ppp/p7/3Np3/P1Pp4/8/1PN1PPPP.text:
White jumps into d5 with the knight.

Our pawn structure is solid, and the d5-knight is not an issue.

We develop our bishop to f5, controlling e4.

rnbqkbnr/1p3ppp/p7/3pp3/P1P5/2N2N2/1P2PP.text:
White’s most natural reaction is to drop back to f3. 

Even so, our center is mobile, and we can bully the knights with our pawns.

With 7…d4 we destabilize the queenside knight.

rnbqkbnr/1p3ppp/p7/3pp3/P1P5/2N5/1PN1PPP.text:
White may choose 7.Nc2, but our center is mobile.

Sometimes simply pushing is strong, and so is 7...d4.

rnbqkbnr/1p3ppp/p7/4p3/P1PpN3/5N2/1P2PPP.text:
The knight may try e4, thinking it’s safer. 

Unfortunately for White, it isn’t -  next comes 8...f5!

rnbqkbnr/1p4pp/p7/4p3/P1PpNp2/5N2/1P2PPP.text:
The knight never finds a good square in this variation. 

We attack it with our bishop, developing with tempo.

rnbqkbnr/1p4pp/p7/4pp2/P1Pp4/5NN1/1P2PPP.text:
After 9.Ng3, the knight remains a target.

We push our f-pawn again, attacking it.

The good news is that our f-pawn also controls e3, discouraging White from playing their usual e3 setup.

rnbqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/3p4/P1PP4/5N2/1P2P.text:
And now comes the premature 4.a4. 

It stops …b5, but gives us the 
b4-square and doesn’t develop a piece.

That’s why I recommend the immediate 4...c5, challenging the center right away. 

White usually chooses between 5.cxd5, 5.e3, or 5.Nc3. 

If they take on c5, we recapture with the bishop and develop quickly.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White plays the Queen’s Gambit. 

We’re prepared and enter the QGD.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/2PP4/5N2/PP2PPP.text:
In this study we’ll emphasize the 3.Nf3 move order. 

Many 3.Nc3 lines are either inaccurate or simply transpose back to 3.Nf3 anyway.

We get ready to capture on c4 by playing 3...a6.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to this new study, added post-launch based on the 7th most popular move after 3...a6: 4.a4. 

The idea is to stop any …b5 plans. 

However, 4.a4 gives up the b5-square and is actually premature - White falls behind in development trying to prevent …b5.

White begins with the queen’s pawn.

We mirror with ours.

r1r3k1/pbp1qppp/n3pn2/P2p4/1b1P4/1Q3NP1/.text:
We defend once more, with ...c5 to come at the right time. 

We need to think about the b-file pressure as well, so ...Rab8 will also exert counter-pressure on the queen.

r2q1rk1/p1p1bppp/b1n1pn2/P1Pp4/1p1P4/5NP.text:
Our knight has the c6-square to land on. 

We've got moves like ...Rb8 to defend the b4-pawn and get out of the diagonal, ...Ne4 to centralize the knight and ...Qe8 to defend the c6-knight if Qa5.

r2qkb1r/1bpn1ppp/p3pn2/1p1p4/P2P4/4PNP1/.text:
Our pawn chain is already sufficiently defended. 

After this point, White has to think about developing their queenside pieces since 4. e3 blocked the bishop in. 

This isn't an easy problem to solve.

r2qkb1r/pbpn1ppp/4pn2/3p4/P2P4/2P2NP1/4P.text:
I like going for quick development here since the bishop is on b7 and it could come under fire soon.

Also, ...Be7 and castling is always good. 

The position is balanced. 

If White targets our b7-bishop with their rook, we slide it forward one square.

r4rk1/pbp1qppp/n3pn2/P2p4/1b1P4/1Q3NP1/1.text: And after our pawn is attacked with the rook...

r4rk1/pbp1qppp/n3pn2/P2p4/1b1P4/1QN2NP1/.text:
11...Na6 is a solid move that covers many weaknesses and freezes the a5-pawn.

We'll continue with ...Rab8 and ...Bd6 back to fight for control of the e5-square and have our rook threaten the queen on the b-file to a greater capacity.

rn1q1rk1/p1p1bppp/b3pn2/P1Pp4/1p1P4/5NP1.text: If 10.Re1, aiming to go e4 at some point...

rn1q1rk1/p1p1bppp/b3pn2/P1PpN3/1p1P4/6P1.text:
Ne5 is a typical idea, preventing …Nc6.

We challenge the knight immediately with 10...Nfd7 - if we take it, we win the c5-pawn.

rn1q1rk1/p1pNbppp/b3p3/P1Pp4/1p1P4/6P1/1.text: That's why White will have to take on d7...

rn1q1rk1/pb2bppp/4pn2/P1ppN3/1pPP4/6P1/1.text:
We've got 9...c5, weakening the d4-pawn which supports the knight. 

We've got ...Qc7 to develop the queen, clearing the way for ...Rd8. 

We're not worried about the tension on d5 because we've got two minor pieces on that square.

rn1q1rk1/pbp1bppp/4pn2/P1Pp4/1p1P4/5NP1/.text:
If White played a5, it makes sense they push c5 - trying to isolate our b-pawn.

So we switch gears: c5 and a5 weaken the light squares, and our bishop can take a strong diagonal from a6, x-raying the f1-rook.

rn1q1rk1/pbp1bppp/4pn2/P2p4/1P1P4/5NP1/1.text:
After the pawn takes...

We recapture.

rn1q1rk1/pbp2ppp/4pn2/P2p4/1b1P4/1Q3NP1/.text:
This move attacks our dark-squared bishop and x-rays the one on b7… 

But we calmly defend the attacked bishop with 10...Qe7.

rn1qk2r/pbp1bppp/4pn2/P2p4/1p1P4/2P2NP1/.text:
8. c3 is also possible here.

We should just castle - our 
b4-pawn is defended.

rn1qk2r/pbp1bppp/4pn2/P2p4/1pPP4/5NP1/1P.text:
White can go for c4 now.

We simply castle.

rn1qk2r/pbp1bppp/4pn2/P2pN3/1p1P4/6P1/1P.text:
White always has this Ne5 idea.

But we can castle - it doesn’t create any real pressure yet.

rn1qkb1r/1bp2ppp/4pn2/p2p4/P2P4/2N2NP1/1.text:
I suggest we control the b4-square here and stop the a-pawn's march up the board.

Next: ...Be7, ...0-0, ...Nbd7, ...Ba6, ...c5. 

A very easy plan to execute.

rn1qkb1r/1bp2ppp/p3pn2/1p1p4/P2P4/4PNP1/.text: If 7.a4 to attack the pawn chain...

rn1qkb1r/pbp2ppp/4pn2/1p1p4/P2P4/5NP1/1P.text:
White may try to get rid of our annoying b-pawn - usually the only logical plan.

But after 6…b4, we continue being irritating, controlling the c3-square.

rn1qkb1r/pbp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/P2P4/2P2NP1/4P.text: If the pawn takes, the b-file becomes fully open and the c3-pawn is backwards.

rn1qkb1r/pbp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/PpPP4/5NP1/1P2.text:
White gains access to the c4 break once we push …b4. 

Yet we simply take en passant.

rn1qkb1r/pbp2ppp/4pn2/P2p4/1p1P4/5NP1/1P.text:
If White delays moving the c-pawn, I recommend a different approach as well.

We start with simple development, 7...Be7.

rn1qkbnr/1bp2ppp/p3p3/1p1p4/3P4/4PNP1/PP.text:
After White castles...

If there’s no direct pressure, we simply develop with 6...Nf6. 

Then we castle - simple and strong.

rn3rk1/p1pqbppp/b3p3/P1Pp4/1p1P4/6P1/1P2.text: And we'll recapture with the queen, with ...Nc6 to come and defend the b4-pawn, ...Rab8, and even ...b3 ideas to use the b4-square for our pieces.

rn3rk1/pbp1qppp/4pn2/P2p4/1b1P4/1Q3NP1/1.text:
11.Bd2 aims to remove our b4-bishop so the one on b7 becomes vulnerable. 

11…Na6 is a solid defensive answer.

rn3rk1/pbp1qppp/4pn2/P2p4/1b1P4/1QN2NP1/.text:
If 11.Nc3, White doesn't add pressure on our bishops so we can be a bit safer. 

Still, I like 11...Na6 here.

rnbqkb1r/p1p2ppp/4pn2/1p1p4/3P4/5NP1/PPP.text:
White often castles here after completing kingside development.

If instead White plays 5.a4, we just push …b4 - leading us back to main-line positions.

We place our bishop on b7 to coordinate our queenside. 

Next comes …Nbd7 and …c5 if allowed. 

Whether White develops the bishop or knight makes no difference: we develop, castle, and play …c5.

rnbqkbnr/2p2ppp/p3p3/1p1p4/3P4/4PNP1/PPP.text:
White may still fianchetto. 

But remember: one of the points of …b5 is that it supports …Bb7 as well.

rnbqkbnr/p1p2ppp/4p3/1p1p4/3P4/4PNP1/PPP.text:
White may go after the b5-pawn with 4.e3, but this is short-sighted - it blocks the dark-squared bishop, which normally belongs on g5.

We solve the problem with 4...a6. 

If White increases the pressure with 5.a4, then 5...b4 escapes the attack and controls c3.

rnbqkbnr/p1p2ppp/4p3/1p1p4/3P4/5NP1/PPP1.text:
White continues logically with 4.Bg2.

Only now do we bring out our knight to f6. 

When there are no direct issues to address, we focus on simple development.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/3P4/5N2/PPP1PPPP.text:
Instead of entering known territory, White may play this vague developing move. 

It could lead to London-type positions, Torre ideas with Bg5, or just flexible setups - but it doesn’t reveal much.

So we calmly play 2...e6. Our plan is simple: if 3.c4, then 3...a6 and we return to our Chapter 4 territory.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/3P4/5NP1/PPP1PP.text:
But White may insert 3.g3, going for something unique - dark-square control with the knight and d-pawn, and light-square control with the g2-bishop.

Against this, I recommend completely preventing c4 with 3...b5. 

This takes Catalan players out of their comfort zone. 

…Bb7 also activates our light-squared bishop.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to Chapter 5! 

Here we deal with 2.Nf3 move-orders. 

White may go for a g3–fianchetto or something more unconventional, like an early 3.Bg5 supported by the knight on f3.

White begins with the queen’s pawn.

We reply with …d5, aiming for our usual QGD setups.

3r1rk1/pb1nqppp/1p2pn2/2p5/3PN3/2PB1N2/P.text:
Rather we'll place a rook on d8 to x-ray many of White's pieces on the d-file. 

The position is fairly equal. 

...h6 is a safe defensive move to keep a piece out of g5. 

...Nd5 is also a good move to centralize the knight.

r2qk2r/1b1nbppp/pp2pn2/8/3PN3/3B1N2/PP3P.text:
White has an IQP they won't easily get rid of. 

We'll continue with ...0-0, ...b5 to expand on the queenside, and we'll develop the queen depending on what White does. 

If they trade on f6, Nxf6+, we can recapture with the knight and develop the queen to d6.

r2qkb1r/1b1n1ppp/pp2pn2/2pp4/3PP3/2PB1N2.text:
White manages to play their desired move, 9.e4, but it weakens their d4-pawn.

We may not win it immediately, but we will isolate it with 9...cxd4 - because Nxd4 runs into …Nc5, hitting both the bishop and the e4-pawn.

r2qkb1r/1b1n1ppp/pp2pn2/3p4/3PP3/3B1N2/P.text:
If White recaptures on d4...

Taking on e4 favors us, since we isolate the d-pawn.

r2qkb1r/1b1n1ppp/pp2pn2/8/3PN3/3B1N2/PP3.text: White recaptures with the knight, centralizing a piece.

r3k2r/pp1nqppp/4pn2/2pp4/3P4/2N1PN2/PPP2.text:
White has traded Black's worst piece in symmetrical d4 d5 positions: the light-squared bishop. 

We'll castle kingside and expand on the queenside with ...a6 and ...b5, taking advantage of the fact that the c3-knight is badly placed.

r4rk1/pb1nqppp/1p2pn2/2p5/3PN3/2PB1N2/PP.text: And after the knight recaptures, we're not going for massive trades in the center.

r4rk1/pb1nqppp/1p2pn2/2pp4/3PP3/2PB1N2/P.text:
e4 arrives. 

Since e5 is a threat, we capture on e4, but only once. 

We don’t want to move the f6-knight because it helps defend h7.

rn1qkb1r/1b3ppp/pp2pn2/2pp4/3P4/2PBPN2/P.text:
You’ll often see 8.c3 as White tries to keep the center solid.

We develop our other knight, 8...Nbd7.

rn1qkb1r/1b3ppp/pp2pn2/2pp4/3PP3/3B1N2/P.text: In essence, it looks like we've stopped e4.

rn1qkb1r/1b3ppp/pp2pn2/3p4/2pPP3/3B1N2/P.text:
Because we can chase one of the pieces that supports the e4-pawn. 

We'll be taking on e4 next.

White's dark-squared bishop is still buried on c1 and soon the attacked one will be on f1 as well.

rn1qkb1r/1bp2ppp/pp2pn2/3p4/3P4/3BPN2/PP.text:
Eventually White might get e4 in...

But only by allowing us counterplay in the center with the 7...c5 pawn break!

rn3rk1/pb2qppp/1p2pn2/2pp4/3P4/2PBPN2/PP.text:
10.Re1 appears to support e4. 

We bring our knight out to d7.

rnb1k1nr/ppp1qppp/4p3/3p4/2PP4/5N2/PP2PP.text:
5.c4 is a good move, a logical pawn break to undermine our center.

We don’t go for …Qb4+ because White can simply meet it with Qd2, defending b2. 

Instead, we bring out the knight to f6, enabling castling and reinforcing the e4-square.

rnb1k1nr/ppp1qppp/4p3/3p4/3P4/2N2N2/PPP1.text:
White may go 5.Nc3 immediately. 

This blocks the c-pawn, but White’s idea is a fast e4 break.

We develop with 5...Nf6 and challenge that plan.

rnb1k1nr/ppp1qppp/4p3/3p4/3P4/2P2N2/PP2P.text:
5.c3 stops …Qb4+, but White is heading toward a c3–d4–e3 London structure without the London bishop - making the setup far less convincing.

With 5...Nf6 we increase control over e4, so e3 is the most likely follow-up.

rnb1k1nr/ppp1qppp/4p3/3p4/3P4/4PN2/PPP2P.text:
5. e3, allowing Qb4+, is the most popular continuation. 

So we give the check and target the b2-pawn.

rnb1k1nr/ppp1qppp/4p3/3p4/3P4/5NP1/PPP1P.text:
This move is too slow. 

It aims for a Bg2 setup, but it allows 5…Qb4+ while White is far behind in development.

We’re fully justified in going pawn-hunting!

rnb1k1nr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/1q1P4/4PN2/PPPN.text:
Blocking the check with 6.Nbd2  is the main reply. 

White stays coordinated and willingly gives up the b2-pawn to activate the rook.

We can take on b2 and remain a pawn up.

rnb1k1nr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/3P4/3BPN2/PqPN1.text:
7.Bd3 develops. 

If 7.Rb1 instead, the a2-pawn hangs.

e4 becomes an idea in many of these positions, so we should place our knight on f6 to fight for the square.

rnb1k1nr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/3P4/5NP1/PqPNPP.text:
And White still has to go Bg2 and 0-0 to develop. 

If Bg2, we can even go 7...Nc6 for ...Nb4.

If our queen is attacked with Rb1, taking on a2 is strong.

rnb1k2r/pp2qppp/4pn2/1Bpp4/3P4/2N1PN2/PP.text:
Bb5+ is the most popular response.

But this check accomplishes nothing - we simply block the check with our bishop.

rnb1k2r/ppp1qppp/4pn2/3p4/2PP4/2N2N2/PP2.text:
Once the c-pawn moves, it’s natural for White to place the knight on c3.

Against 6.Nc3, we follow a similar plan to the 6.e3 lines and castle.

rnb1k2r/ppp1qppp/4pn2/3p4/2PP4/4PN2/PP3P.text:
You may also face 6. e3. 

Again, ...Qb4+ isn't relevant anymore.

rnb1k2r/ppp1qppp/4pn2/3p4/3P4/2N1PN2/PPP.text:
Many players resort to 6.e3 because 6.e4 is no longer possible.

This is a small admission that 5.Nc3 may not have been ideal.

Meanwhile, we do have a pawn break: 6…c5 undermines d4. 

If White takes on c5, they lose control of e5, which is often White’s key square in these QP structures.

rnb1k2r/ppp1qppp/4pn2/3p4/3P4/2P1PN2/PP3.text:
This becomes an inferior London. 

We continue in a principled way, castling our king.

rnb1k2r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/3P4/3BPN2/PqPN1.text:
White castles.

We castle as well. 

Being a pawn up, our job is simply to finish development.

rnb2rk1/p3qppp/1p2pn2/2pp4/3P4/2PBPN2/PP.text:
White develops the knight.

From d2 it supports e4 and c4.

We continue with 9...Bb7, an excellent square - reinforcing e4 and making the pawn push difficult.

10.Re1 is the usual way White prepares the advance.

rnb2rk1/pp2qppp/4pn2/2pp4/3P4/2PBPN2/PP3.text:
White castles and keeps playing typical London moves. 

We respond with 8...b6 -  we want to use b7 for our bishop, since the f7–e6–d5 chain is currently locked.

rnb2rk1/pp3ppp/4pn2/2PpN3/8/3BP3/q1PN1PP.text:
If White resolves the tension with a capture…

We slide our queen to a5. The idea isn't to go after the pawn, it is to get the queen back into a safer square where it helps defend the Black position.

rnb2rk1/pp3ppp/4pn2/2ppN3/3P4/3BP3/PqPN1.text:
White may try to relieve the pressure on d4 by moving the queen away from b2. 

But whenever the rook slides to b1, we can grab yet another pawn, 10...Qxa2.

rnb2rk1/pp3ppp/4pn2/q1PpN3/8/1N1BP3/2P2P.text: 12.Nb3 defends c5 and attacks the queen...

rnb2rk1/ppp1qppp/4pn2/3p4/2PP4/2N1PN2/PP.text:
The reason being is that Nc3 and e3 are interchangeable many times.

So we can support d5 with 7...Rd8 and place the rook opposite White's queen.

rnb2rk1/ppp1qppp/4pn2/3p4/2PP4/4PN2/PP3P.text:
So we'll just castle. 

The position is about equal. 

We'll go ...b6, ...Bb7 and ...c5 at some point, with a stable position.

rnb2rk1/ppp1qppp/4pn2/3p4/3P4/2PBPN2/PP3.text:
d3 is the best square for White's light-squared bishop in these positions. 

And …c5 is our thematic break to undermine d4.

rnb2rk1/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3pN3/3P4/3BP3/PqPN1.text:
9.Ne5 is a popular try: since White controls the e5-square, they may try to get a knight there. 

But this isn’t the right moment - White should have tried pawn breaks or activated other pieces. 

9…c5 undermines the d4-pawn, as we’ve done throughout the course.

rnb2rk1/ppq2ppp/4pn2/2PpN3/8/1N1BP3/2P2P.text:
But we've got pressure against the knight on e5. 

...Nbd7 will challenge that knight successfully. 

With the queen on c7, the ...Bd7-c6  maneuver becomes possible. 

Black is up a pawn and should have long-lasting pressure against the doubled c-pawns.

rnbqk1nr/ppp1Bppp/4p3/3p4/3P4/5N2/PPP1PP.text:
Trading is the most logical continuation. 

After we recapture with the queen, ideas of Qb4+ come into play.

rnbqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p3pn2/3p4/3P4/3BPN2/PPP.text:
White may castle, preparing their main break: e4.

That’s why we play 5...b6, aiming to develop our bishop to b7 - trying to make e4 harder to achieve.

rnbqkb1r/2p2ppp/pp2pn2/3p4/3P4/3BPN2/PPP.text:
White may reinforce e4... 

But so do we, 6...Bb7 is coming.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/3P4/3BPN2/PPP2.text:
As seen in the previous study, Bd3 is very typical when White places many pawns on dark squares.

4...a6 is our best move, transposing back to the course. 

If c4, then …dxc4 and …b5.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/3P4/5N2/PPP1PPPP.text:
2.Nf3 is very flexible and keeps White’s intentions hidden. 

We must be ready for everything.

Once again, we go 2...e6 to remain prepared to transpose into known QGD territory.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p2B1/3P4/5N2/PPP1P.text:
3.Bg5 attacks our queen.

In this course, whenever Bg5 appears, our standard answer is 
…Be7, blocking the attack.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/3P1B2/5N2/PPP1P.text:
This is the London System with 2. Nf3 and 3. Bf4. 

Refer to Chapter 6 for this one!

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/3P4/4PN2/PPP2PP.text:
3.e3 is a very rare move order. 

You won’t face this often, and you don’t need to memorize much. 

White usually sets up pawns on e3, d4, c3 with the bishop on d3 - but the dark-squared bishop becomes passive, so this opening shouldn’t concern us.

We develop our knight to f6 and wait for White’s next step.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to the second study of Chapter 5! 

Here we cover the Torre Attack and some other unconventional 3rd-move options from White.

White starts with 1.d4, claiming space in the center. 

We mirror with 1...d5.

rnbr2k1/p1p1qppp/1p2pn2/3p4/2PP4/2N1PN2/.text:
We end the variation with 8...b6 and will look to play  ...Bb7 and ...Nbd7 for our c5-pawn break. 

The position is fairly stable, but after a few pawn trades in the center Black's pieces are more active on the queenside and the bishop's diagonal on b7 may even become open if the d5-pawn comes off the board.

rnbr2k1/ppp1qppp/4pn2/3p4/2PP4/2N1PN2/PP.text: After 8.Qc2 it looks like a fairly normal Queen's Gambit Declined Position.

1rb2rk1/p1q3pp/3bpn2/1pppN3/3PnB2/2PBPN2.text:
We'll also get to support our knight on e4. 

You've got ideas of ...b4 and ...c4. 

If dxc5, we recapture with the knight and attack the bishop on d3. 

We have to keep our king safe and attack on the queenside.

1rb2rk1/p1qn1ppp/3bp3/1pppN1P1/3PnB2/2PB.text:
White increases pressure on e4…

We reinforce the knight with 12...f5.

If White avoids en passant, we maintain a strong outpost on e4.

1rb2rk1/p1qn1ppp/3bpn2/1pppN1P1/3P1B2/2P.text:
If White advances with g5, they do gain space, but the pawn also takes away an important square from their pieces.

We jump to e4 with our knight.

1rb2rk1/p1qn2pp/3bpP2/1pppN3/3PnB2/2PBPN.text: If White does take on en passant...

1rb2rk1/ppqn1ppp/3bpn2/2ppN3/3P1BP1/2PBP.text:
London structures can get sharp quickly - White attacks on the kingside.

Our counter is to attack on the queenside, 10...b5 is our next move!

r1b1k1nr/ppR2ppp/2n1p3/1B1p4/3P4/q3PN2/P.text: White may try to attack the knight...

r1b1k1nr/ppR2ppp/2nqp3/1B1p4/3P4/4PN2/P2.text:
But this move attacks the rook and defends the knight. 

White is lost.

r1b1k2r/p1pn1ppp/1p1qpn2/3p4/3P4/2PBPN2/.text:
White castles. 

As I said, Nbd2 is equally likely - London players follow their system.

We fianchetto.

r1b1k2r/p1qn1ppp/1p2pn2/2pp4/3P4/2PBPNP1.text: White goes for Standard London development.

r1b1k2r/pppn1ppp/3qpn2/3p4/3P4/2PBPN2/PP.text:
This move is very common. 

It’s interchangeable with Nbd2 and can transpose.

We go for …b6 and …Bb7.

r1b1k2r/pppn2pp/3qpp2/3p4/3P1P2/2P1P3/PP.text:
9.e3 builds a Stonewall, but with no knight capable of reaching e5. 

It’s not a strong setup.

We castle.

r1b1k2r/ppqn1ppp/3bpn2/2pp4/3P4/2PBPNB1/.text:
After White castles... 

We can now take on g3 - and we should.

Exchanging bishops helps reduce White’s control of e5. 

Also, after 8.0-0, hxg3 does not activate the rook on the h-file.

r1b1k2r/ppqn1ppp/4pn2/2pp4/3P4/2PBPNP1/P.text:
White recaptures. 

We continue improving our position with 9...b6, our bishop will soon be developed on b7.

r1b2rk1/ppp3pp/1n1q1p2/3p3Q/3PpP2/2P1P3/.text:
And like I said, we control the c4-square. 

...Be6 will follow. 

One of the only productive things White could do is castling kingside, but after ...Be6 they' ll be tasked with playing something useful once again. 

Our moves are easier to play because of strong our central control.

r1b2rk1/pppn2pp/3q1p2/3p3Q/3PpP2/2P1P3/P.text:
This isn't ideal coordination for White. 

We also control f3 so Nbd2 to f3 isn't possible. 

c4 seems like the only option for White, which we can begin to play against with ...Nb6 and ...Be6. 

We'll have a complete grip on the position.

r1b2rk1/pppn2pp/3q1p2/3pp2Q/3P1P2/2PBP3/.text:
White has no strategic solution and goes for mate. 

After 11…e4, the bishop gets chased from the diagonal and no longer pressures h7 - a key idea of any Stonewall.

r1b2rk1/pppn2pp/3qpp2/3p4/3P1P2/2PBP3/PP.text:
If White tries 10.Bd3 pressure... 

We control e5 - so we push and aim for this pawn break.

r1b2rk1/ppq1bppp/4pn2/2p1N3/2NPpP2/2P1P1.text:
We can just move our bishop away. 

We've got a nice d5-square to work with: we'll play ...Nd5 and if White tries setting up discoveries with f5, we'll just get out of the way with ...Qd8.

r1b2rk1/ppq2ppp/3bpn2/2p1N3/2NPpP2/2P1P1.text: Even though White could jump into c4 and attack our bishop...

r1b2rk1/ppqn1ppp/3bp3/2p1N3/3PpP2/2P1P1B.text:
White may try to attack the pawn.

But we’re perfectly fine if we simply defend it with 11...Nf6.

r1b2rk1/ppqn1ppp/3bp3/2ppN3/3PBP2/2P1P1B.text:
If White gives up their important light-squared bishop...

We recapture and welcome the concession.

r1b2rk1/ppqn1ppp/3bpn2/2ppN3/3P1B2/2PBPN.text:
White brings the knight to f3, adding more control over e5. 

Without losing time, we set up queenside counterplay, starting with 9...Rb8.

r1b2rk1/ppqn1ppp/3bpn2/2ppN3/3P1P2/2PBP1.text:
9.f4 reinforces the knight on e5 even more.

But this allows us to also get a knight into a central square.

r1bqk2r/ppp1n1pp/2nb1p2/3pP3/5B2/3NP3/PP.text:
White may trade…

But …f6 and …e5 is a dream pawn break against the London. 

We recapture.

Here, White has already lost the d4-pawn - meaning their grip on e5 is gone.

r1bqk2r/ppp1n1pp/2nb4/3pp1B1/8/3NP3/PPPN.text:
White may try to recover something strategically with a pin.

But there’s no real way to exploit our position after Bg5. 

We simply activate our bishop.

r1bqk2r/ppp1n1pp/2nbpp2/3p4/3P1B2/3NP3/P.text:
White develops and aims for Nf3. 

But one reason to play …Nc6 early is to prepare …e5.

7…e5 hits the bishop, gains space, and opens lines for our pieces.

r2q1rk1/ppp1n1pp/2nb4/3ppbB1/8/3NP3/PPPN.text:
Our rook is even active on the semi-open f-file. 

A short-term plan is to unpin and improve the queen: ...Qe8 for ...Qg6.

Of course, our pawn center is mobile and strong: if 11. 0-0, 11...e4 is a strong move.

r2qk2r/ppp1n1pp/2nb4/3ppbB1/8/3NP3/PPPNB.text: And after White puts their bishop on the suboptimal e2-square...

r3k2r/pbpn1ppp/1p1qpn2/3p4/3P4/2PBPN2/PP.text:
The knight develops to d2. 

Fortunately, in this variation we control e5, so White’s plan of planting a knight there won’t work.

We castle.

r3k2r/pbqn1ppp/1p2pn2/2pp4/3P4/2PBPNP1/P.text:
And we go for sound development as well. 

Our bishop helps control the e4-square. Play may continue with Qe2 and ...0-0. 

We'll take on e4 if White pushes e4 and quickly get our f-rook into d8.

r4rk1/pb1n1ppp/1p1qpn2/2p5/3PN3/2PB1N2/P.text: And after the knight recaptures in the center attacking our queen...

r4rk1/pb1n1ppp/1p1qpn2/2pp4/3PP3/2PB1N2/.text:
After 11.e4...

We take, removing the tension.

r4rk1/pbpn1ppp/1p1qpn2/3p4/3P4/2PBPN2/PP.text:
White’s only counterplay is to prepare the e4-pawn push. 

We strike with 10…c5.

r4rk1/pbqn1ppp/1p2pn2/2p5/3PN3/2PB1N2/PP.text:
We won't go for trades in the center, rather we'll keep our pieces as they are. 

If White doesn't take on c5, we'll take on d4. 

If they take on c5, we'll trade bishop and knight on e4 and only then recapture on c5 with the knight. 

We've got a rook coming into the d8-square and we have a stable middlegame.

rnb1k1nr/ppR2ppp/4p3/3p4/3P4/q3PN2/P2N1P.text:
White cannot even take this pawn...

After 9...Nc6 the rook is trapped.

rnb1k1nr/ppp2ppp/3qp3/3p4/3P4/2N2N2/PPP1.text:
White may choose fast knight development, aiming for a quick e4. 

But Nc3 blocks the c-pawn, so we must focus on controlling e4.

Our solution is to develop with 5...Nf6, controlling the e4-square.

rnb1k1nr/ppp2ppp/3qp3/3p4/3P4/2P2N2/PP2P.text:
Playing the pawn to c3 aims to develop the queen and prevent …Qb4+. 

We simply develop the kingside with 5...Nf6 and prepare to castle.

rnb1k1nr/ppp2ppp/3qp3/3p4/3P4/4PN2/PPP2P.text:
5.e3 is standard London play, activating the light-squared bishop and queen.

But 5.c3 was also possible, especially since after the bishop trade on d6.

5.e3 allows us to throw in a check on b4 with the queen.

rnb1k1nr/ppp2ppp/4p3/1N1p4/3P4/4PN2/PqP2.text:
Jumping to b5 might be White's idea...

But it’s quickly refuted with 7...Qb4+. 

If 8.Qd2, then …Qe7.

rnb1k1nr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/1q1P4/2N1PN2/PP.text:
Nc3 is also very unstable.

It allows us to take on b2, putting pressure on two pieces.

rnb1k1nr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/1q1P4/2P1PN2/PP.text:
This block doesn’t work - there will be too much pressure on White’s undeveloped queenside.

After we take on b2, we attack the rook.

rnb1k1nr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/1q1P4/4PN2/PPPN.text:
White could block and develop the knight. 

This is very sound because it argues that Black will lose valuable development time hunting pawns.

rnb1k1nr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/3P4/2P1PN2/Pq1N.text:
And when the knight moves so the queen can defend it...

We capture on c3. 

Essentially, c3 was played only to be taken.

rnb1k1nr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/3P4/2q1PN2/P2N1.text:
The rook might try to get active, and White may claim compensation…

But queens excel at hitting multiple weaknesses by sliding to a3. 

a2 becomes the next target.

rnb1k1nr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/3P4/4PN2/PqPN1P.text:
Yet we want to be able to take and refute White's gambit, in essence. 

Our plan is simple: Escape with the queen via a3 to e7, and play Nf6 and castle. Capturing on a2 is possible, but not recommended.

rnb1k1nr/ppp2ppp/4p3/qN1p4/3P4/2P1PN2/P4.text:
The queen defends c7. 

We're kicking the knight out soon with ...a6 and developing with ...Nd7. 

White doesn't have compensation.

rnb1k2r/p1p2ppp/4pn2/1pNp4/3P4/2q5/P2NPP.text: The knight has to block or the rook falls.

rnb1k2r/p1p2ppp/4pn2/1pNp4/3P4/q1P2N2/P3.text:
Once again, only one square remains. 

We now take on c3 with check.

rnb1k2r/p1p2ppp/4pn2/1pNp4/3q4/8/P2NPPPP.text:
And now we can take on d4. 

We're up two pawns out of the opening. 

It's now time to convert.

rnb1k2r/ppp2ppp/3qpn2/1N1p4/3P4/5N2/PPP1.text:
Many players lash out with this attacking move - but it’s a huge blunder. 

We reply with a queen check,
attacking both the knight and the b2-pawn.

rnb1k2r/ppp2ppp/3qpn2/3p4/3P1P2/3B1N2/PP.text:
White will usually defend with the queen, placing it on a square that normally belongs to the knight in London setups. 

White is still fine; the position remains equal.

We castle.

rnb1k2r/ppp2ppp/3qpn2/3p4/3P4/2P1PN2/PP3.text:
White can continue with standard London pawn-and-piece play.

We develop another piece, 6...Nbd7. 

White has spent a lot of time moving pawns, so we might even prepare central counterplay.

rnb1k2r/ppp2ppp/3qpn2/3pN3/3P4/2P5/PP2PP.text:
White may try 6.Ne5, though it’s odd - the knight is the only developed piece.

Since the pawn is still on e2, we can answer with 6…Nfd7 and later …f6 to chase it.

rnb1k2r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/1q1P4/2N2N2/PPP.text:
Once the knight blocks...

We attack the knight on c3 with pressure on the rook (though it is defended by the queen, so we don’t take it). 

The real issue is that White has few good squares here…

rnb1k2r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/N2P4/5N2/PqP1PP.text:
8.Na4 is the only safe square. 

We go for 8...Qa3, attacking the knight once again.

rnb1k2r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/N2P4/q1P2N2/P3P.text:
c3 does defend the knight for one more move…

But with the pawn still on e2, 9…b5 is possible. 

White runs into problems by not developing the e-pawn early.

rnb1k2r/pppn1ppp/3qp3/3pN3/3P1P2/2P5/PP2.text:
White reinforces their knight with 7.f4.

This early Stonewall attempt allows us …f6. 

It’s a one-piece attack that is easily repelled.

rnb1k2r/ppq2ppp/3bpn2/2pp4/3P4/2PBPNB1/P.text:
White may bring the bishop to d3, their dream square in the London.

And again, we develop the queenside with 7...Nbd7, also defending the c5-pawn - exactly as explained in the video.

rnb2rk1/p1p2ppp/1p1qpn2/3pN3/3P1P2/3B4/P.text:
Expect this move. 

White centralizes the knight.

rnb2rk1/p4ppp/1p1qpn2/2ppN3/3P1P2/3B4/PP.text:
And now we should go for 9...c5, undermining d4.

A nice way of reducing the pressure in the position is to go for a trade with ...Ba6, removing one of White's best and most aggressive pieces. 

...a6 to keep a piece out of b5 is also an option in the future, trying to play for ...Nc6 and a stable queenside.

rnb2rk1/ppp2ppp/3qpn2/3p4/3P1P2/3B1N2/PP.text:
White castles. 

With our f7–e6–d5 pawn chain, the best development for our light-squared bishop is via b7 or a6, so 8...b6 is our move.

rnb2rk1/ppq2ppp/3bpn2/2ppN3/3P1B2/2PBP3/.text:
White develops the other knight. 

We  continue with 8...Nbd7,  developing while maintaining pressure on c5.

rnb2rk1/ppq2ppp/3bpn2/2ppN3/3P4/2PBP1B1/.text:
Some players secure the bishop on g3 and prepare f4.

We develop the knight to d7 and keep everything defended. 

On d7 it doesn’t block the queen’s view of c5, and it can reroute to f6 later.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/3bpn2/2ppN3/3P1B2/2PBP3/.text:
London players rarely take on c5. 

They usually reinforce the pawn and create the c3–d4–e3 triangle.

We play 7…Qc7, keeping pressure on the diagonal without losing sight of the c5-pawn.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2ppp/3bpn2/3pN3/3P1B2/3BP3/P.text:
White brings the bishop to d3. 

We counter with 6…c5 immediately.

rnbqk1nr/ppp2ppp/3Bp3/3p4/3P4/5N2/PPP1PP.text:
First, we check what happens if White accepts the trade.

If they do, we’re happy - we’ve traded off White’s best piece: the London Bishop. 

Our queen lands on d6, eyeing b4. 

Our plan is simple: develop, castle kingside, and then expand on the queenside with …c5, …b6, and so on.

rnbqk1nr/ppp2ppp/3bp3/3p4/3P1B2/4PN2/PPP.text:
White may defend the bishop with 4.e3, hoping that if we take on f4, they recapture with the pawn and strengthen e5.

So we do not capture. 

Instead we place a knight on f6. 

This allows White the tricky Ne5 idea.

rnbqk1nr/ppp2ppp/3bp3/3p4/3P4/5NB1/PPP1P.text:
4.Bg3 is the most common move. 

London players like falling back so that hxg3 opens the h-file if we take.

We simply continue developing and play 4...Nf6.

rnbqk1nr/ppp2ppp/3bp3/3pN3/3P1B2/8/PPP1P.text:
White may place the knight on e5 early, but if it arrives before we play …Nf6...

We can kick it out immediately.

Since White isn’t optimally placed, we can prepare the …e5 break. 

…f6 is also possible because the pawn on e2 stops Qh5+ ideas.

rnbqk1nr/ppp3pp/3bpp2/3p4/3P1B2/3N4/PPP1.text:
The knight must retreat to d3 to protect the bishop.

We continue developing with 
5…Ne7 - our kingside is now fully developed.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/3bpn2/2pp4/3P4/2P1PNB1/PP.text:
Many players won’t take on c5, so you’ll often see 6.c3. 

Our defense is to build a bishop –queen battery with 6...Qc7.

rnbqk2r/ppp1n1pp/3bpp2/3p4/3P1B2/3NP3/PP.text:
White continues in typical London fashion with 6.e3.

We develop our other knight to c6.

This blocks our c-pawn for now, but White’s setup is also suboptimal because their bishop usually belongs on d3.

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/3bpn2/3p4/3P1B2/3BPN2/PP.text:
If White continues with a typical London setup, we’re completely fine. 

This line is much less tricky than 5.Ne5. 

I suggest we simply trade bishops.

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/3bpn2/3p4/3P4/4PNB1/PPP2.text:
White goes for the usual e3.

We respond with 5…c5, our thematic break against the London.

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/3bpn2/3pN3/3P1B2/4P3/PPP.text:
Because our knight sits on f6 and White has played e3, we cannot kick the knight from e5 with …f6. 

This is a serious line played even by top GMs.

We should castle early to avoid any potential tactics.

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/3P1P2/3B1N2/PPP.text:
White ends up with doubled f-pawns but also strong control of e5. 

We develop the queen with tempo, 6...Qd6.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/3P4/5N2/PPP1PPPP.text:
White may go 2.Nf3.

We play 2…e6, keeping the option to face c4. 

We don’t know whether White will choose Bf4, c4, or g3, so …e6 ensures we can always transpose into familiar territory. 

If we play 2...Nf6, White could enter a Catalan, and without our pawn on e6 we cannot steer the game back to our course.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/3P1B2/5N2/PPP1P.text:
But White may instead bring the bishop out immediately and take us into the London. 

Since this move order is different, we can also do something different.

We challenge the bishop on f4 right away by playing 3...Bd6.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to our first study of this chapter. T

he 2.Bf4 London is a simple approach, and you won’t see many deviations - especially when White follows with 3.e3.

White opens with 1.d4. 

We reply with 1…d5, ready for a Queen’s Gambit structure.

r2q1b1r/p1Q1kppp/4pn2/1B6/1n1PbB2/N3P3/P.text:
The queen takes on c7 with check, it had no other squares to go to.

We trade queens.

r2qk2r/pp3ppp/2p1p3/n2n1b2/Q2P1B2/P1P1P3.text:
We recapture with the knight, which is now nicely placed on the d5-square.

We are putting pressure on the c3-pawn and the bishop on f4. 

...Qb6 and castling are the ideas here, with ...Rc8 preparing c5.

r2qk2r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/n2P1b2/Q2P1B2/P1P1P.text: White gets rid of the doubled c-pawns.

r2qk2r/ppp2ppp/2n1pn2/3p1b2/1bPP1B2/1QN1.text:
This position is a transposition to
 5. Qb3 Nc6 6. Nc3 Bb4

The plan is to play ...a5, going for the queenside expansion. 
 
Trading off the dark-squared bishop is also an idea. 

If White's queen ever moves out of the protection of the c3 knight, we will capture the knight and double White's c-pawns.

r2qk2r/ppp2ppp/2n1pn2/3p1b2/1bPP1B2/PQN1.text:
White attacks our bishop. 

We capture on c3 to maintain better control over e4.

r2qk2r/ppp2ppp/2n1pn2/3p1b2/2PP1B2/PQP1P.text:
White recaptures. 

We maneuver our knight to a5, hitting the queen.

r2qk2r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/n2p1b2/Q1PP1B2/P1P1P.text:
White gives a check forking the king and the knight on a5.

We block with our c-pawn - now the queen defends the knight.

r2qkb1r/pQp2ppp/2n1pn2/3p1b2/2PP1B2/4P3/.text:
Capturing on b7 is a common mistake - White is now in trouble. 

We jump with our knight to b4, threatening to fork the king and rook.

r2qkb1r/pQp2ppp/4pn2/1B6/1n1PbB2/N3P3/PP.text:
White tries to attack our king with 9.Bb5 +.

We calmly step out to e7 - there are no threats.

r2qkb1r/pQp2ppp/4pn2/3p1b2/1nPP1B2/N3P3/.text:
White plays 7.Na3, defending c2.

We take on c4 and free up the 
e4-square for our bishop.

r2qkb1r/pQp2ppp/4pn2/5b2/1nBP1B2/N3P3/PP.text:
White recaptures. 

We attack both the queen on b7 and the weak pawn on g2 with 8...Be4.

r2qkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n1pn2/3p1b2/2PP1B2/1QN1.text:
White develops the knight. 

We pin it, strengthening our control of the e4-square.

r2qkb1r/pppn1ppp/4pn2/3p4/3P1B2/3QPN2/PP.text:
Again this flexible ...Nbd7 move. 

We will again finish up development and go c7-c5 (or the more solid ...c6). 

The position is balanced.

r2qkb1r/pppnpppp/5n2/3p4/3P1B2/3QP3/PPP2.text:
Now I like this flexible move, 5...Nbd7. 

From here, we try to play ...e6, ...c5 (or even ...c6), develop and castle.

rn1q1rk1/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p1b2/1bPP1B2/2N1P.text:
We simply castle, with the plans of ...Ne4. 

Play can develop in many ways here, but keep in mind the following ideas:

1. Ne4 jump
2. c7-c5 followed by ...Qa5
3. ...Bxc3, damaging White's pawns

rn1qk2r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p1b2/1bPP1B2/1QN1P.text:
b3 is a common square for the queen. 

6. a3 is always met with 6... Bxc3.

rn1qk2r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p1b2/1bPP1B2/2N1PN.text: White frenquently plays this move in these variations.

rn1qkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p1b2/2PP1B2/4P3/P.text:
A typical move in Queen’s Pawn openings.

We respond with 4...e6, preparing to develop the dark-squared bishop.

rn1qkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p1b2/3P1B2/3BP3/P.text:
White may challenge our light-squared bishop. 

We trade on d3, the upside is that exchanging this bishop reduces White’s attacking chances on our king.

rn1qkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p1b2/3P1B2/4PN2/P.text:
White develops the knight to f3 first.

We respond with 4...e6 - aiming to develop the dark-squared bishop and build an e6–d5 structure. 

5.c4 becomes another move order.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p1b2/2PP1B2/1Q2P3.text:
White brings out the queen early, targeting b7. 

We don’t need to defend the pawn and instead play 5...Nc6.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p1b2/2PP1B2/2N1P3.text:
White develops the knight behind the c-pawn.

We play a common idea in these structures - 5...Bb4, pinning the knight to the king and strengthening our control of e4.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p1b2/3P1B2/3BPN2/.text:
White fights for e4 with Bd3. 

As usual, we take on d3.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p4/3P1B2/4P3/PPP2.text:
White opens the diagonal for the light-squared bishop.

Our idea is to mirror White and play 3...Bf5, getting our bishop out of the pawn chain.

We don’t want it stuck behind our pawns.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/3P1B2/8/PPP1PPPP.text:
White immediately develops the dark-squared bishop, so e3 won’t trap it. 

White also gains control over e5.
