This is clearly the London, which means we can safely play 2...Nf6 without worry of transpositions.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
In this study we cover the 2.Bf4 London, usually followed by 3.e3. 

It’s one of the most common amateur setups because the ideas are simple. 

We answer with 3...Bf5 to develop our light-squared bishop early.

White begins with the Queen’s Pawn Opening.

We mirror with 1…d5, ready for a QGD structure.

lessons.title: 1. d4 d5 (2. Bf4, 3. Nf3 Move Order)

1r1qkb1r/Q1pn1ppp/4pn2/3p1b2/2PP1B2/5N2/.text:
If White chooses to capture the pawn on a7...

We take on b2 - now the knight on b1 is hanging.

1r1qkb1r/p1Qn1ppp/4pn2/3p1b2/2PP1B2/5N2/.text:
White takes another pawn. 

We trade queens.

1r2kb1r/p1Bn1ppp/4pn2/3p1b2/2PP4/5N2/PP2.text:
White recaptures. 

We take on b2, attacking the knight.

2q1kb1r/Q1Bn1ppp/4pn2/2Pp1b2/3P4/5N2/Pr2.text: White tries to close the position, but cannot defend both threats.

3qkb1r/Q1Bn1ppp/4pn2/3p1b2/2PP4/5N2/Pr2P.text:
Taking on c7 with the bishop loses.

We step out of the attack, 8...Qc8. 

There are two threats: …Rxb1 and …Rb7, attacking queen and bishop.

4k2r/p1Bn1ppp/4pn2/3p1b2/1bPP4/5N2/Pr1NP.text:
And with ...Bb4 we pin the knight on d2. 

We can always capture the pawn on a2 later. 

With ...Ne4 coming it is very hard for White to untangle this position.

4kb1r/p1Bn1ppp/4pn2/3p1b2/2PP4/5N2/Pr1NP.text: White steps out of the attack.

r2q1rk1/pp1nbppp/2p1p3/8/3P1P2/2NQ1N2/PP.text:
We castle. 

The next moves will be ...Qc7 to connect the rooks and get the knight into the game with ...Nf6 or ...Nb6.

r2qk2r/1pp1bppp/1n2pn2/5b2/p2P1B2/4PN2/P.text:
We prepare to castle. 

With the plans of ...Ne4 and ...c5 Black has a very comfortable game here.

r2qk2r/pp1nbppp/2p1p3/5b2/3P1P2/2NB1N2/P.text:
The bishop isn't placed well on c4, so White may elect to trade it.

We accept the trade since we don't want our pawn structure to be disrupted.

In addition, this trade favors Black, because we get rid of White's attacking chances, and our pawns are already on light squares.

r2qkb1r/1pp2ppp/1n2pn2/p4b2/3P1B2/1Q2PN2.text:
White castles. 

We push 9…a4 to chase the queen off the b-file.

r2qkb1r/1pp2ppp/1n2pn2/p4b2/P2P1B2/1Q2PN.text:
White stops the pawn. 

We want to trade queens to improve our b6-knight, so 9...Qd5 is our move.

r2qkb1r/pQpn1ppp/4pn2/3p1b2/2PP1B2/5N2/P.text:
White grabs the “free” pawn - this is the most popular try.

We attack the queen and get our rook on the semi-open file.

r2qkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p1p3/5b2/2BP1P2/2N2N2/.text:
White now eyes our king after 10.Re1. 

We must be careful about d5 pushes. 

We reduce the rook’s scope by preparing ...0-0 with 10...Be7.

r2qkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/5b2/2QP1B2/2N1PN.text:
White opens the diagonal for the light-squared bishop.

8...Qb6 is our next move.

Our queen on b6 is very active, pressuring b2. 

Tactics often revolve around controlling b4 - White can blunder easily.

r2qkb1r/ppp2ppp/1n2pn2/5b2/3P1B2/1Q2PN2/.text:
White retreats. 

We play 8...a5, looking to later  attack the queen with …a4.

r2qkb1r/pppn1ppp/4pn2/3p1b2/2PP1B2/1Q2PN.text:
Another option is 6.e3, delaying pressure on d5. 

We usually take on c4.

r2qkb1r/pppn1ppp/4pn2/3p1b2/2PP1B2/1QN2N.text:
White ignores the pawn and instead increases pressure on d5.

We remove the pressure by taking on c4.

r2qkb1r/pppn1ppp/4pn2/5b2/2BP1B2/1Q2PN2/.text:
White recaptures with the bishop. 

We try to eliminate the bishop pair with 7...Nb6.

r2qkb1r/pppn1ppp/4pn2/5b2/2QP1B2/2N2N2/P.text:
White recaptures and attacks our c-pawn. 

We defend it by pushing it one square.

r3k2r/1pp2ppp/4pn2/p2n1b2/Pb1P4/4PNB1/1P.text:
Making it harder for White to develop naturally. 

This is a classic idea in this line - occupy the b4 square. 

We have a greater piece activity, we will castle next and centralize the rooks with ...Rfd8 and ...Rac8.  

The knight will be placed well on e4.

r3k2r/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/5b2/1b1P1B2/1PN1PN.text:
Now we pin the knight. 

Black has a very good position now. 

White's doubled b-pawns are soft, and with ...Nd5 coming it is easy for us to put pressure on White. 

The b4-square is also perpetually ours.

r3kb1r/1pp2ppp/1n2pn2/p2Q1b2/P2P1B2/4PN2.text:
White trades. 

We recapture and our knight becomes nicely centralized.

r3kb1r/1pp2ppp/4pn2/p2n1b2/P2P4/4PNB1/1P.text: White wants to keep the bishop pair.

r3kb1r/pp1n1ppp/1qp1p3/3n1b2/2QP1B2/2NBP.text:
Centralizing the knight here is good, gaining control of the crucial b4-square with both the bishop and the knight. 

An idea is to just let White capture on f5 because the pawn on b2 hangs. 

White must be careful!

r3kb1r/pp1n1ppp/1qp1pn2/5b2/2QP1B2/1PN1P.text:
White may try to defend b2 - this is a subtle blunder.

We pin the knight with our queen; …Nb6 and …Bb4 are unstoppable.

r3kb1r/pp1n1ppp/1qp1pn2/5b2/3P1B2/1QN1PN.text:
White wants to trade queens because their king might become vulnerable. 

We’re happy to trade.

r3kb1r/pp1n1ppp/1qp1pn2/5b2/N1QP1B2/4PN2.text:
White attacks our queen, but this is also a mistake. 

We check the king, 9...Qa5+.

r3kb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p1p3/q2n1b2/2QP1B2/2N1P.text:
Black is very active here with ...Bb4 coming.  

For instance, after 11. a3 we can still play 11... Bb4, because the rook on a1 is undefended.

r3kb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/q4b2/2QP1B2/2N1PN.text: White has to retreat, othervise the attack is even harder to defend with ...Nd5 coming.

rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1p3/5b2/2BP1P2/2N2N2/P.text:
White castles.

We develop the knight; from d7 it can later go to f6 or b6.

rn1qkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p1b2/2PP1B2/5N2/P.text:
White challenges our d5-pawn in a Queen’s Gambit fashion.

We support with 4…e6; our bishop is nicely placed outside the pawn chain.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/4p3/3n1b2/2BP1B2/2N1PN2.text:
White recaptures the pawn. 

We get rid of White’s strong dark-squared bishop.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/4p3/5b2/2BP1P2/2N2N2/PP.text:
White recaptures. 

We play 8…c6, guarding d5 and b5.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p1b2/2PP1B2/1Q3N2.text:
A natural continuation from White, attacking b7 is 5.Qb3. 

We set a trap by leaving the pawn hanging and play 5...Nbd7.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p1b2/2PP1B2/2N2N2.text:
5.Nc3 is a different approach where White develops the queenside knight first.

We take on c4 - something we’re used to doing.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/5b2/2pP1B2/2N1PN2/.text:
White tries to regain the pawn by opening up their light-squared bishop.

We centralize the knight, 6...Nd5, looking to win the bishop pair.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/5b2/Q1pP1B2/2N2N2/.text:
White may try to regain the pawn with Qa4+. 

We block the check with our c-pawn.

rn2kb1r/pp3ppp/1qp1pn2/5b2/2QP1B2/2N2N2/.text:
And we play the traditional 7...Qb6, with ...Be7 and castling next. 

Our bishop stands dominant on f5, and White won't get their standard London play out of this opening.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p4/3P1B2/5N2/PPP1.text:
White develops the knight in typical London fashion. 

Ne5 may come later.

We want to play …e6, but first we develop our bishop to f5 so it doesn’t get stuck.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/3P1B2/8/PPP1PPPP.text:
This setup is the London System.

White plays 2.Bf4 to control e5.

2...Nf6 is solid - we support d5 and control e4.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to Study 3. 

Some London players develop the kingside knight first. 

It’s mostly a matter of preference, but it gives us extra time - White’s queenside development is delayed.

White starts with the Queen’s Pawn. 

We reply with 1…d5, ready for the Queen’s Gambit.

lessons.title: 1. d4 d5 (2. Bf4 Nf6 3. Nc3) - The Jobava London

r1b1k2r/pp3ppp/2n1p3/q1Pp4/4nB2/P1PQPN2/.text:
With 9...Ne4 we should be winning some of those doubled isolated c-pawns.

...Nxc5 is coming with a tempo on the queen almost no matter what. 

...0-0 will come eventually, and we'll continue playing against the c-pawns.

r1bq1rk1/1p1n1ppp/p1p1pn2/b2p4/3P1B2/N1P.text:
We play 9...c6 with the idea of retreating the bishop to c7 and trading off White's strong f4 bishop. 

Black has ideas of ...b5 and ...c5, devleoping with ...Bb7 too.

r1bq1rk1/pp1n1ppp/4p3/2bp4/8/2NBP1N1/PPP.text:
We get the king to safety. 

We're not afraid of Qh5 on h7 because we have ...g6, and since we have the dark-squared bishop our dark squares will be safe.

A neat idea is to bring the bishop back to e7 so the knight can land on c5. 

Black is better out of the opening.

r1bqk2r/1pp2ppp/p1n1pn2/b2p4/Q2P1B2/N1P2.text:
White retreats.

We activate our f-knight to e4 - threatening to take on c3 and win the rook after bxc3.

r1bqk2r/2p2ppp/p1n1p3/bp1p4/Q2PnB2/N1P2N.text:
We end the variation with 9...b5, attacking the queen. 

The moves ...g5 and ...f5 are definitely a plan, going for the attack. 

White will be excessively passive as we attack on the kingside. 

Black is much better.

r1bqk2r/pp1n1ppp/4p3/2bp3n/8/2NBP1B1/PPP.text:
White usually brings the bishop back.

We take anyway.

r1bqk2r/pp1n1ppp/4pn2/2Pp4/1b3B2/2NBP3/P.text:
Supporting the knight on c3 is the most popular move, so here’s the antidote:

We capture on c5 with the bishop. 

8.Nb5 isn’t good for White because of 8…e5 and 9…a6.

r1bqk2r/pp1n1ppp/4pn2/2bp4/5B2/2NBP3/PPP.text:
White may castle and seem perfectly developed with no obvious weaknesses.

But we’ll go after the bishop pair with 8...Nh5. 

The f4-bishop is one of White’s best pieces.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2n1pn2/bN1p4/Q2P1B2/2P2N.text:
White develops a knight. 

We push the knight to a worse square with 7...a6, c3 isn't available anymore.

rnb1k2r/pp3ppp/4pn2/q1Pp4/5B2/P1PQP3/2P2.text:
8.Qd3 defends for one more move and prepares Qb5+.

We block the diagonal with 8...Nc6 to prevent Qb5+. 

We’re not letting the pressure fade.

rnb1k2r/pp3ppp/4pn2/q1pp4/3P1B2/P1P1PN2/.text:
And if you can tell, White cannot really defend the c3-pawn! 

If 8Qd3, ...c4! 

If Qd2, ...Ne4!

rnbq1rk1/1pp2ppp/p3pn2/b2p4/3P1B2/N1P1PN.text:
White gets on with kingside development.

We also bring our knight into the game, 8...Nbd7.

rnbqk2r/1pp2ppp/1b2pn2/pN1p4/PP1P1B2/2P5.text:
But here comes 7...a5, disrupting the advanced pawns on the queenside.

The b4-pawn will be very weak. ...Qe7 and ...Nc6 are ideas to attack the b4-pawn.

If bxa5, ...Bxa5 and Black gets everything they want, because White's queenside is destroyed.

rnbqk2r/1pp2ppp/p3pn2/b2p4/3P1B2/N1P1P3/.text:
White must retreat to a passive square. 

We castle.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/4pn2/2Pp4/1b3B2/2NBP3/PPP.text:
White trades.

We don’t rush to take on c5. 

We instead play 6...Nbd7, aiming to take on c5 with the knight.

If 7.Nf3, we may play ...Bxc3, doubling the pawns, then …Nxc5. 

If 7...Ne2, then …Bxc5, bringing our bishop back.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/4pn2/2Pp4/5B2/P1P1P3/2P2P.text:
If White takes on c5, they’re left with tripled, very weak pawns. 

This is the second most popular option after the bad 7.Nf3.

7…Qa5 puts pressure on all the pawns.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/4pn2/2pp4/3P1B2/P1P1PN2/2.text: Keep in mind the most popular move, 7. Nf3, runs into ...Qa5.

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/1b2pn2/1N1p4/PP1P1B2/2P5.text: White is trying to trap our bishop on b6.

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/1N1p4/1b1P1B2/2P5/P.text:
And when White blocks, attacking our bishop...

We defend c7 from a5.

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/1b1P1B2/2NBP3/P.text:
White places their light-squared bishop on an active square - the most popular move after the pin.

We challenge White’s center immediately with our typical 5...c5.

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/1b1P1B2/P1N1P3/.text:
White attacks our bishop. 

As planned, we capture and damage the queenside structure.

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/3P1B2/P1P1P3/2P.text:
White recaptures.

We strike with 6…c5, opening the diagonal for the queen and targeting the weak queenside pawns.

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/bN1p4/1P1P1B2/2P5/P.text:
White expands on the queenside, attacking our bishop. 

We retreat the bishop to b6.

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/bN1p4/3P1B2/2P1P3/P.text:
White opens the diagonal for the light-squared bishop. 

We attack the knight with 6...a6.

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/bN1p4/Q2P1B2/2P5/PP.text:
White threatens discovered attacks with the knight.

We cover the diagonal and defend the bishop with 6...Nc6. 

We’re now ready for …a6 and …b5 if we want it.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p4/3P1B2/2N5/PPP1.text:
White develops the queenside knight early. 

This is the Jobava London - unusual because blocking the c-pawn is rarely ideal in d4/d5 openings. 

Still, White gets active piece play.

We continue with the standard move 3...e6, opening our bishop’s diagonal.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/1N1p4/3P1B2/8/PPP1.text:
White attacks c7 - very typical in Jobava lines.

We defend by developing the bishop with check.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/3P1B2/2N1P3/PP.text:
White prepares to develop the light-squared bishop. 

We develop with 4...Bb4, with the idea of capturing on c3 and damaging White’s pawn structure.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/3P1B2/8/PPP1PPPP.text:
White immediately chooses to develop the London bishop. 

We develop our knight naturally, 2...Nf6, eyeing central squares.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to the last study in the London chapter! 

Here we look at the Jobava London System, popularized by Baadur Jobava. 

It’s defined by the early 3.Nc3, before any c4 commitment.

White begins with the central d-pawn. 

We mirror with 1…d5.

r1b2rk1/P4ppp/2n5/3p4/1P2p1nq/2P1P3/P1B1.text:
Our queen arrives at the h4 square, and together with the knight, they attack the undefendable h2 square.

Checkmate is now unstoppable.

Good game!

r1bq1rk1/P4ppp/2n2n2/3p4/1P2p3/2P1P3/P1B.text:
White accepts the sacrifice but... 

The follow-up check with the knight opens the queen’s diagonal…

r1bq1rk1/P4ppp/2nb1n2/3p4/1P2p3/2P1P3/P1.text:
White falls for it - we’re winning.

This bishop sacrifice on h2 is the famous Greek Gift.

r1bq1rk1/p3bppp/1Pn2n2/3p4/1P2p3/2P1P3/P.text:
White captures, and instead of recapturing...

We set a trap: 10...Bd6!

r1bq1rk1/pp2bppp/2n2n2/2Pp4/1P2p3/2P1P3/.text:
The bishop steps out of the way.

We now address the queenside clamp: 9…b6 undermines the structure and forces White to react.

r1bq1rk1/pp2bppp/2n2n2/2Ppp3/1P6/2PBP3/P.text:
White castles as well.

Although 8…e4 concedes d4 and f4, it gains space and tempo, prepares e5 for the knight, and restricts White’s light-squared bishop. 

We’re taking over!

r1bqk2r/pp2bppp/2n2n2/2Ppp3/1P6/2PBP3/P3.text:
White develops the final kingside piece. 

7.Nf3? loses to 7...e4.

We finally castle.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/2Pp4/8/2PBP3/PP3P.text:
White chooses 5.dxc5, relieving tension and grabbing a pawn.

Now our plan begins: 5...e5, taking over the center and eyeing c5 with the f8-bishop.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n2n2/2Ppp3/1P6/2PBP3/P4.text:
White’s entire point was to hold the pawn.

That’s fine - our central control is strong, we’re almost fully developed, and ready to castle.

We continue with 6...Be7.

r2q1rk1/pppn1ppp/3b1n2/3pNp2/3P1P2/4P3/P.text:
We castle and will get our knight into e5 soon enough.

e4 will be a permanent outpost for us, while e5 won't be a permanent outpost for White because we can even go ...f6 at some point to kick the knight out. 

We have plans of ...c6 and ...g6 to consolidate our pawns. 

If at any point White trades on f5, you'll have similar ideas revolving around control of e4.

r2qk2r/pp3ppp/2nbpn2/2ppNb2/3P1P2/2PBP3/.text:
8.Ne5 is one of White’s main Stonewall ideas.

We don’t fear it - our pieces develop around it and we keep firm control of e4.

We continue with 8...Qc7.

r2qk2r/pppn1ppp/3b1n2/3pNp2/3P1P2/4P3/PP.text: If White gets their knight to e5 as is their plan in the Stonewall...

r2qkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/5bB1/2BP3N/2N5/P.text: White moves the knight to the edge of the board with goals of capturing our bishop.

r2qkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p1pnb1/6B1/2BP3N/2N5/P.text:
We move the bishop away from the dangerous f5 square, and are ready to capture with the h-pawn if the trade happens.

Apart from that, our plan is simple:
Develop the bishop to e7, castle, and enjoy a much better position being up a pawn.

Sounds great!

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/2pp1b2/3P1P2/2PBPN.text:
White may castle. 

We prepare castling as well, 7...Bd6 comes next.

r2qkb1r/pppn1ppp/4pn2/5bB1/2BP4/2N2N2/PP.text:
White castles. 

With our king still in the center, White wants d5 and pressure on the e-file.

That’s why 8...c6 is important - it adds another defender to d5.

r2qkb1r/pppn1ppp/5n2/3p1p2/3P1P2/4PN2/PP.text:
White often just castles...

We develop our remaining kingside minor piece to prepare castling.

r3k2r/ppq2ppp/2nbpn2/2ppNb2/3P1P2/2PBP3/.text:
If White avoids the bishop trade and moves the queen…

We go for the bishop trade, forcing White to move the queen again.

r4rk1/ppq2ppp/2nbpn2/2ppN3/3P1P2/2PQP3/P.text:
And we can castle. 

Expect Stonewall players to go Nd2-Ndf3. 

However, White's hole on e4 cannot be ignored. We've got plan of ...Rac8, ...a6, ...b5 and ...Ne4 at the right time.  We have a positional edge not only because of our e4 control but because of our piece quality: the bishop on c1 is dead.

rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/4pn2/2pp1b2/3P1P2/2PBPN2.text:
6.c3 is most popular, connecting the pawns.

We develop the knight to c6 after 
…c5. 

If Bxf5, exf5 followed by …Bd6 and …g6 is excellent.

rn1qkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p1b2/3P1P2/3BP3/P.text:
White tries to trade our active bishop.

4…e6 is key - we don’t mind trading, since a pawn on f5 becomes a shield and strengthens our grip on e4.

rn1qkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/5b2/2BP4/2N2N2/PPP.text:
White continues developing and prepares to castle.

Now we play 6…e6, opening the bishop and defending f7.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p1B2/3P1P2/4P3/PP.text:
This is the most common continuation.

After 5...exf5 our control of e4 is overwhelming - an outpost for the entire middlegame and endgame.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p1b2/3P1P2/3BPN2/.text:
Instead, White may continue with 5.Nf3, targeting e5.

But this overlooks 5…c5!, our thematic pawn break. 

We already equalize.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/5bB1/2BP4/2N2N2/PP.text:
7.Bg5 pins our knight, but this won’t work.

We develop our b-knight to d7, defending f6, and keeping a solid extra pawn.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/3p1p2/3P1P2/4PN2/PP.text:
The kingside knight is usually White’s first developed minor piece. 

If they ever pressure f5 with Qd3, then …g6 holds everything.

If the pawn remains untargeted, we simply develop - the knight is best on d7 because it may go to f6 later to support the other knight on e4.

rnb1kb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/5q2/8/2N1BN2/PPP2Q.text:
A developing move by White, blocking the queens from seeing eachother.

But it simply loses.

rnb1kb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/8/3q4/2N1BQ2/PPP3P.text:
6.Be3 develops with tempo - White’s whole idea.

Since we’re two pawns ahead, we’re happy to trade queens, so we offer the exchange on g4.

rnb1kb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/8/6q1/2N1B3/PPP2QP.text:
White avoids it, as expected…

But we insist with 7...Qf5.

rnb1kb1r/ppp1pppp/8/5q2/6n1/2N1BN2/PPP2Q.text:
8...Ng4! forks White's queen and bishop, and we are guaranteed to trade a piece.

After that, we will develop the kingside, castle, and then develop the queenside.

Now you know how to fight against the Blackmar-Diemer gambit!

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/2pp4/3P4/2PBP3/PP3P.text:
Again White sets up the classic triangle of dark-square pawns.

We continue with 4…Nc6 - no need to block our bishop with …Nd7. We still leave c5 hanging.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p4/3P1P2/4P3/PPP3.text:
Very aggressive! 

3.f4 supports e5 and is central to Stonewall setups. 

But if White now plays c4, they'd be totally overextended.

We strike immediately with 3...Bf5, claiming the light squares.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p4/3P4/3BP3/PPP2P.text:
White develops the bishop to d3, the usual square in QP positions.

3...c5 is a very interesting idea! 

If White takes, we have …e5 ideas with strong central control.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/8/3P4/2N2N2/PPP3PP.text:
If 5.Nxf3, White has a small lead in development and wants to castle quickly.

Since defending with …e6 wasn’t needed earlier, we develop the light-squared bishop to f5 first.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/8/3P4/2N2Q2/PPP3PP.text:
If White recaptures with the queen, offering yet another pawn, this is even worse. 

White is lost.

We simply capture - now two pawns up.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/8/3Pp3/2N2P2/PPP3P.text:
White’s idea is to give up the e-pawn, trade on f3, and accelerate development.

We take on f3 and leave White with choices.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/3P4/4P3/PPP2PPP/.text:
2.e3 looks dubious, blocking the c1-bishop, but White may aim for a Stonewall with several dark-square pawns and Bd3. 

They may also still go for c4, so we don’t over-commit with …Bf5.

We develop naturally with 2...Nf6.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
2.e4 is the Blackmar–Diemer Gambit. 

White sacrifices a pawn to speed up development - but with precise play, the move is simply bad.

We accept the pawn and go up material.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/3Pp3/2N5/PPP2PPP/R.text:
White develops with tempo, attacking e4. 

We defend and develop with 2...Nf6.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to the first study of Chapter 7! 

Here and in the next study we cover White’s second-move deviations. 

In this one, we look at 2.e3 and 2.e4.

White fights for the center with 1.d4.

We respond symmetrically.

3rkbnr/pp2ppp1/1qn4p/8/3PQ2B/1P5P/P1P2PP.text: So if the queen retreats to the wrong square...

4kbnr/pp2ppp1/1qn4p/8/3rQ2B/1P5P/P1P2PP1.text:
We're winning a bishop. 

Of course, White isn't forced to go to e4. 

But even if 11. Qf3 had been played, 11...Nxd4 would have been a tempo on the queen as well, with a winning advantage.

r1b1k1nr/pp1nBpp1/1qp4p/3p4/3Pp3/1P2P3/P.text: After the trade, we get rid of White's only active piece.

r1b1k1nr/pp2ppb1/2n4p/2qp2p1/8/1PP1PNB1/.text:
White could also go for development. 

The nice thing is that their queenside is under attack by our bishop and queen, so they cannot easily develop it.

r1b1k2r/pp1nnpp1/1qp4p/3p4/3Pp3/1P2P3/P1.text:
We recapture with our knight. 

We'll be playing ...f5 and ...Nf6 after the f-pawn moves. 

We'll castle kingside and go for an attack on that side of the board.

r1b1k2r/pp2ppb1/2n2n1p/2qp2p1/8/1PP1PNB1.text:
We should just develop as well though. 

Amazingly, the engine gives Black an advantage with moves like ...h5 for ...h4, but this is really sharp. 

You could also centralize the knight with ...Ne4, castle kingside, and continue attacking the weak points with your pieces.

r1b1kbnr/pp1n1pp1/1qp4p/3p4/3Pp2B/1P2P3/.text:
The knight must retreat. 

We develop and challenge the h4-bishop with our own, 8...Be7.

r1b1kbnr/pp1n1pp1/1qp4p/3pP3/7B/1P2PN2/P.text:
White captures, but this trade favors us.

We take on e5 with the knight.

r1b1kbnr/pp1n1pp1/1qp4p/3pp3/3P3B/1P2PN2.text:
The bishop goes to e2 since Bd3 is impossible because of e5.

We still attack the f3-knight with our e-pawn - our pawn chain grants us space and central control.

r1b1kbnr/pp3pp1/2p4p/3pN3/1q5B/1P2P3/P1P.text:
But we can go after the bishop. 

We'll get the bishop pair and get our queen into f6. 

We'll have a slight positional edge.

r1bqk2r/1p1nbpp1/p3pn1p/2pp4/3P3B/2NBPN2.text:
If White prepares e4…

We chase the bishop from d3 with 9...c4.

r1bqk2r/1p1nbpp1/p3pn1p/3p4/2pP3B/2N1PN2.text: No matter where the bishop goes...

r1bqk2r/1p2bpp1/p3pn1p/2np4/7B/2NBPN2/PP.text:
Black has a better position and one extra pawn in the center, thus more central control. 

We'll continue with ...0-0, ...b6 and ...Bb7.

r1bqk2r/1ppnbpp1/p3pn1p/3p4/3P3B/2NBPN2/.text:
When White castles…

8…c5 is already very strong. 

We’re threatening to chase the bishop from d3.

r1bqk2r/3nbpp1/p3pn1p/1p1p4/2pP3B/2N1PN2.text:
We have a lot of space on the queenside and a robust pawn structure; meanwhile White's pieces aren't so well-coordinated. 

...Bb7 and ...0-0 are in the horizon, and we can even consider queenside play because we're so far advanced on that side of the board.

r1bqkb1r/1ppn1pp1/p3pn1p/3p4/3P3B/2NBPN2.text:
7.Bd3 is the most popular continuation.

We unpin the knight with 7..Be7, gaining more control of e4.

r1bqkb1r/pppn1pp1/4pn1p/3p4/3P3B/2N1PN2/.text:
The bishop retreats to h4, keeping the pin. 

White may consider 7.Bb5, pinning our d7-knight.

So we play 6…a6, preventing Bb5 and preparing …c5.

r1bqkb1r/pppn1ppp/4pn2/3p2B1/3P4/2N1PN2/.text:
White plays 5.e3 to activate the light-squared bishop.

We gain a tempo with 5...h6, asking the bishop a question.

r1bqkb1r/pppnpppp/5n2/3p2B1/3P4/2N2N2/PP.text:
White continues developing.

We strengthen the center with 4...e6, opening the diagonal for the dark-squared bishop.

r3kb1r/pp1n1pp1/1qp2n1p/3p1b2/3P3B/2P2N2.text:
White develops their bishop to e2, and we see one benefit of …Bf5 - we control d3, preventing Bd3.

Our dark-squared bishop goes to a strong diagonal via d6.

r3kbnr/pp1n1pp1/1qp4p/3p1b2/3P3B/2P2N2/P.text:
White brings the knight out. 

We mirror the development, 9...Ngf6.

r3kbnr/pp2ppp1/1qn4p/3Q4/3P3B/1P5P/P1P2P.text:
White may try to exchange pawns to avoid structural damage... 

But 10…Rd8 activates the rook - 
…Rxd4 is coming.

r3kbnr/pp3pp1/1qn1p2p/3pN3/3P3B/1P6/P1P1.text:
And now we put pressure on the pawn. 

10...Qxd4 allows 11. Qb5+. 

But after 10...Nc6, we've got ideas of bringing a rook into c8 and developing our knight from g to e7. 

We've got pressure against the center and White's pieces, like the h4-bishop, don't have meaningful roles.

r4rk1/pp1n1pp1/1qpb1n1p/3p1b2/3P3B/2P2N2.text:
And we castle too. 

We're going to centralize the rooks.

If the bishop goes to g3, we'll go for a trade. 

We've got superior piece placement and so we should have a stable edge in the middlegame.

rn2kbnr/pp2ppp1/1q5p/2pp4/3P2bB/1P2PN1P/.text:
White tries to provoke a capture. 

Here, we should take on f3 - the d4-pawn becomes weak.

rn2kbnr/pp2ppp1/1q5p/2pp4/3P2bB/1P2PN2/P.text:
White may unpin the knight.

We play 7…e6 to connect the pawn chain. 

We have ideas of …Bxf3 and cxd4.

rn2kbnr/pp2ppp1/1q5p/2pp4/3P3B/1P2PQ1P/P.text:
The queen recaptures. 

White attacks d5, we attack d4.

We take on d4 - it looks equal, but it isn’t.

rn2kbnr/pp2ppp1/1q5p/3Q4/3p3B/1P2P2P/P1P.text:
The problem is that when White takes on d5, the queen isn't safe.

We develop the knight and support d4 while clearing the way for 
…Rd8.

rn2kbnr/pp3pp1/1q2p2p/2ppN3/3P2bB/1P2P3/.text:
White may misplay with a centralized knight and a discovered attack. 

We gladly take on e2.

rn2kbnr/pp3pp1/1q2p2p/2ppN3/3P3B/1P2P3/P.text:
When the queen recaptures, it no longer defends d4.

We take on d4 - but the isn't to win the pawn on d4 right away.

rn2kbnr/pp3pp1/1qp4p/3p1b2/3P3B/2P5/PP1N.text:
White starts queenside development.

We do the same, 8...Nd7 - our pieces go to more natural squares.

rnb1k1nr/pp2ppb1/7p/2qp2p1/8/1PP1PNB1/P4.text:
White blocks the diagonal. 

We don't want to take on c3; instead, we continue developing and play 9...Nc6 - it improves our control of e5 and d4.

rnb1kbnr/pp2pp2/1qp4p/3p2p1/3P4/5NB1/PPP.text:
The bishop drops to g3.

We remove the defender of d4 by pushing our g-pawn once again.

rnb1kbnr/pp2pp2/1qp4p/3pN3/3P2p1/6B1/PPP.text:
The knight centralizes to e5, but the square is unstable - we will remove one of its defenders.

We take on d4 with the queen and  already are a pawn up. 

All we need now is to catch up in development.

rnb1kbnr/pp2pp2/2p4p/2qpN3/6p1/4P1B1/PPP.text:
Our queen is quite active on c5. 

Our next move will be ...Bg7 to protect the diagonal. ...Nd7 is good to challenge the e5-knight, and ...h5 to support our advance g4-pawn will help us keep that pawn there. 

All we have to do is catch up in development and use our extra pawn in the middlegame.

rnb1kbnr/pp2pp2/7p/2qp2p1/8/1P2PNB1/P1P2.text:
The bishop must go to g3 - only move.

Now we hit the rook by completing the fianchetto.

rnb1kbnr/pp2ppp1/1q5p/2Pp4/7B/1P3N2/P1P1.text:
Another natural reaction to ...c5 is for White to take it.

We'll recapture with the queen, with some pressure against the c-pawn.

rnb1kbnr/pp2ppp1/1q5p/2pp4/3P3B/1P2PN2/P.text:
White may refuse to capture and simply support d4.

We pin the defender with 6...Bg4 - adding central pressure before 
…e6.

rnb1kbnr/pp2ppp1/1qp4p/3p4/3P3B/1P2P3/P1.text:
White may defend b2 by pushing it, but that creates plenty of dark-square weaknesses.

Since the knight isn’t on f3 to fight for e5, we can play 5…e5 here.

rnb1kbnr/pp2ppp1/1qp4p/3p4/3P3B/1P3N2/P1.text:
Pushing the pawn is the natural way to defend it.

We immediately undermine d4 with our c-pawn - this also frees the c6-square for our knight.

rnb1kbnr/pp2ppp1/1qp4p/3p4/3P3B/4P3/PPP2.text:
White may defend b2 with 5.Qc1, but the queen is passive.

Without Nf3, we can undermine d4 in a very tricky way, with 5...e5 - White should not capture.

rnb1kbnr/pp2ppp1/1qp4p/3p4/3P3B/5N2/PPP1.text:
Another defense is 5.Qc1. 

The queen isn’t happy here.

We attack the bishop with 5…g5. 

The point is simple: …g4 wins the d4-pawn - White cannot prevent it.

rnb1kbnr/pp2ppp1/7p/2qp4/7B/1P2PN2/P1P2P.text:
White continues developing, so expect 7.e3.

With 7...g5, we gain a tempo and prepare a great diagonal for our dark-squared bishop.

rnb1kbnr/pp3pp1/1qp4p/3p4/3P3B/2P5/PP3PP.text:
White usually recaptures with the e-pawn. 

That gives White's queen extra squares, but Black’s queen is far more active.

With 7...Bf5, our development becomes harmonious.

rnb1kbnr/pp3pp1/1qp4p/3pP3/7B/4P3/PPP2PP.text: Many players will fall for this one.

rnb1kbnr/pp3pp1/1qp4p/3pp3/3P3B/1P2PN2/P.text:
White targets our e5-pawn. 

We defend with 6...Nd7 - the same ...Qb4+ trick remains possible.

rnb1kbnr/pp3pp1/1qp4p/3pp3/3P3B/2P1P3/PP.text:
The most popular response is defending with c3. 

We take on d4.

rnb1kbnr/pp3pp1/2p4p/3pP3/1q5B/1P2P3/P1P.text: But as we've seen, the bishop is falling.

rnb1kbnr/pp3pp1/2p4p/3pP3/1q5B/4P3/PPP2P.text: This check picks up the bishop.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p2B1/3P4/2N5/PPP1.text:
3.Bg5 targets f6 and tries to ruin our pawn structure.

We defend with 3…Nbd7, ready to recapture on f6 with the knight.

rnbqkbnr/pp2ppp1/2p4p/3p4/3P3B/4P3/PPP2P.text:
4.e3 is the most popular move, connecting White’s pawn chain.

And this is where our setup shines - we attack the vulnerable b2-pawn with the queen after the early bishop development.

rnbqkbnr/pp2ppp1/2p4p/3p4/3P3B/5N2/PPP1P.text:
White may go for simple development with 4.Nf3. 

We can attack b2 with the queen here as well.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1ppp1/7p/3p4/3P3B/8/PPP1PPPP.text:
The natural reaction is to keep the pin.

We answer with 3...c6, defending d5 and giving the queen a diagonal - on b6 we will attack b2.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p2B1/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP.text:
2.Bg5 is an immediate attempt to annoy us, pinning the e-pawn. 

The bishop won’t stay there long.

We kick it with 2…h6.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/3P4/2N5/PPP1PPPP.text:
Another move you’ll face after 1.d4 d5 is 2.Nc3, the Veresov. 

White wants a quick e4.

We develop the kingside knight to f6 first.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to the last study of this chapter! 

Here we analyze positions where White’s second move is either 2.Bg5 or 2.Nc3.

White begins with the Queen’s Pawn opening.

We respond symmetrically with 
1…d5.

r1bqkb1r/pp3pp1/2n2n1p/2p1p3/N1Pp4/3P1NP.text:
First we play 8...h6, disallowing Bg5 by White before we continue developing.

As we have shown, 3.g3 by White has lead them nowhere. 

Now they have a stuck knight on a4, a lack of space and it is not clear how they will continue.

On the other hand, we are ready to develop the bishop to d6 and castle, with a better position.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/2n5/2p1p3/N1Pp4/3P1NP1/P.text:
Instead, White develops normally. 

We mirror with 7...Nf6.

r2q1rk1/1b1n1ppp/p2b1n2/1ppP4/8/2N1PNP1/.text:
13...b5 grabs more space on the queenside.

Now the knight on c3 is also a target for our pawns. The position is -1.0.

White should definitely trade the knights on d5!

r2q1rk1/1b1n1ppp/p2b4/1ppP4/4P3/5NP1/PB3.text:
15.e4 grabs more space in the center and defends d5.

However, White would love to push e5 and completely take control of the center, which would be a huge problem!

15...Re8 stops it and targets e4.

r2q1rk1/1b1n1ppp/pp1b1n2/2pN4/2P5/4PNP1/.text:
White captures with the knight, opening up the dark-squared bishop.

We go for the knight trade.

r2q1rk1/1b1n1ppp/pp1b1n2/2pP4/8/2N1PNP1/.text: If White chooses not to trade the knights on d5, we simply continue with our plan.

r2q1rk1/1b1n1ppp/pp1b4/2pP4/8/4PNP1/PB3P.text:
And White finally recaptures with the pawn.

Now we begin our queenside expansion. 

The 3-1 pawn majority is enormous - plus we now have a passed c-pawn.

r2q1rk1/1b1n1ppp/pp1bpn2/2pP4/2P5/2N1PNP.text:
For that reason, White tries to close down the center and grab more space with 12.d5.

We capture, planning ...b5 and ...c4 when the pawn recaptures.

r2q1rk1/1bpn1ppp/pp1bpn2/3p4/2PP4/1PN1PN.text:
White activates the rook to the c-file, preparing for potential pressure if the file opens.

We connect our rooks as well with 10...Qe7. 

This line is highly positional - both sides improve everything before committing.

r2q1rk1/1bpn1ppp/pp1bpn2/8/2PP4/2N1PNP1/.text:
White castles as well...

Now we strike with 11...c5!, grabbing space and creating tension.

White shouldn’t capture - it helps us activate our pieces.

r2qk2r/1bpn1ppp/pp1bpn2/8/2PP4/2N1PNP1/P.text:
White continues with their plan.

We castle.

r2qkb1r/1b1n1ppp/p3pn2/1pp5/3P4/2N1PN2/P.text:
Having no need to capture and make it easier for White to coordinate pieces, we simply develop and support the c5-square with our knight.

Next, we will play ...Rc8, ...Be7 and castle. 

The engine claims that the position is equal, but from a human standpoint I would argue that we are already better!

r2qr1k1/1b1n1ppp/p2b4/1p1P4/2p1P3/5NP1/P.text:
16...c4 defends our pawn and frees up the c5-square as an excellent outpost for our pieces.

Our play will definitely focus on the queenside with ideas of bringing the rook and trying to utilize the 3-1 pawn advantage.

However, White will focus on the two strong center pawns, probably bring the rooks to the center and try to push!

It's a balanced but extremely sharp game with a lot of chances for both sides.

r2qr1k1/1b1n1ppp/p2b4/1ppP4/4P3/5NP1/PBQ.text: White activates the queen, connects the rooks and defends the pawn on e4, while also putting pressure on our c-pawn.

r4rk1/1bpnq1pp/pp1bp3/3p1p2/2PPn3/1PNBPN.text:
However, 12...f5 completely solidifies the knight!

Now we have a lot of space on the board and have made it impossible for White to capture on e4, as ...fxe4 would activate our rook and simply give us too much advantage.

White will probably rely on capturing on d5 and opening up the c-file. 

We'll play our other knight to f6 and maybe even go for ...c5.

r4rk1/1bpnqppp/pp1bp3/3p4/2PPn3/1PNBPN2/.text: White improves the position of their bishop and targets our knight, with possible ideas of trading.

r4rk1/1bpnqppp/pp1bpn2/3p4/2PP4/1PN1PN2/.text:
White keeps optimizing their pieces and might aim for e4 soon, which would be very strong for them.

We prevent that with 11...Ne4!, our most active piece, solidly supported.

rn1q1rk1/1bp2ppp/pp1bpn2/3p4/2PP4/1PN1PN.text:
White strikes in the center, gaining space with all pieces developed.

We finish piece development with 9...Nbd7, controlling key central squares.

rn1qk2r/1bp2ppp/pp1bpn2/3p4/2P5/1PN1PN2/.text:
Before the battle begins, the kings must be safe...

White castles.

So do we.

rn1qk2r/1bp2ppp/pp1bpn2/3p4/2PP4/1PN1PNP.text:
White goes for a double fianchetto - let’s learn the antidote.

We start by capturing on c4, opening our bishop.

rn1qk2r/1bp2ppp/pp1bpn2/8/2PP4/2N1PNP1/P.text:
As White wants to fianchetto on g2, they recapture with the pawn.

This way they also keep pawns in the center, which is always important.

However, having played 9.bxc4, White now has only 2 pawns on the queenside, while we have 3.

We finish queenside development with 9...Nbd7.

Next we want to castle and play for the critical ...c5 push, supported by the knight.

rn1qkb1r/1b3ppp/p3pn2/1pp5/3P4/2N1PN2/PP.text: White has been passive enough and strikes in the center!

rnbqk2r/1pp1bppp/p3pn2/3p4/2PP4/2N1PN2/P.text:
We develop, ready to castle.

You know how to play this position!

rnbqk2r/1pp2ppp/p2b1n2/3p4/3P4/2N1PN2/PP.text:
However, after 6...Bd6 we have developed the kingside and are ready to castle with little to no problems in the position.

Notice how this position is almost the same as the positions of Chapter 2, with the c1-bishop being stuck as a difference!

That means that this way of playing is far from optimal for White.

rnbqk2r/1pp2ppp/p2bpn2/3p4/2P5/1PN1PN2/P.text:
White develops naturally on the long diagonal. 

After 6...b6 our own bishop will soon reach b7 as well.

rnbqk2r/1pp2ppp/p2bpn2/3p4/2PP4/1PN1PN2/.text:
White challenges the center early.

We prevent the c5 expansion and prepare to fianchetto with 6...b6.

rnbqk2r/2p2ppp/pp1bpn2/3p4/2P5/1PN1PN2/P.text:
White completes kingside development.

We fianchetto our light-squared bishop.

rnbqk2r/2p2ppp/pp1bpn2/3p4/2PP4/1PN1PN2/.text:
White completes queenside development by fianchettoing their bishop.

We do the same.

rnbqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p3pn2/3P4/8/2N1PN2/PP1P.text:
White captures on d5…

We recapture, maintaining healthy central control.

rnbqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p3pn2/3p4/2P5/1PN1PN2/P.text:
White prevents ...dxc4 and prepares to recapture with the pawn. 

The dark-squared bishop wants to head to b2, since it has no other good square.

We continue developing. With no Bg5 issues, 5...Bd6 is perfectly placed.

rnbqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p3pn2/3p4/2P5/2N1PN2/PP.text:
5.Be2 does nothing to stop our idea and loses a tempo.

We continue with 5...dxc4.

rnbqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p3pn2/3p4/2PP4/2N1PN2/P.text: 5.d4 simply transposes the position back to Chapter 3.

rnbqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p3pn2/8/2B5/2N1PN2/PP1P.text:
White recaptures, but this is what we wanted.

6...b5! hits the bishop and opens b7 for ours.

rnbqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p4n2/3p4/3P4/2N1PN2/PP3.text: White continues with the natural 6.d4, placing another pawn in the center and grabbing space.

rnbqkb1r/2p2ppp/p3pn2/1p6/8/2N1PN2/PP1PB.text:
The bishop retreats.

Before developing our light-squared bishop, we take more space with 7...c5!, grabbing full queenside control.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/2P5/2N1PN2/PP1.text:
White mirrors our development.

And we implement our classic idea with 4...a6! 

We want to capture on c4 and expand on the queenside with ...b5 and ...Bb7.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/8/2p1p3/N1Pp4/3P2P1/PP2P.text:
White opens the diagonal for the bishop.

We choose 6...Nc6, an active developing move. 

We don’t mind doubled c-pawns - White would be trading their only active piece!

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3P4/8/2N5/PP1PPPPP/.text: If White chooses to capture the pawn on d5 immediately...

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/2P5/2N1P3/PP1P1.text:
3.e3 is the main move and White’s best plan here.

Of course, 3.d4 simply transposes to the QGD structures we already know.

We develop with 3...Nf6, reinforcing the center.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/2P5/2N3P1/PP1PP.text:
3.g3 is actually a mistake - let’s see why.

White wants to fianchetto, but before they finish developing:

We immediately play 3...d4!, kicking the knight from c3. 

If White isn’t precise, trouble comes quickly.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/8/2PpN3/6P1/PP1PPP1.text: 4.Ne4 centralizes the knight and it looks like White is doing fine...

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/8/N1Pp4/6P1/PP1PPP1.text:
White may retreat to the rim.

Now we seize space with 4...e5!, something rarely possible in these structures. 

Our light-squared bishop will develop smoothly.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3p4/8/2N5/PP1PPPPP/R1.text:
We simply recapture. White has made it easier for our light-squared bishop to develop!

We have already seen positions like this in earlier chapters.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/4p3/N1Pp4/6P1/PP1PPPB.text:
White keeps developing, but the knight remains stuck on a4.

We solidify with 5...c5, taking away the b4 square.

rnbqkbnr/ppp3pp/4p3/5p2/2PpN3/6P1/PP1PPP.text:
But 4...f5 traps the knight!

All of the squares the knight could escape to are covered by our pawns and pieces.

Oops!

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/4p3/8/2P5/2N5/PP1PPPPP.text:
White develops the queen’s knight and adds pressure on d5.

We calmly continue with 2...d5, now properly supported. 

White has different options, but everything eventually leads back to the main line - other attempts are either inferior or already seen in previous chapters!

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/2P5/8/PP1PPPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to Chapter 8! 

In this and in the next chapter, we will analyze what to do when White opens with the English (1.c4) instead of the traditional Queen’s pawn systems.

Chapter 8 covers White’s setup with knights on c3 and f3, followed by 3.e3.

White opens with the 4th most popular move in chess, 1.c4, discouraging the immediate ...d5. 

1...e6 prepares the central break we want.

1r1q1rk1/p1p2ppp/4pn2/4n1N1/b7/P1P3P1/PB.text:
14...Ne5 proves our whole point. 

We have neutralized all of White's threats and have huge threats of our own!

...Nc4 and ...Qd2 both pressure the bishop on b2, which is pinned and blocked in by White's own pawn!

...Qd2 even attacks the knight on g5!

The evaluation of this position is -6. We are winning!

1r1q1rk1/p1pn1ppp/4pn2/6N1/b1p5/P5P1/PB1.text:
White moves the bishop away, but that is not the end of their troubles.

Out of nowhere, 13...c3 attacks the pinned bishop on b2! 

We also clear the c4-square for our knight to reroute to.

1r1q1rk1/p1pn1ppp/4pn2/6N1/b7/P1P3P1/PB2.text: Having no other choice, White captures.

r1b1k2r/1pp1qppp/1n2p3/p2n4/P7/3R1NP1/1P.text:
11...Qe7 simply moves the queen out of the way and threatens our knight to come to b4 again.

White has already castled but needs to deal with our threats and develop the dark-squared bishop.

On the other hand, we are yet to castle and figure out the development of our own light-squared bishop.

One of the plans could be to go for a quick ...f6 and ...e5, opening the diagonal for the bishop!

r1b1k2r/ppp1bppp/1n2pn2/8/2p1q3/5NP1/PP1.text:
And we simply develop our bishop to e7 and are ready to castle and develop our light-squared bishop, centralize the rooks and enjoy a comfortable position!

The computer claims it's equal but we have more activity and space.

I would much rather play Black here!

r1b1kb1r/1pp2ppp/1n2pn2/p1q5/P1p5/5NP1/1.text:
In the variation with Ne5 on move 
7...Qe4 was recommended, trying to trade queens.

That's also fine here, but since White has commited their queenside with a4, ...Qc5 is more active with possible plans of queenside play in the future.

Next, we will develop and castle!

r1b1kb1r/1pp2ppp/1n2pn2/p7/P1pq4/5NP1/1P.text: With no better move, White retreats.

r1b1kb1r/ppp2ppp/1n2pn2/8/2p1q3/5NP1/PP1.text: White passively retreats, but keeps the queens alive.

r1b1kb1r/ppp2ppp/1n2pn2/8/2pq4/5NP1/PPQP.text:
White admits they have no better option and retreats, attacking our queen.

Since we want our c4-pawn to survive, we try trading queens with 8...Qe4, as that would remove one of White’s attackers from c4. 

If White captures, we will have a knight in the center of the board with no problems in the position.

r1bq1rk1/1pp2ppp/3b1n2/p3p3/P1Q5/5NP1/1P.text:
...And we castle, with an equal position.

Even though White has regained the pawn, they have let us develop and grab some space in the process!

The queen on c4 can easily become a target for moves like ...Be6. 

Also, we will develop our queen, move our rooks to the center and battle!

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/1n2pn2/8/2p5/P4NP1/PBQP.text:
...White develops the queen, putting pressure on the key c4-pawn. 

But it is defended, for now.

With no ...b5 and ...Bb7 idea being possible here, we simply develop our bishop to d7. 

In the future, we might try to reroute it to a4 and pressure White’s queen. 

We must not forget about the undefended b7-pawn, as it can become a target in many positions!

r1bqk1nr/1pp2ppp/1n2p3/p7/P1p5/R4NP1/1PQ.text:
Naturally, White recaptures with the rook.

After 8...Nf6 we have developed the kingside and are ready to castle. 

In the future, we might centralize the knight on f6 and possibly jump to the dangerous b4-square.

r1bqk2r/1pp2ppp/1n1b1n2/p3p3/P1N5/5NP1/1.text:
White finally takes the c4-pawn.

Since we don’t want White to trade for our bishop on d6, we capture on c4.

r1bqk2r/1pp2ppp/1n1bpn2/p7/P1p5/N4NP1/1P.text:
However, White targets the c4-pawn with the now well-known 9.Na3.

As we don’t have a good way of defending c4 in this variation, we choose to grab space with 9...e5 instead. 

Now our light-squared bishop can come to life!

r1bqk2r/1pp2ppp/1n2p3/p2n4/P1p5/R2P1NP1/.text:
And White has had enough of our c4-pawn! 

10.d3, although a simple move, changes a lot. 

Now we are left with very few options…

The most logical one is simply to capture, as it was very hard to defend c4!

r1bqk2r/1pp2ppp/1n2p3/p2n4/P1p5/R4NP1/1P.text:
...and we do just that!

We'll castle, try to place the knight on the b4-square and deal with White's d3- or b3-pawn breaks, probably by capturing!

r1bqk2r/1pp2ppp/1n2p3/p2n4/P7/3R1NP1/1PQ.text:
This is the other point of the rook lift to a3. 

White now activates the rook on the central d-file and is pinning our knight to our queen!

r1bqk2r/1pp2ppp/1n2pn2/p7/P1p5/R4NP1/1PQ.text:
The rook recaptures, as bxa3 would only double White’s pawns and ruin their queenside pawn structure. 

Also, the rook supports the d3-square if White wants to challenge our c4-pawn with d3.

Since White has committed with a4, 9...Nfd5 centralizes our knight and threatens to jump to b4, which would be an excellent outpost!

r1bqk2r/1ppnbppp/p3pn2/8/2Q5/2N2NP1/PP1P.text: But as soon as White finally captures the c4-pawn...

r1bqk2r/2pnbppp/p3pn2/1p6/2Q5/2N2NP1/PP1.text:
...Here comes 8...b5, with tempo on the queen!

Next, we will play ...Bb7 and castle.
 
In the future, we might even consider queenside expansion with ...b4 and ...a5.

The position is sharp but equal!

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/1n2pn2/8/2p5/P4NP1/PB1PP.text:
Having captured on a3 with the pawn, White now has room to activate their own bishop on the b2-square.

Once we bring the king to safety…

r1bqk2r/pppn1ppp/4pn2/8/2p5/P4NP1/P2PPPB.text:
Forced.

We get the knight out of d7, 7...Nb6.

Now our queen and light-squared bishop have room to develop. 

Also, we add another defender to the c4-pawn.

r1bqkb1r/1pp2ppp/1n2pn2/p3N3/P1p5/6P1/1P.text:
Here comes Ne5 once again, with an attack on c4. 

But we know what to do!

The queen is active on d4, attacks the knight, and defends c4 at the same time.

r1bqkb1r/1pp2ppp/1n2pn2/p7/P1p5/5NP1/1PQ.text:
8.Rd1 places the rook on the central d-file with ideas of going for the d3-break in the future.

We develop with 8...Bd6 and block any potential pins from White on the d-file later on. 

Since White hasn’t made any serious threats yet and has little control of the center, we might decide to take some central space ourselves!

r1bqkb1r/1pp2ppp/1n2pn2/p7/P1p5/N4NP1/1P.text:
The knight is developed to the edge of the board, and now two pieces are pressuring our c4-pawn. 

It’s not easy to defend, so…

We remove the knight! 

As we can see, the c4-pawn is a critical pawn in the position, and we should do everything in our power to keep it alive, as it greatly restricts White’s development!

r1bqkb1r/1ppn1ppp/p3pn2/8/2Q5/5NP1/PP1PP.text:
The pawn falls… 

But 7...b5 comes with tempo again, allowing us to develop the bishop on the next move.

r1bqkb1r/1ppn1ppp/p3pn2/8/Q1p5/2N2NP1/PP.text:
Before doing anything else, White brings the king to safety. 

We complete kingside development, 7...Be7, and are ready to castle.

r1bqkb1r/2pn1ppp/p3pn2/1p6/8/5NP1/PPQPPP.text: The queen moves out of the way.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/1n2pn2/4N3/2p5/6P1/PPQP.text:
White might implement the now familiar Ne5 idea again. 

By attacking the c4-pawn one more time, White also puts pressure on b7 and makes it harder for us to develop.

However, we have 7...Qd4! 

We suddenly centralize the queen, defend our pawn, and attack the e5-knight at the same time!

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/1n2pn2/8/P1p5/5NP1/1PQP.text:
White tries to create play on the queenside and kick out our knight…

7...a5 simply prevents a5 from White. 

The queenside is successfully locked!

r1bqkb1r/pppn1ppp/4pn2/8/2p5/5NP1/PPQPPP.text:
6.Qc2 develops the queen and puts pressure on the currently undefended c4-pawn!

And we make use of our early ...Nd7 idea and play 6...Nb6. 

Our c4-pawn is now defended, and our queen and light-squared bishop have room to develop.

r1bqkb1r/pppn1ppp/4pn2/8/2p5/N4NP1/PP1PP.text:
Instead of activating the queen, White might try to increase the pressure on our pawn with the knight on move 6.

Once again, we remove the knight, now forcing White to double their pawns on the a-file!

r1bqkb1r/pppn1ppp/4pn2/8/Q1p5/5NP1/PP1PP.text:
Having castled, White might choose to bring out the queen now, with similar ideas to what we saw in the 5.Qa4 variation. 

In this line, White chooses to capture immediately before moving the knight to c3.

We prepare ...b5 with 6...a6.

r1bqkbnr/1pp2ppp/1n2p3/p7/P1p5/N4NP1/1PQ.text:
This line is similar to the main line. 

White attacks the c4-pawn with one more piece, making it hard for us to defend.

That’s why we remove the knight!

r1bqkbnr/1ppn1ppp/p3p3/8/Q1p5/2N2NP1/PP1.text:
After 6.Nc3, 6...b5 would be a blunder! 

The knight could simply capture, and 7...axb5 would leave our rook hanging. 

Whenever we are trying to play ...b5, we must always look out for tactics like this, especially with our rook being undefended and the White bishop controlling this dangerous diagonal!

So we just continue developing instead, 6...Nf6.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/1n2p3/8/P1p5/5NP1/1PQPP.text:
As in the main line, White tries to kick our knight out. 

We won’t let them, 6...a5!

r1bqkbnr/pppn1ppp/4p3/8/2p5/5NP1/PP1PPPB.text:
White has completed kingside development and castles. 

We develop the kingside knight to its natural square.

r1bqkbnr/pppn1ppp/4p3/8/2p5/5NP1/PPQPPPB.text:
Another approach for White is 5.Qc2, developing the queen to a safer square and targeting our c4-pawn.

This is where ...Nd7 becomes useful, as we now defend c4 from b6.

r1bqkbnr/pppn1ppp/4p3/8/Q1p5/5NP1/PP1PPP.text:
Instead of going for the safer route and castling, White chooses a more aggressive approach. 

5.Qa4 pins our knight to our king, making ...Nb6 impossible, and attacks c4 at the same time. 

It’s hard to defend c4 now…

Although a calm-looking move, 5...a6 prepares ...b5 in the future, defending the c4-pawn. 

If White captures now and we push ...b5, that would actually speed up our queenside development, as we’ll soon see.

r2q1rk1/pBpn1ppp/4pn2/6N1/b1p5/P5P1/PB1P.text:
...And our precise play may cause White to blunder! 

Bxb7 is a huge mistake. Let’s exploit it!

We move the rook out of danger and attack the bishop on b7. 

Notice that White has three pieces on the open b-file! 

White should never have opened it.

r2q1rk1/pp3ppp/1np1pn2/8/b1N5/P1Q3P1/PB1.text:
However, should White choose to capture on c4...

We trade on c4.

r2q1rk1/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/1b6/2Q5/P5P1/PB1PP.text:
And this is the key idea to remember!

Even though we lost the c4-pawn, we have 13...Bb5, attacking the queen and targeting the e2-pawn behind her!

The only way for White to defend against that is to trade on f6 and play Qe4.

However, with the two weak pawns on the queenside against our three, that might not be the best idea!

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/1n2pn2/4N3/b1p5/P1Q3P1/P.text:
However, White plays 11.Qc3, lining up with the bishop on b2 and still defending the pawn. 

Our b7-pawn is still hanging!

11...c6 blocks the bishop from capturing on b7.

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/1n2pn2/6N1/b1p5/P5P1/PB1.text:
White moves the queen away, but keeps it on the b1–h7 diagonal, recreating the checkmating threat.

Luckily, 11...Nbd7 reinforces the knight on f6. 

Now if Bxf6 happens, we will recapture with the knight and cover the h7-pawn. 

We are safe for now…

r2q1rk1/pppb1ppp/1n2pn2/4N3/2p5/P5P1/PBQ.text:
One of White’s ideas is 10.Ne5. 

White is targeting both of our pawns on c4 and b7 at the same time! 

However, this is a slight inaccuracy.

Let’s continue with our idea of hitting the queen on the c2-square!

As we can see after 10...Ba4, White’s d2-pawn is weak, and pushing the queen away from it may allow us to capture it.

r2q1rk1/pppb1ppp/1n2pn2/6N1/2p5/P5P1/PBQ.text:
Another approach for White at the beginning of the middlegame is 10.Ng5. 

Aside from threatening to win the b7-pawn, White is threatening something even more poisonous: Bxf6 followed by Qxh7# is a huge checkmating idea!

That’s why 10...Ba4 is the key move to remember in this variation. 

We move the bishop with tempo, counterattacking White’s queen.

r2qkb1r/1bpn1ppp/p3pn2/1p6/8/5NP1/PPQPPP.text:
And we activate our bishop on b7.

Next, we will develop the dark-squared bishop, castle, and possibly play on the queenside with ...Rc8 and ...c5.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/2P5/5NP1/PP1PPP.text:
The Nf3–g3 setup is definitely an interesting idea by White. 

With the bishop on the long h1–a8 diagonal, White aims for better central control and a generally safer king. 

However, 3.g3 loses a tempo and allows us to capture on c4! 

Other moves like 3.e3 or 3.b3 were already covered in Chapter 7.

Since White’s bishop is going to g2, it will be harder for White to regain the c4-pawn. 

We will probably try to hang on to it.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/8/2p5/5NP1/PP1PPPBP.text:
White continues developing. 

The position clearly resembles Catalan-like structures.

4...Nd7 is perhaps an unusual developing move, bringing out the queenside knight and temporarily blocking some of our own pieces. 

However, we plan to place the knight on b6 to defend the c4-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/4p3/8/2P5/5N2/PP1PPPPP.text:
Instead, with 2.Nf3, White chooses a move order that can transpose into many different openings. 

We grab space in the center with 2...d5.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/2P5/8/PP1PPPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to Chapter 9! 

 In this chapter, just like in the previous one, we will cover the English with 1.c4 by White. 

However, in Chapter 9 we focus on White placing the kingside knight on f3 and often playing g3 on the third move. 

As we will see, one of our key ideas is capturing on c4 and playing around our c4-pawn.

White plays the English Opening. 

We reply with 1...e6, ready to transpose into the QGD if White plays 2.d4.

1nbqkbnr/r1p2ppp/p3p3/1p2N3/2p5/2N3P1/PP.text:
We simply slide out of danger, with plans of ...Bb7. 

The position is equal but sharp!

1rbqkbnr/2pn1ppp/p3p3/1p6/P3Q3/5NP1/1P1P.text:
We simply slide one square, supporting the pawn on b5.

Although we lack in development, we'll make use of White bringing out the queen early and develop with tempo!

Moves such as ...Ngf6 and ...Bb7 attack the queen and activate our pieces at the same time.

2rqkb1r/1b1n1ppp/p3pn2/1pp5/3P4/5NP1/PPQ.text:
And we put our plan in motion! 

Now the c-pawn is supported by our rook.

We would like to capture on d4 as that would open up an attack on White's queen!

After that, we'll develop the dark-squared bishop, maybe even to c5, and castle.

We are better in this position.

r1bqkbnr/1ppn1ppp/p3p3/8/2Q5/5NP1/PP1PPP.text:
White opts for the calmer approach, finishing kingside development and getting ready to castle.

We move forward with our plan. 

Don’t forget to develop the bishop immediately after playing 6...b5, as the rook on a8 is vulnerable!

r1bqkbnr/1ppn1ppp/p3p3/8/P1Q5/5NP1/1P1PP.text:
White plays 6.a4, thinking they’ve stopped us from achieving our ...b5 push! 

But have they?

Absolutely not! 

Despite 6.a4, we still push on the queenside with similar plans! 

Let’s see why 6...b5 is possible.

r1bqkbnr/2pn1ppp/4p3/1p6/2Q5/5NP1/1P1PPP.text:
We simply recapture!

Although our own rook is hanging, White's queen and rook are attacked at the same time!

White can't defend both. Oops!

r1bqkbnr/2pn1ppp/p3p3/1P6/2Q5/5NP1/1P1PP.text: If White chooses to capture, thinking that's exactly what they wanted, they are losing on the spot!

r1bqkbnr/2pn1ppp/p3p3/1p6/8/5NP1/PPQPPPB.text:
The queen moves out of the way.

And we finally develop the bishop to b7. 

In the near future, we might be looking to expand on the queenside with moves like ...c5.

r1bqkbnr/2pn1ppp/p3p3/1p6/P3Q3/5NP1/1P1P.text: Instead of blundering, White moves the queen out of the way to the center of the board and hits our rook on a8.

r1bqkbnr/pppn1ppp/4p3/8/2Q5/5NP1/PP1PPP1.text:
Naturally, the queen captures.

And here is our main 5...a6 idea! 

As we already know, we want to play ...b5 with tempo on the queen, followed by ...Bb7.

r2qk1nr/pb1n1ppp/4p3/1pp5/2p5/Q4NP1/PP1P.text:
We move forward with our plan!

Now we will finish kingside development and castle.

There could be some ...b4 ideas in the future, expanding on the queenside even more, so White has to be careful!

r2qk2r/1b1n1ppp/p3pn2/1pb5/8/5NP1/PPQ1PP.text:
We've now activated the bishop and are ready to castle!

Apart from that, the rook is coming to c8, our bishops are very active, and the queen is ready to jump into the game! 

Who wouldn't like this position?

r2qk2r/1b1nbppp/p3pn2/1pp5/8/1P3NP1/PBQP.text:
We can take a moment to expand on the c-file because 10...c5 is sufficiently supported. 

We'll continue with ...Qb6 and 
...0-0. 

Our rooks will most likely have to be centralized in open or semi-open files like the d- and c-files.

r2qk2r/1bpnbppp/p3pn2/1p6/8/1P3NP1/PBQPP.text: White will surely continue with Bb2.

r2qkb1r/1b1n1ppp/p3pn2/1pP5/8/5NP1/PPQ1P.text: If White chooses to capture instead of defending with the rook, this only helps us.

r2qkb1r/1b1n1ppp/p3pn2/1pp5/3P4/5NP1/PPQ.text: The rook defends, with plans of maybe capturing now and pinning our knight to our queen.

r2qkb1r/1b1n1ppp/p3pn2/1pp5/P7/5NP1/1PQP.text:
We expand on the queenside.

The b5-pawn is nicely protected by the a6-pawn, and we wouldn't mind a rook trade on the a-file should it open up.

We have excellent play on the queenside and might follow it up with moves like ...Qb6. 

Of course, we will develop with ...Be7 and ...O-O first.

r2qkb1r/1bpn1ppp/p3pn2/1p6/3P4/5NP1/PPQ1.text:
White strikes in the center! 

But this plays directly into our hands…

Now the ...c5 push is even more potent! 

It challenges White’s undefended d-pawn and threatens to open up the c-file and attack White!

r2qkb1r/1bpn1ppp/p3pn2/1p6/8/1P3NP1/P1QP.text:
White could also choose to play 9.b3 and develop the bishop to the b2-square. 

After 9...Be7 our plan remains the same: expand on the queenside, develop and castle! 

Again, in this line we can specifically consider putting the rook on the c-file, as White has not played a4.

r2qkb1r/1bpn1ppp/p3pn2/1p6/P7/5NP1/1PQPP.text:
White is trying to undermine our queenside pawn structure!

But we just continue with our plan...

r2qkbnr/1bpn1ppp/p3p3/1p6/8/5NP1/PPQPPPB.text:
Once White castles…

We simply develop the kingside knight to f6. 

However, that gives White time to challenge our queenside!

rn1qk1nr/pbp2ppp/4p3/1p6/2p5/Q4NP1/PP1PP.text:
White also fianchettos their light-squared bishop. 

We somehow need to block the queen’s vision of the f8-square in order to castle. 

The best way to do that would be ...c5, expanding on the queenside at the same time!

But we need to support it first with 7...Nd7.

rnbqk1nr/p1p2ppp/4p3/1p6/2p5/Q4NP1/PP1PP.text:
Instead, White goes ahead with their plan and captures with the queen on a3. 

Having played ...b5 with tempo, we now have room to develop our queenside bishop to b7!

rnbqk1nr/ppp2ppp/4p3/8/Q1p5/b4NP1/PP1PPP.text:
Instead of recapturing immediately and doubling their a-pawns, White brings out the queen and checks! 

They will probably capture the bishop with the queen next.

5...b5 is a smart move! 

Even though it seems like we are giving away a pawn with check, Qxb5 would be met by ...c6! 

The queen would be deflected from the bishop and we would save it.

rnbqkbnr/1pp2ppp/p3p3/8/2p5/2N2NP1/PP1PP.text:
With no good way to stop our plan, White continues development.

After 5...b5 we have a nice cluster of pawns on the queenside! 

However, with the light-squared bishop being on g2, there is always danger on the h1–a8 diagonal.

rnbqkbnr/2p2ppp/p3p3/1p2N3/2p5/2N3P1/PP1.text: That's why White centralizes the knight and puts pressure on our rook on a8.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/2P5/5NP1/PP1PPP.text:
The move 3.g3 is the traditional English approach by White, delaying d4. 

As in the last study, we know what to do!

We take on c4, with hopes of ...a6 and ...b5 in the next few moves. 

White now has three main options.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/8/2p5/2N2NP1/PP1PPP.text:
Another 4th-move idea for White instead of bringing out the queen early is to develop the knight to c3. 

The knight now covers the b5-square and makes it difficult to push ...b5 right away.

However, this approach is more passive and gives us everything we want!

That’s why we play the key 4...a6 move! 

Now ...b5 will be supported by a pawn.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/8/2p5/N4NP1/PP1PPP1.text:
And the third possibility we will analyze in this chapter is 4.Na3. 

White attacks our c4-pawn from the edge of the board instead of with the queen. 

As we have seen in the previous study, more often than not we will capture this knight!

4...Bxa3 removes the attacker.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/8/Q1p5/5NP1/PP1PPP1.text:
The queen activates to the edge of the board and forks our king and pawn.

Rather than blocking with the bishop, we block with the knight. 

The knight on d7 will serve as great reinforcement for the other knight on f6, since we are planning to develop our light-squared bishop to b7 anyway, as you will see.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/4p3/8/2P5/5N2/PP1PPPPP.text:
Instead of the QGD, White develops the knight to f3. 

As we know, 2.Nf3 is extremely flexible, leaving White with many options to choose from in the future.

We move forward with 2...d5.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/2P5/8/PP1PPPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to the second study of Chapter 9! 

In this study, we will go over the 4th-move deviations by White, such as 4.Qa4+, 4.Nc3 and 4.Na3. 

More often than not, White will opt for the 4.Bg2 approach, but it’s important to know these lines as well!

White opens with 1.c4.

1...e6 signals that we are prepared for QGD! But White has other plans…

1r1qkb1r/1b1n1ppp/p3pn2/1pp5/5B2/3P1NP1/.text: The bishop develops and attacks our rook.

1r1qkbnr/1b1n1ppp/p3p3/1pp5/8/3P1NP1/PPQ.text:
The 10.d3 idea for Bf4 shouldn't be concerning. 

The rook can just go to c8. 

We continue with kingside development, 10...Ngf6.

1r1qkbnr/1bpn1ppp/p3p3/1p6/8/5NP1/PPQPPP.text:
The queen is forced back.

We expand normally with 9...c5 - this is the structure you should expect.

1rbqkbnr/2pn1ppp/p1Q1p3/1p6/8/5NP1/PP1PP.text:
That’s why White often castles. 

After 8…Bb7, fianchettoing our bishop…

2rqkb1r/1b1n1ppp/p3pn2/1pp5/5B2/3P1NP1/P.text:
And the rook goes opposite the queen. 

This line isn't that common. 

You should spend most of your brain power memorizing more popular move orders like the previous studies or stuff like in Chapter 1-2 and the Anti-London. 

But if you ever do get something like this, the ideas stand. ...Be7, 
...0-0, ...Qb6 for queenside control.

r1b1kb1r/3n1ppp/pqN1p3/1ppB4/8/6P1/PPQPP.text: White could insert this capture to defend for one more move...

r1b1kb1r/3n1ppp/pqN5/1ppp4/8/6P1/PPQPPP1.text:
But after we recapture, the knight will be lost on the next move. 

It simply cannot get out.

r1bq1rk1/1p1nbppp/p3pn2/2p5/8/2N2NP1/PPQ.text:
And we'll castle kingside as well.

We have ideas of ...Qc7 and ...b5 to activate our pieces on the queenside. 

We'll go ...Bb7 but we'll always keep in mind that our rook could be attacked with a knight discovery, so we have to be careful.

r1bqkb1r/1p1n1ppp/p3pn2/2p5/8/2N2NP1/PPQ.text:
White develops the other knight and prepares to castle. 

We prepare castling as well, 8...Be7.

r1bqkb1r/1p1n1ppp/p3pn2/2p5/8/5NP1/PPQPP.text:
Let’s say they castle… 

Then 8...b5 is very strong.

r1bqkb1r/3n1ppp/p1N1p3/1ppn4/8/6P1/PPQPP.text:
Some players may be tempted to continue attacking.

But after 10...Qb6 the knight on c6 is completely trapped.

r1bqkb1r/3n1ppp/p3pn2/1pp1N3/8/6P1/PPQPP.text:
If White tries a discovered attack…

We simply block on d5, 9...Nd5.

r1bqkbnr/1p1n1ppp/p3p3/2p5/8/2N3P1/PPQPP.text:
7.Nc3 is best now. 

The knight controls key squares but cannot jump into them effectively.

We develop with 7...Ngf6, controlling e4 and d5.

r1bqkbnr/1p1n1ppp/p3p3/2p5/8/5NP1/PPQPPP.text:
White may also try to just develop the kingside as soon as possible.

Without the c-knight, we gain full control over d5 with 7...Ngf6.

r1bqkbnr/1ppn1ppp/p3p3/8/2Q5/5NP1/PP1PPP.text:
White may ignore the …b5 idea - or forget that it works, and caslte.

Even so, we are safe.

We play 6...b5 with tempo on the queen.

r1bqkbnr/1ppn1ppp/p3p3/8/8/6P1/PPQPPPBP/.text:
Many grandmasters bring the queen back to avoid …b5 with tempo. 

Their queen and bishop are well placed, which is why engines like the position for White.

I suggest 6…c5, gaining space and controlling d4. 

If White plays d4, we take.

r1bqkbnr/2pn1ppp/p1Q1p3/1p6/8/5NP1/PP1PP.text:
If the queen attacks our rook on a8…

7...Rb8 steps out of danger and makes …Bb7 come with tempo. 

If Ne5, then …Ne7 wins for Black because the queen will be chased and eventually distracted from defending the e5-knight.

r1bqkbnr/pppn1ppp/4p3/8/2Q5/6P1/PP1PPPBP.text:
Once White captures on c4…

We continue with our main idea 
5…a6, preparing …b5. 

But we must be careful: since White hasn’t played Nf3, a premature …b5 leaves the a8-rook vulnerable.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/2P5/6P1/PP1PPPB.text:
White completes the fianchetto and puts pressure on the center. 

As we’ve learned, we capture on c4 aiming to follow with …a6 to defend the pawn.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/8/Q1p5/6P1/PP1PPPBP.text:
But White has other plans! 

4.Qa4+ checks the king and attacks our c4-pawn. 

We cannot defend it.

We block with 4...Nd7, keeping the option of …Nb6.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/4p3/8/2P5/6P1/PP1PPP1P.text:
Rather than 2.d4 and entering QGD territory, White goes for a classical English setup with 2.g3 and Bg2.

We continue with 2...d5.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/2P5/8/PP1PPPPP/RNB.text:
In the last study of Chapter 9, we look at the possible 2.g3 move. 

Instead of the flexible 2.Nf3, White quickly develops the light-squared bishop, controls the h1–a8 diagonal, and prepares to recapture on c4 early.

White begins with the English and takes space in the center. 

We reply with 1...e6, supporting the …d5 push.

r1b1k2r/pppnQppp/3b1n2/1B1P4/8/2N5/PP1P1.text:
White takes. 

We recapture, and we’re castling next.

r1b1k2r/pppnbppp/5n2/1B1P4/8/2N2N2/PP1P1.text:
White may prepare castling themselves. 

We now castle, with the idea of ...Nb6 to put pressure on the d5-pawn.

r1b1kb1r/ppp1qppp/1nn5/1B6/8/1QN2N2/PP1P.text:
We can disrupt their coordination with 8...Qe7+. 

All the options of dealing with this check are unpleasant. 

Be2 makes the bishop retreat. 

Ne2 places the knight on a worse square, and moving the king loses castling rights.

r1b1kb1r/ppp1qppp/1nn5/8/8/1BN2N2/PP1PQP.text:
If the queen blocks, Black has more useful moves to make before the queen trade.

9...Bg4, for example, carries the positional threat of doubling the f-pawns.

r1b1kb1r/ppp1qppp/2n5/8/1n6/2N2Q2/PP1PBP.text:
The other knight can join the party. 

If Nd5, we trade knights on d5 and attack the queen with ...Be6. 

At any rate, we want to go ...Be6 and play ...0-0-0 to place our rook opposite the king.

r1b1kbnr/p3q1pp/2p2p2/3pP3/5P2/8/PP4PP/R.text:
9...f6 successfully undermines it. 

...Nh6 for ...Nf7 will help us add pressure on e5, but White really cannot defend it if not with awkward queen moves. 

The queen on d4 could be targetted with ...Nh6 to f5. And the queen on e2 could be forced to e5 with ...fxe5. 

Our c6-d5 structure is hard to undermine, so we'll control the center the entire game.

r1b1kbnr/p3qppp/2p5/3pP3/5P2/8/PP4PP/RNB.text:
9. f4 defends e5, yet it's not enough to keep things together. 

The e5-pawn is overextended.

r1b1kbnr/pp2qppp/2N5/3pP3/8/8/PP3PPP/RNB.text:
The most natural continuation is for White to trade on c6 and defend e5 momentarily. 

Once we recapture, we’re attacking e5 and we have fixed our structure, which is now the solid c6–d5 pawn chain.

r1b1kbnr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/3qP3/3p4/5N2/PP3PP.text:
We've got superior piece play and pressure, e5 will surely fall. 

Our d4-pawn cannot be easily dislodged. 

White could try trading with Qb3 to defend the e5-pawn. 

But taking on b3 with ...Bb4+ and ...Bc5 ideas to overprotect d4 is good enough. ...Nge7 for ...Ng6 is an idea to attack e5.

r1b2rk1/pp3ppp/2n2b2/q7/3P4/1QN2N2/PP3PP.text:
And after the knight blocks…

We can win the d-pawn back, 12...Nxd4.

r1b2rk1/pp3ppp/8/q7/3b4/1QN5/PP3PPP/R3KB.text:
And the bishop recaptures.

The king is in a pretty tough spot in the middle of the board. 

If 0-0-0, the king is put on the open c-file and moves like ...Be6 to attack the queen exist.

If Be2, ...Be6 and ...Rae8 are ideas. 

Going for the d-pawn isn't a good choice for White.

r1b2rk1/pppBbppp/5n2/3P4/8/2N2N2/PP1P1PP.text:
Giving up the bishop to remove our knight is an idea White may have. 

But this just gives us the bishop pair, allowing us to get the pawn back quite quickly.

r1bq1rk1/pp2bppp/2n2B2/3p4/3P4/1QN2N2/PP.text:
So just to illustrate that idea…

We can recapture and we’re attacking d4. 

Many players go for this continuation because it looks natural, but trading d-pawns isn’t an equal trade: Black is up in development and has a safer king!

r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/2n2b2/3N4/3P4/1Q3N2/PP3P.text:
11.Nxd5 is losing because of Black’s better pieces and White’s less safe king. 

The refutation begins with 11...Qa5+.

r1bqk2r/pp2bppp/2n2n2/2p5/2Pp4/3P1N2/PP2.text:
Still, we should just prepare castling. 

We'll play moves like ...h6 to control the g5-square and if Bf4, ...Bd6 to trade bishops.

We can even go ...a5 to control the b4-square even further.

r1bqk2r/pp2bppp/2n2n2/3p2B1/3P4/1QN2N2/P.text:
The 9.Bg5 move is still popular even if it isn’t a pin. 

The idea is to try to remove the defender of d5.

But we can just castle, because if White takes on f6, we recapture with the bishop and the e-file is open. 

Besides that, the bishop and knight would be attacking d4 in return.

r1bqk2r/pppn1ppp/3b1n2/1B1P4/8/2N5/PP1PQ.text:
Hence White may try to continue causing coordination issues by giving another check.

But the check doesn’t achieve anything, we can just block with the queen.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n2n2/2p5/2Pp4/3P1N2/PP2.text: White may put a rook on the e-file, but they don't even have a useful discovered check!

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n2n2/3p4/3P4/1QN2N2/PP3.text:
White has to defend d4.

We should break any potential Bg5 pins with 8...Be7 and get ready to castle.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/1nn5/1B6/8/1QN2N2/PP1P1.text: If White tries developing actively by creating a pin on one of the knights...

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/1nn5/8/8/1BN2N2/PP1P1PP.text:
White’s most natural attempt of developing and playing d4, 8.Nf3 runs into our next move.

We can give a check, 8...Qe7+ and force a piece into e2.

r1bqkb1r/pppn1ppp/5n2/1B1P4/8/2N5/PP1P1P.text:
White will usually try to make winning back the d-pawn difficult. 

But we’ll argue that if we get to castle, the pin will be eradicated and we’ll take the d5-pawn in no time.

So we prepare castling with 6...Bd6.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/2ppP3/2PP4/5N2/PP3.text:
If d4…

We can take the pawn, e5 is now really weak.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/2n5/2ppP3/3P4/5N2/PP3PPP.text:
White could develop their knight now, supporting d4 and e5. 

And we can insert the capture here to misplace the knight on d4.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/2n5/3pP3/3N4/8/PP3PPP/RN.text:
White takes. 

The knight on d4 no longer defends the e5-pawn, so we can attack it with our queen, 7...Qe7.

This is what I meant by misplacing the knight, there will be two attackers on e5.

r3k2r/ppp1bppp/1nn5/8/6b1/1BN2N2/PP1P1PP.text:
After 10...Bxe7, all our pieces are out. 

We still have the positional threat of capturing on f3. 

It's hard to stop this plan and it's tough for White to develop. 

We've got options of castling either kingside or queenside, depending on what White does. 

...0-0 may be better if there's pressure on f7, but if Bd1, ...0-0-0.

r3kb1r/ppp1Qppp/1nn5/8/6b1/1BN2N2/PP1P1P.text: If White is forced to initiate the queen trade, they will help Black develop.

r4rk1/ppp1bppp/5n2/3P4/6b1/2N2N2/PP1P1PP.text:
We can go for the positional threat of doubling the f-pawns and we're getting a rook into d8 soon enough to win the d5-pawn back.

Because of the bishop pair, Black has a slight edge in this position.

r4rk1/pppqbppp/2n2n2/8/2BP2b1/2N1BN2/PP3.text:
We're going to be centralizing the rooks. 

We've got ideas of ...a6 to keep pieces out of b5. 

...Bd6 will also improve our bishop's diagonal. 

We've got a middlegame that's about equal, but we've got some pressure against the IQP.

rn1q1rk1/ppp1bppp/5n2/8/2BP2b1/2N1BN2/PP.text:
White could now add a defender to d4. 

And we can add an attacker, 9...Nc6.

rnb1kb1r/ppp1qppp/8/3n4/8/2N2Q2/PP1PBPPP.text:
The most natural way for White to block runs into more threats. 

After 7...Nb4 we threaten ...Nc2+.

rnb1kb1r/ppp1qppp/8/8/1n6/2N2Q2/PP1PBPPP.text: If the king is forced to stop ...Nc2, this isn't good news for White.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1bppp/5n2/3p4/2PP4/2N2N2/PP2.text:
When White moves their light-squared bishop, this should be our cue to capture. 

It's time to take on c4 and make White have to move their bishop again.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1bppp/5n2/8/2BP4/2N2N2/PP3PP.text:
White now captures. 

White has lost some time in this operation.

And we can pin the f3-knight with 8...Bg4, provoking another bishop move to unpin! 

Most importantly, there’s pressure on d4.

rnbqk1nr/1pp2ppp/8/p3p3/1bPpP3/P2P4/1P1B.text:
If White wants to pressure the bishop…

We’ll just take on d2. 

Black’s position is solid because we’ll go for a dark-square complex, placing all our pawns on dark squares. 

The dark-squared bishop was White’s good bishop.

rnbqk1nr/1pp2ppp/8/p3p3/2PpP3/P2P4/1P1QN.text:
Once White recaptures, the queen won’t be so relevant on the dark squares, so it will most likely have to move again.

With 8...f6 we “connect four”. 

The d4-pawn that spearheads the structure is super powerful.

rnbqk1nr/1pp3pp/5p2/p3p3/2PpPP2/P2P4/1P1.text: Undermining the pawn chain with 9.f4 is not an easy task.

rnbqk1nr/ppp2ppp/8/4p3/1bPpP3/3P4/PP1BNP.text:
And once they block… 

Our idea is to defend the bishop with the a-pawn, going for complete dark-square control.

rnbqk2r/1pp3pp/5p1n/p3p3/2PpPP2/P2P4/1P1.text:
We have ideas of ...Ng4. 

The queenside knight's journey will be ...Nd7 to c5. 

The queen will also operate on the safe dark squares with ...Qd6. 

We'll castle kingside and enjoy our stronger central control and superior pawn chain.

rnbqk2r/ppp1bppp/5n2/3p4/2PP4/2N2N2/PP3P.text:
White may continue development, delaying the light-squared bishop’s development. 

But we’ll also delay the capture on c4 and just get castled.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/5n2/2p5/2Pp4/3P1N2/PP2BP.text:
After White castles, they have completed kingside development. 

However, sometimes being in a hurry to do something in chess makes you ignore other things that may be going on. 

In this case, the center.

7...Nc6 supports the central structure and helps control the critical b4-square.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/5n2/3p4/3P4/1QN5/PP3PPP/.text:
White could play 7.d4 to develop their dark-squared bishop. 

They also control some key squares with their d4-pawn.

But we can attack White’s center with a tempo as well with 7...Nc6.

After declining the gambit, Black gets natural development and a rather safe position. 

Symmetrical positions are often safe.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/1n6/8/8/1BN5/PP1P1PPP/R.text:
We force the bishop back. 

And we can develop our other knight to c6, controlling the d4-square.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/1n6/8/8/1QN2N2/PP1P1PPP.text:
White may just continue with development. 

But our development is much more active, 7...Nc6, with ideas of gaining tempi on White’s pieces.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/1B1P4/8/8/PP1P1PPP/.text:
5.Bb5+ isn’t the most popular, but it’s very logical because it may give Black some coordination issues.

But we’ll just block with the knight on d7. 

We won’t have any coordination issues because our knight will go to b6, where it will pressure the d5-pawn.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/3P4/8/2N5/PP1P1PPP/.text:
5.Nc3 is the most popular move.

But this just allows us to take on d5. 

6.Nxd5 presents no problems, so let’s just focus on other moves.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/3p4/2PP4/2N5/PP3PPP.text:
White could add an attacker, but the pawn is defended by two pieces.

If there isn’t anything more productive to do, development is the name of the game: 5...Be7 is our continuation. 

You’ll notice there is tension between the d5- and c4-pawns. 

We want to keep the tension until White moves their f1-bishop, to make them move it again to recapture on c4.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/8/3n4/2B5/2N5/PP1P1PPP/.text:
The first one we should see is 6.Bc4. 

Here, we can attack the c4-bishop by retreating the knight to b6.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/8/3n4/8/1QN5/PP1P1PPP/R.text:
6.Qb3 attacks the knight as well, however, it places the queen on a vulnerable square.

For instance, 6...Nb6 controls the c4-square, which prevents Bc4, and also blocks the queen’s view of b7, which enables ideas like ...Be6.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/8/3n4/8/2N2Q2/PP1P1PPP/.text:
6.Qf3 is another way of adding an attacker on the d5-knight, but this isn’t particularly good.

6.Qf3 is refuted by a check on e7 with the queen. 

This will disrupt White’s coordination. 

If Nge2, the bishop on f1 is blocked and White’s development isn’t promising.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/2p5/3P4/8/1Q6/PP1P1PPP/R.text:
White usually takes on d5.

We recapture, and, as a result, we have a symmetrical pawn structure. 

Both sides have an isolated queen’s pawn. 

But our d-pawn controls the c4-square, which prevents Bc4.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/4p3/2pPP3/8/8/PP1P1PPP/R.text:
White can go for this capture. 

But going for exchanges isn’t always a good thing. 

Sometimes, trades help the other side.

In this case, the trades help us. 

We recapture and have two strong pawns controlling the center.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/4p3/2ppP3/2P5/5N2/PP1P1P.text:
White can develop the kingside knight. 

Yet we can add control of the d4-square a bit more with 4...Nc6.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/8/2p5/2Pp4/3P1N2/PP2BPPP.text:
White could continue with their plan of kingside development before anything else. 

But we’re quite happy with how things have turned out in the center and can continue with 6...Nf6.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/8/2ppP3/3P4/8/PP3PPP/RNB.text:
White can try pushing and supporting e5. 

But our c-pawn already controls d4.

We can add pressure on d4 with 5...Nc6. 

We don’t need to capture on d4 right away because the structure will collapse on itself, unforced.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/8/3p4/8/1QN5/PP1P1PPP/R1.text:
White can develop with a tempo, attacking the pawn on d5. 

But we can just defend it with our knight.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3P4/2P5/8/PP1P1PPP/.text:
White could choose to take with the e-pawn. 

We will, of course, recapture.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3P4/4P3/8/PP1P1PPP/.text:
3.cxd5 is the most popular move. 

White’s idea is that they’re taking our central pawn with a flank pawn.

We’ll recapture, of course.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/2P1P3/2N5/PP1P1.text:
3.Nc3 is a bad move. 

It also neglects the d4-square. 

We can push our pawn up to d4 with tempo.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3pP3/2P5/8/PP1P1PPP.text:
White can try to gain some space with 3.e5. 

As we’ll see, this pawn lacks support.

Gaining space and controlling d4with 3...c5 is good for us here.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/8/2PpP3/8/PP1PNPPP/.text:
There are no good squares for the knight, but e2 is the lesser evil.
