Still, on e2 it blocks the f1-bishop and really just clutters the White position.

We can support the d4-pawn with 4...e5.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3P4/8/8/PP1P1PPP/RNBQ.text:
The most popular continuation that you should expect is White just trading both pawns on d5. 

At this point, you’ll want to avoid 4...Qxd5, because 5.Nc3 will come with a tempo.

Instead, you should attack the pawn with the knight, 4...Nf6 is our move.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3p4/2P5/5N2/PP1P1PPP/.text:
White may also play with 4.Nf3, going for kingside development before anything else. 

But this neglects the center, which gives us an opportunity.

We can prevent White from going d4. 

If we go 4...d4 ourselves, we control the c3-square, preventing Nc3. 

Pawn pushes like this are only possible when we’re confident we’ll be able to hold on to the pawn.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3p4/2PP4/8/PP3PPP/RNB.text:
White could try to put their pawn on d4. 

This is quite sound, White wants to control the center.

We can just be solid and defend d5 one more time with our knight, 4...Nf6.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3p4/4P3/1Q6/PP1P1PPP/.text:
And this is officially the Orthoschnapp Gambit. 

White is inviting you to take on e4. 

If you take, their idea can be Bc4 to attack f7.

Declining the gambit with 1...c6 is safe. 

We don’t want to allow White quick development with tempi.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/4p3/2PpP3/3P4/PP2NPPP.text:
5.d3 is the most popular move.

But we’ve got 5...Bb4+. White will have to block with their bishop.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/8/2Pp4/3P1N2/PP3PPP/R.text:
After White goes d3 to support their c4-pawn…

We can also defend our own pawn with 5...c5. 

It seems our pawn duo is quite solid in the center and cannot be easily attacked.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/4p3/8/2P1P3/8/PP1P1PPP.text:
Now White plays 2.e4, going for maximum control of d5. 

This is the Steiner Variation of the French. 

These moves don’t really stop ...d5, since our pawn push is sufficiently supported.

I suggest we follow through with 2...d5, the pawn break that’s most natural in our setup.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/2P5/8/PP1PPPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to Chapter 10! 

We’re going to see what happens if White plays the English, but chooses to play e4 on move 2. 

This transposes into the French, Steiner Variation. 

The idea is maximum control of d5.

It may not be the best approach, since we can play ...d5 anyway, but we have to be prepared because White can play a gambit.

White begins with 1.c4, the English.

And we respond with 1...e6.

r1q1k2r/pp1nbpp1/2p1pn1p/3p1b2/2PP1B2/1Q.text:
Since our queen is on c8, White wants to capture on d5 and open up the c-file for the rook. 

Before going to battle, we castle…

r1q1k2r/pp2bppp/n1p1pn2/3p1b2/2P4N/1QNP2.text:
Some people will go for this positional approach and hunt your bishop.

We can therefore push the pawn and attack the c3-knight. 

The knight will have to spend at least a couple of moves before becoming relevant again.

r1q1k2r/pp2bppp/n1p1pn2/5N2/2Pp4/1QNP2P1.text:
Even though White can insert this capture…

We just recapture, and our f-pawn controls the e4-square. 

White still has to move the knight away.

r1q1k2r/pp2bppp/n1p2n2/3p1b2/8/1QNP1NP1/.text: This is a direct transposition to 6. c4 and 7. cxd5.

But our king will get castled soon enough.

White may go for Re1 to play e4. 

A good plan for Black is to play ...Rd8, since after e4, we can play ...dxe4 and open up the d-file for our rook.

r1q1k2r/pp2bppp/n1p2n2/5p2/N1Pp4/1Q1P2P1.text: If the knight goes to the rim...

r1q1k2r/ppn1bppp/2p2n2/5p2/N1Pp4/1Q1P2P1.text:
Rest assured, it won't be a good piece on a4. 

We've got ...Ne6 to support the d4-pawn and control the c5-square even more. 

...0-0 is also coming and our pieces have more natural squares. 

The g2-bishop is blunted by our c6-b7 pawn chain.

r1q1kb1r/pp1n1pp1/2p1pn1p/3p1b2/2PP1B2/1.text:
White takes control of the h2–c7 diagonal. 

The bishop on f4 now covers some important dark squares in our position.

Since developing to d6 is impossible now, we develop the bishop to e7, ready to castle.

r1q1kb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/3p1b2/2PP4/1QN2.text:
Now White strikes in the center! 

However, that loosens up the e4- and c4-squares, which we can use to our advantage soon.

We play 8...h6 to control the g5-square.

r1q2rk1/pp1nbpp1/2p1pn1p/3P1b2/3P1B2/1QN.text:
...and White puts their plan in motion with cxd5.

However, let’s not allow them to open the c-file! We capture with the e-pawn instead, keeping it closed and maintaining a grip on the e4-square. 

Also, we might have ideas of placing our knight on the c4-square, which we also control.

r1q2rk1/pp1nbpp1/2p2n1p/3pNb2/3P1B2/1QN3.text:
Having their own control of the e5-square, White jumps there with the knight, grabbing even more space.

Instead of trading on White’s terms, we rotate our knight to the queenside, 12...Nb6 is our move.

r1q2rk1/pp2bpp1/1np1bn1p/P2pN3/3P1B2/1QN.text: The a-pawn still attacks our knight and grabs more space on the queenside...

r1q2rk1/pp2bpp1/1np2n1p/3pNb2/P2P1B2/1QN.text:
13.a4 expands on the queenside and tries to kick our knight out.

Before White achieves that, we support the c4-square one more time with 13...Be6. 

Our knight will be ready to jump there!

r1q2rk1/pp2bpp1/2p1bn1p/P2pN3/2nP1B2/1QN.text:
...But we go 14...Nc4, maintaining a solid position and attacking the a5-pawn.

The position is balanced, but could become quite sharp, with possibility of a knight trade happening at any moment!

r1q2rk1/pp2bppp/n1p2n2/3p1b2/8/1QNP1NP1/.text:
A useful resource by us is 10...Na6.

We develop the knight to the edge of the board with the simple plan of placing it on c5.

From there it will target White's queen and add protection to the critical e4 square.

Next, we might have plans of ...Re1, ...Rb1 (to defend our b-pawn) and going for the mentioned ...Bh3 trade!

r2q1rk1/pp1nbppb/2n1p2p/3pP3/2pP4/1NP2NP.text:
We can force the knight back. 

White's attempt to defend their center have allowed us to gain space on the queenside. 

We'll now attack with ...b5 and ...b4, supported by ...a5 if needed. 

White doesn't have counterplay on the kingside because our h7-bishop is a strong defender.

rn1q1rk1/pp1nbppb/4p2p/2ppP3/3P4/2P2NP1/.text:
White can “connect four”  to defend. 

11 ...Nc6 adds another attacker on d4.

rn1q1rk1/pp2bppb/5n1p/2pp4/8/1N1P1NP1/PP.text:
But we can use our c-pawn to control the d4-square, and get ready to bring our knight out from b to d7. 

...Re8 is also an idea to contest the e-file. 

Black has good development and space.

rn1q1rk1/ppp1bpp1/4pn1p/3p1b2/4P3/3P1NP1.text:
After 8.e4, we don’t take the pawn. 

Rather, we use that h7-square we prepared for our bishop.

rn1q1rk1/ppp1bppb/4pn1p/3P4/8/3P1NP1/PPP.text:
If White trades…

Recapturing with the pawn keeps a strong pawn in the center. 

You’ll notice White still has to develop the dark-squared bishop.

rn1q1rk1/ppp1bppb/4pn1p/3pP3/8/3P1NP1/PP.text:
Many players get excited and think that 9.e5, gaining space and kicking the knight out of f6, is a good move.

But e5 is usually only good when White has attacking chances on the kingside. 

Here, it’s actually Black who is attacking!

We escape danger with 9...Nfd7.

rn1q1rk1/pppnbppb/4p2p/3pP3/3P4/5NP1/PPP.text:
The center is overextended. 

The pawns have advanced too much and White will not be able to hold it together.

After 10...c5 and with ...Nc6 coming, the center will be attacked and undermined.

rn1qk2r/pp2bpp1/2p1pn1p/3P1b2/8/3P1NP1/P.text:
If White takes… 

We still recapture with the e-pawn to keep the c-file closed.

rn1qk2r/pp2bpp1/2p2n1p/3p1b2/8/1Q1P1NP1/.text:
But there’s a slight nuance that works in our favor. 

Since the knight is on d2, we can play 8...Qb6.

This move is possible because Be3 cannot be played. 

We can defend b7 and propose a queen trade.

rn1qk2r/pp2bppp/2p1pn2/3P1b2/8/3P1NP1/PP.text:
White can always insert the trade on d5.

And we should recapture with the e-pawn to keep the c-file closed. The reason for this is that after a move like Qb3, we will defend our b7-pawn by placing our queen on the c-file, and we don’t want a rook coming to c1 to drive us away.

rn1qk2r/pp2bppp/2p1pn2/3p1b2/2P5/1Q1P1NP.text:
It’s also quite possible that White doesn’t insert the trade on d5. 

Instead, they could just go after the b7-pawn.

Our antidote is the same: we defend with 7...Qc8 because we want to avoid getting attacked by the dark-squared bishop.

rn1qk2r/pp2bppp/2p2n2/3p1b2/8/1Q1P1NP1/P.text:
So if 8.Qb3… 

We just defend b7 with 8...Qc8.

rn1qk2r/ppp1bpp1/4pn1p/3p1b2/2P5/3P1NP1/.text:
Some people decide on the c4-pawn break only after Nbd2. 

This is a logical move, in a way, because the d2-knight supports the c4 expansion.

We reinforce d5 with our c-pawn.

rn1qk2r/ppp1bpp1/4pn1p/3p1b2/8/3P1NP1/PP.text:
This is a natural move designed to support the e4-pawn break.

Realistically, we cannot stop e4 from being played. 

So kingside castling and simple development is the best strategy.

rn1qk2r/ppp1bppp/4pn2/3p1b2/2P5/3P1NP1/P.text:
White could undermine our d5-pawn with the move c4. 

With 6...c6, we create the strong “diamond” pawn structure.

rn1qk2r/ppp1bppp/4pn2/3p1b2/8/3P1NP1/PPP.text:
6.Nbd2 is the most common idea after 5.d3. 

The point is to support the e4- and c4-pawn breaks.

Here I recommend that, before castling, we create a safe square for our bishop with 6...h6. 

The light-squared bishop is our “London bishop”, and we should take care of it as much as we can.

rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3p1b2/2P5/1Q3NP1/.text: White activates their own queen first, with pressure in the center, as well as on the undefended b7-pawn.

rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3p1b2/2P5/5NP1/PP.text:
4...c6 is an inferior way of handling the pressure on d5, and that's why you shouldn't play it. 

This is because it gives White some chances for an advantage.

rn1qkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p1b2/2P5/5NP1/PP1.text:
White creates tension in the center!

We have to defend the d5-pawn.

4...e6 is the right move, natural and solid, supporting d5. 

We also open up the diagonal for our dark-squared bishop.

rn1qkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p1b2/8/5NP1/PPPPP.text:
White has chosen the calmer route and castles without creating tension in the center. 

This simply poses no problems for us; we will open up the diagonal for our dark-squared bishop, develop the other knight, sometimes be even more solid with ...c6, and castle!

Just like 3.e3 or 4.e3 is played after Bf4 in the London, here we play 4...e6, connecting the pawns after taking the bishop out.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p1b2/2P5/1Q3NP1/P.text:
5.Qb3 by White activates the queen and puts pressure on the weak points in our position.

5...Qc8 is an important move to remember! 

Although we relinquish some control of the d5-square, 5...Qc8 is the best defensive move against the pressure on b7.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p1b2/8/3P1NP1/PPP.text:
5.d3 is the most popular move and the one worth preparing against.

In the London, the bishop usually goes to d3 and aims at h7. 

But when there’s a pawn on g6, the bishop goes to e2. 

In the Reverse London, we would love for our dark-squared bishop to have a long diagonal as well. 

But White has a pawn on g3, so there’s no use playing ...Bd6, we instead play 5...Be7.

rn2k2r/1p2bpp1/1pp2n1p/3p1b2/8/3P1NP1/PP.text:
Our rook becomes active on the semi-open a-file. 

We'll continue with ...c5, to control the d4- and b4-squares, and with ...Nc6 to develop. 

We'll also castle and play ...Rfd8. 

Our pieces have better activity.

rn2k2r/pp2bpp1/1Qp2n1p/3p1b2/8/3P1NP1/PP.text: And if White trades, as they often do...

rn2kb1r/pp2pppp/1qp2n2/3p1b2/2P5/1Q1P1NP.text: Instead, White wants to kick out our queen from b6 with 7.Be3!

rn2kb1r/pp2pppp/1qp2n2/3p1b2/2P5/1Q3NP1/.text:
We defend with our queen.

We wouldn't mind a queen trade on the b6-square, as it would bring our rook on a8 to life.

rn2kb1r/pp3ppp/1qp1pn2/3p1b2/2P5/1Q1P1NP.text: We continue naturally, though, maintaining a solid position.

rn2kb1r/pp3ppp/1qp1pn2/3p1b2/2P5/1Q1PBNP.text:
White develops their dark-squared bishop with tempo, leaving us with no better choice but to trade on b3 now, as anything else would be passive.

It seems that White has achieved everything they wanted out of the opening. Therefore 4...c6 is not the right approach!

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p4/8/5NP1/PPPPPPB.text:
White has developed rapidly and is already prepared to castle.

However, having placed no pawns in the center of the board, White allows us to develop our bishop before playing ...e6! 

The bishop will be very active on the f5-square, instead of being blocked in by our own pawns.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/8/5NP1/PPPPPP1P/.text:
White continues with 2.g3, delaying the moves d4 and c4, but developing the kingside quickly. 

We’ll develop naturally, 2...Nf6.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/5N2/PPPPPPPP/RNB.text:
Greetings! 

Welcome to the very last chapter of our QGD course for Black, Chapter 11! 

In this chapter, we will cover the lines after 1.Nf3, the Réti Opening by White. 

The first study deals with White developing their kingside before grabbing space in the center, which allows us to play 3...Bf5, the so-called Reverse London.

Instead of placing a pawn in the center, White opts for 1.Nf3, the third most popular opening move in chess. 

White doesn’t want to commit to any specific opening yet and can transpose to many different playing styles on move 2.

We respond naturally with 1...d5, putting a pawn in the center.

rnq1k2r/pp2bppp/2p1pn2/3p1b2/2P5/1QNP1NP.text:
White will usually develop. 

And many times we have this move, 8...Na6, to attack the queen.

rnq1k2r/pp2bppp/2p2n2/3p1b2/8/1QNP1NP1/P.text:
White castles, with ideas of activating the rook on the central e-file. 

We get our king to safety too.

rnq1kb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/3p1b2/2P5/1QN2NP1.text:
A normal developing move, pressuring the center. 

We develop ourselves, 7...Nbd7.

rnq1kb1r/pp3ppp/2p2n2/3p1b2/8/1QNP1NP1/P.text:
8.d3 by White brings the bishop on c1 to life. 

In the future, White might try to go for the e4 break.

For now, we simply develop, 8...Be7.

rnq1kb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3P1b2/8/1Q3NP1/PP1.text:
White tries to use the “absence” of our queen from d8 to take on the center!

We take back. 

Now our queen and bishop form a battery on the h3–c8 diagonal, with possible ideas of ...Bh3 in the future, trading for White’s useful light-squared bishop and possibly starting an attack.

rnq1kb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p1b2/2P5/1Q3NP1/P.text:
Another line worth exploring is 
6.O-O by White. 

Instead of capturing right away, they bring the king to safety first.

We reinforce the center with 6...c6.

rnq1kb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/3p1b2/8/1QN2NP1/PP1.text:
The knight on c3 puts even more pressure on the d5-square! 

7...c6 is forced now, strengthening the center with a pawn. 

Now we’ve defended everything in the position and are ready to develop and castle!

rnq2rk1/pp2bppp/2p2n2/3p1b2/8/1QNP1NP1/P.text: Once White has activated the rook and prepares e4....

1rbqkb1r/2p1pppp/p1n2n2/1p6/8/NP3NP1/3PP.text:
We simply move out of the way, neutralizing both threats.

Next, we'll activate our bishop to b7, play ...e6 and ...Be7 or ...Bd6 and castle.

Equal position!

2kr1b1r/1ppq1ppp/p1n1bn2/4p3/8/2N2NP1/PP.text:
...And we castle.

This different approach by us and quick queenside castling allows us to launch an attack on the kingside with moves like ...h5!

Also, our queen and bishop make a battery that can be used for an h3 trade, as we've seen in the previous study.

B1b1kb1r/4pppp/pqp2n2/1p2n3/2p2P2/N5P1/P.text: The king gets out of check...

B1b1kb1r/4pppp/pqp2nn1/1p6/2p2P2/N5P1/PP.text:
...And we simply bring the knight back to the kingside.

Next, we will play ...Bd7 to defend the c6-pawn before attacking the imprisoned bishop with ...Qa7 and finally capturing it. 

We are winning.

Bye, bye, bishop!

B1bqkb1r/2p1pppp/p4n2/1p2n3/2p5/N5P1/PP1.text:
With no better option now, White accepts the sacrifice.

But 8...c6 completely cuts off the bishop’s mobility! 

Now all that’s left is to take it.

B1bqkb1r/4pppp/p1p2n2/1p2n3/2p2P2/N5P1/P.text:
White lashes out with 9.f4, trying to deflect the knight from defending the c6-pawn. 

But that simply doesn’t work.

The queen delivers check and defends c6 at the same time. 

Now our knight is free to move!

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/4N3/Q1p5/6P1/PP1P.text:
But a simple 7...c6 crushes all of White's hopes.

Our queen from h1 protects the c6 square, so White can't even try to sacrifice the knight with Nxc6.

We are crushing here! 

White is lost.

r1b1kb1r/ppp1pppp/2N2n2/3q4/Q1p5/6P1/PP1.text:
White takes on c6, but that doesn’t save them. 

We simply capture the rook on h1, unafraid of possible discovered attacks on c6 by White.

r1b1kb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/4N3/Q1p5/6P1/PP1PP.text: With no better option, the White knight retreats to e5, with a discovered check from the queen.

r1bqkb1r/1pp1pppp/p1n2n2/8/2p5/5NP1/PPQP.text:
White develops the queen and puts pressure on our pawn on c4.

We can let them take it! 6...e5 grabs crucial space in the center and prepares to develop our pieces with tempo once White takes the pawn on c4.

r1bqkb1r/1pp1pppp/p1n2n2/8/2p5/N4NP1/PP1.text:
Another path to our c4-pawn might be the common 6.Na3 move by White.

That allows the ...b5 push. 

Although we will open the diagonal for White’s bishop on g2, they have to be very careful, as you will see.

r1bqkb1r/1pp1pppp/p1n2n2/8/Q1p5/5NP1/PP1.text: You might wonder why White doesn't activate the queen on a4, instead of attacking the pawn from c2.

r1bqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p1n2n2/4p3/2Q5/5NP1/PP1.text:
Naturally, the queen captures.

And our light-squared bishop comes out to e6 with an attack on the queen! 

Notice how in the previous chapters we usually played ...b5 and developed our bishop to b7. 

Since White has chosen this move order, we instead grab central space and activate the bishop on e6!

r1bqkb1r/2p1pppp/p1n2n2/1p2N3/2p5/N5P1/P.text:
White thinks they’ve tricked us with 7.Ne5, attacking our pinned knight on c6 twice - but this is a big mistake!

We capture the free knight and sacrifice our rook! 

Our idea is that once the bishop captures on a8, we can trap it!

r1bqkb1r/2p1pppp/p1n2n2/1p6/2p5/NP3NP1/P.text:
7.b3 undermines our queenside pawn structure. 

We capture, as we don’t want to allow bxc4.

r1bqkb1r/2p1pppp/p1n2n2/1p6/8/NP3NP1/3PP.text:
White recaptures with the pawn, opening the a-file for the rook with some nasty intentions.

Now Nxb5 is possible, since our a6-pawn is pinned to our rook on a8!

Also, White might have various Ne5 ideas.

r1bqkb1r/2p1pppp/p1n2n2/1p6/Q1p5/5NP1/PP.text:
Because that gives us exactly what we want!

6...b5 protects our c4-pawn and attacks the queen at the same time.

Now we will easily develop to b7 and enjoy an already slightly-better position.

Definitely an inaccuracy by White!

r1bqkb1r/ppp1pppp/2n2n2/4N3/Q1p5/6P1/PP1.text:
Instead of taking the pawn, White might try to exploit the pin on c6 with 5.Ne5. 

But this is a horrible blunder by White.

5...Qd5 is the key move to remember! 

We fork the knight on e5 and the rook on h1, while also adding protection to our knight on c6.

r1bqkb1r/ppp1pppp/2n2n2/8/2Q5/5NP1/PP1PP.text:
White takes the pawn…

And we continue with our plan of controlling the center, 5...e5.

r1bqkb1r/ppp1pppp/2n2n2/8/Q1p5/5NP1/PP1P.text:
Another possibility for White on move 5 is to continue developing with Bg2. 

Since our knight on c6 is pinned, we can’t play ...e5 yet.

That’s why we first develop the light-squared bishop to d7, unpinning.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/4p3/2Q5/5NP1/PP1P.text:
A normal developing move by White, fianchettoing their light-squared bishop. 

Again, as in the main line, we develop the light-squared bishop to e6 instead of b7, with tempo!

r2q1rk1/pp1bbppp/2p2n2/6B1/3Q4/6P1/PP2PP.text:
12.Bg5 is a dangerous move! 

White targets some weak points in our position.

The threat is Bxf6 followed by Qxd7.

We need to be accurate!

r2q1rk1/pp2bppp/2p1bn2/6B1/3Q4/6P1/PP2PP.text:
The light-squared bishop is out of the way and the dark-squared bishop is ready to capture on f6 if needed!

Also, our queen is soundly defended on d8.

We've evaded all problems and have equalized, with plans of kicking out the bishop from g5, centralizing rooks after trading queens, and in the longer run placing our bishop on d5, trying to trade for White's bishop on g2. 

If White doesn't trade queens, Qb6, aiming at b2, is strong.

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/2nbbn2/4p3/Q7/5NP1/PP1PP.text:
...And so do we.

We are developed and have achieved everything we wanted out of the opening!

The position is still equal, however, with a lot of chess to be played.

r2q1rk1/pppbbppp/2n2n2/4p3/2Q5/2N2NP1/PP.text:
And we simply castle and have reached a pleasant position.

Next, we will try to move our bishop to e6 with a tempo on the queen, and then try to go for ...a6, preventing anything from coming to b5.

In some positions in the longer run, we might try to follow up with ...Rb8 and ...b5.

r2qk2r/pp1bbppp/2p2n2/8/3Q4/6P1/PP2PPBP/.text:
The rook is activated and controls the d-file together with the queen on d4.

However, there are no concrete threats yet, so we just castle.

r2qk2r/pppbbppp/2n2n2/4p3/2QP4/5NP1/PP2P.text:
A sharper variation for White might be the quick d4, counter-attacking in the center and trying to open up the board before we get to castle. 

We have to react now!

As we don’t want White to capture, we do.

r2qk2r/pppbbppp/2n2n2/8/2QN4/6P1/PP2PPBP.text:
The knight recaptures, opening up some pressure towards our c6-knight. 

That’s why we trade once again…

r2qk2r/pppbbppp/5n2/8/3Q4/6P1/PP2PPBP/RN.text:
And White recaptures, centralizing the queen. 

Now our b7-pawn is hanging.

So let’s defend it by pushing our c-pawn! 

But we’ve left ourselves vulnerable to some pressure on the d-file by White.

r2qkb1r/1pp2ppp/p1n1bn2/4p3/8/5NP1/PPQPP.text:
The queen moves out of the way. 

White has already moved the queen three times in the opening!

We use White’s slow development to activate our own queen, 8...Qd7.

Since we’ve rapidly developed our queenside pieces, we will make use of that and castle queenside.

r2qkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n1bn2/4p3/Q7/5NP1/PP1PP.text:
The queen moves back to a4, pinning our knight and creating the threat of Nxe5. 

That’s why 7...Bd6 develops and protects the e5-pawn.

r2qkb1r/pppb1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/2Q5/5NP1/PP1P.text:
White brings the king to safety. 

And we simply develop, 7...Be7, getting ready to castle our king as well.

r2qkb1r/pppbpppp/2n2n2/8/2Q5/5NP1/PP1PPP.text:
Now White takes on c4, also getting the queen out of the way of our bishop… 

But that gives us time for our central 6...e5 push!

r3kb1r/1ppq1ppp/p1n1bn2/4p3/8/2N2NP1/PPQ.text: White develops the knight to c3...

rnbqkb1r/1pp1pppp/p4n2/8/2p5/5NP1/PP1PPP.text:
Once White has finished kingside development and castled…

First we bring the knight out to c6, developing and supporting the ...e5 push.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p4/2P5/5NP1/PP1PP.text:
Instead of occupying the center directly with pawns, White puts pressure on it with a flank pawn!

However, we still continue with our usual 3...dxc4 plan. 

We want to play ...a6 and prepare the possible ...b5 in the future. 

As in the previous chapters, the c4-pawn restricts the vital d- and b-pawns from moving forward.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/8/2p5/5NP1/PP1PPPB.text:
The main line is 4.Bg2, with White naturally continuing development.

We also continue with our idea, 4...a6. 

However, with this move order, in the main line playing ...b5 might be too dangerous. 

With White lacking control of the center, we might instead resort to something like ...e5 to grab more central squares and coordinate our pieces more easily.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/8/Q1p5/5NP1/PP1PPP.text:
Instead of developing with 4.Bg2, White might choose to go after our pawn immediately with 4.Qa4+, before we get time to play ...a6.

We simply block with 4...Nc6. 

As you will see in the main line as well, we want to play ...e5 and grab space in the center. 

Our knight supports that square.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/8/5NP1/PPPPPP1P/.text:
2.g3 prepares the kingside fianchetto for White. 

We develop the knight to its natural f6 square.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/5N2/PPPPPPPP/RNB.text:
In the second study of Chapter 11, we will again take a look at the Réti, but this time with White choosing to play c4 on move 3! 

This is a unique move order we haven’t seen yet.

White opens with the Réti, developing the knight to f3. 

We respond by controlling the center with a pawn.
